name: The syntax for the new language additions
explain:
The spelling of every ruled language addition. docs/plan-syntax-additions.md.

  • New words: public, deployment, prev, settings, external, apikey; $tenant.
  • Found: a guard cannot see the caller's tenant today.
  • Ask 4 meets public-path-design ask 8 (a row condition on public).

asks.text: Use ordo evolve for schema changes (render and store the plan), with apply offering at the end to remove prev lines that have landed?
asks.suggest: Yes, one source tree. Old versions are already kept as stored artifacts, so files per version add nothing. evolve also frees ordo plan, which today prints the compiler's artifact.

asks.text: Should public be a reserved word, so no field or entity may be named public?
asks.suggest: Yes. It heads an entity line and an op flag, and a word that is contextual in 3 positions is the kind of rule an agent gets wrong; isPublic serves the field.

asks.text: Should an entity whose rows live only in the deployment's space say so with a deployment line, required before any public mark?
asks.suggest: Yes. The compiler then knows which reads cross the tenant boundary and refuses a tenant-and-deployment join, which two databases cannot serve.

asks.text: ACLs are opt-in. With none, the tenant boundary and the door's op grants decide who reads. Keep public off guarded or acl entities?
asks.suggest: Yes. Public then never overrides a guard; it only goes where nothing guards. To mix public and private rows, use a row condition on public (public-path-design ask 8).

asks.text: May a guard test the caller's own row and tenant ($caller.role, $tenant.plan), compiled to one constant per call?
asks.suggest: Yes. It is the only way to write "every pro tenant reads this" without a link row per tenant per row, and it costs no join.

asks.text: Should one settings { } block replace the unparsed policy blocks as the single spelling for settings?
asks.suggest: Yes. One form carries every layered value and its exposure; policy never parsed, so nothing built changes.

asks.text: Should setting names come only from Ordo's closed catalogue this round, with app-defined settings deferred?
asks.suggest: Yes, for now. An app value readable in op bodies is a different feature with its own determinism rules, and 18ac is about Ordo's settings.

asks.text: Should API keys be issued at runtime against an apikey profile the program declares, naming the ops a key may ever reach and the quota default?
asks.suggest: Yes. The program sets the ceiling and the quota, a tenant issues keys inside it, and no grant ever lives in a file.

asks.text: Should a tenant owner or manager be able to issue API keys for the tenant's own customers by default, through std.space.issueKey?
asks.suggest: Yes. The app's customer is usually a tenant, and the profile already bounds what a key reaches; the deployment owner keeps std.deployment.issueKey.

asks.text: Should a public write op be limited to create mode, with no addressing, converge or delete?
asks.suggest: Yes. An anonymous converge-or-create could overwrite a row by a guessed key; a form only ever makes a new row.

asks.text: Should dropping an orphaned field or entity be a plan choice (ordo plan --drop) and never a line in the source?
asks.suggest: Yes. A drop is an act on one deployment's data with an actor and a confirmation, and can differ between dev and production.

asks.text: Is <- the right mark for a column mapping in an external entity, as the mirror of ->?
asks.suggest: Yes. It says the data comes in, and a stray <- in an expression fails to parse instead of silently meaning less-than-minus.

asks.text: Should per-op settings such as page size wait for 18ac's build, spelled then as op x settings(door.pageSize = 100) =?
asks.suggest: Later. The block covers the app layer now, and the per-op form is best decided with the resolver that reads it.

asks.text: Should external entities be read at the same three levels as the deployment's space (public, signed in, narrowed by a guard)?
asks.suggest: Yes. They have no $space column, so they are the deployment's by construction, and the plan's "which tenants may see it" is then a guard.

asks.text: Should the reserved-word list in definition-language.md §2 be generated from the Keyword enum, ending today's disagreement between them?
asks.suggest: Yes. The document claims it is regenerated and nothing does it; the enum is what the lexer reads, so it is the source.

where: Design: docs/plan-syntax-additions.md. Ruled: all 15 asks. Building now: the public keyword (with public-data, go 2026-10-10). The rest: checklist 27ah (no go); 27ag the reserved-word list; per-op settings owed in 18ac; ordo evolve in 27a.

name: How the public path and API keys work at runtime
sub: Ruled 2026-10-03, all 12 asks
explain:
The runtime design under the ruled public-data model. docs/design-public-path.md.

  • A tokenless call to a public op runs as $anonymous; anything else is refused as today.
  • Public reads are cached and dropped by the existing commit notify.
  • Read layer: same binary in a mode. 11 build steps.

asks.text: Should a public read accept $refine in v1, or only its declared parameters?
asks.suggest: Declared parameters only. Every distinct refinement is a distinct cache key, so an open $refine lets one crawler turn every request into a database read.

asks.text: What should the shipped default for s-maxage on public responses be?
asks.suggest: 60 seconds. A CDN with no purge hook is stale for at most this long after an erasure, and a hooked CDN drops the entry at once anyway.

asks.text: The server must check each widget token with the provider, or a bot just skips the widget. Support Turnstile, reCAPTCHA and hCaptcha, off until a key is set?
asks.suggest: Yes. The widget runs in the browser, but only the server's check with the provider's secret key stops a bot. Each provider is one HTTP call, set per deployment or tenant.

asks.text: What should the shipped default per-address limit on public writes be?
asks.suggest: 10 a minute. A person fills a form a few times at most, and 10 a minute per address costs a tenant little while the developer tunes it.

asks.text: Should the read layer be the same binary in a mode (ordo serve --public-read) rather than a separate service?
asks.suggest: Same binary, in a mode. It needs the artifact, the bus and the cache that already exist; a second service would carry a second copy of the registry loader.

asks.text: Which API key kind ships first: personal keys that act as their issuer, or service keys with a seat of their own?
asks.suggest: Personal keys first. A customer automates what they can already do, every existing guard applies, and no new seat machinery is built.

asks.text: Is an API key sent as the bearer on every call, or exchanged once for a short-lived token?
asks.suggest: Sent directly, resolved in memory. API customers expect that, and it costs the door one hash and one lookup, with no database read.

asks.text: May public on an entity carry a row condition, so drafts stay private without a condition in every public op?
asks.suggest: Yes. One condition on the declaration is checked once instead of remembered in every op. Decide with syntax-additions ask 4, which keeps public off guarded entities.

asks.text: On a public live stream, should Ordo push the fresh result, or send invalidate and let each visitor refetch as today?
asks.suggest: Push the result. A public result is the same for every visitor, so one frame saves every visitor a refetch. The private path keeps today's signal.

asks.text: Should the command log record a public write as $anonymous plus the site label, keeping the caller's address out of the chain?
asks.suggest: Yes, address out. The chain is kept forever and exported with the space; an address there is a behaviour log nobody asked for. The rate limiter holds it for a minute.

asks.text: Should a deploy drop the whole public cache, including entries for ops the deploy did not change?
asks.suggest: Yes, drop everything. A deploy may move rows, the version is in the key anyway, and one rule is easier to trust than a per-op diff.

asks.text: Are per-address rate windows counted per node in v1, accepting that 3 nodes admit up to 3 times the limit?
asks.suggest: Per node in v1. The window bounds cost, and no tenant relies on the exact number. A shared count is one later step.

where: docs/design-public-path.md. Steps 1, 3, 4 built 2026-10-10 (5c6f2fa4). Next: 5 to 10; step 7 uses no client address (ruling 2026-10-06).

name: The language reference and the compiler disagree in 18 places
sub: Ruled 2026-10-03: compiler owes settled syntax; lean marked unbuilt; how-tos fixed now
explain:
Found writing examples/syntax/; the list is that README's Findings.

  • Settled syntax that does not compile, such as text(64) and bare duration.
  • Rules not enforced, such as unbounded and reproducible.
  • Lean syntax not built: enum, each, routines, triggers.
  • 3 how-tos contradicted the reference; 2 are fixed.

Money today (ask 3): a whole number of the currency's smallest unit, so it cannot hold $0.0004 or an exchange rate. decimal is exact but exists only inside calculations. Storing a division in money needs an explicit round. The proposal makes money an exact decimal with no fixed scale, a field may declare places (money(2)), and rounding happens only where the app writes it. It changes the compiler, the planner and the wire's bounds.

asks.text: For settled syntax that does not compile, fix the compiler, and for lean syntax that is unbuilt, mark the reference as not built yet?
asks.suggest: Yes. Settled means the compiler owes it; lean was never promised, so the reference should say plainly that it does not compile today.

asks.text: Should the 3 how-tos be corrected to match the reference now (money in major units, no filter on an unindexed sealed field, passkeys served)?
asks.suggest: Yes, now. They are documents a reader trusts today, and each fix is a few lines with no code.

asks.text: Should money store exact decimals with no fixed precision, written as 29.99, rounded only where the app asks?
asks.suggest: Yes. No financial precision is lost, sub-cent rates fit, and source reads like the wire's "29.99". A field may declare places, such as money(2), when the app wants a fixed scale.

asks.text: A refinement narrows an op's result at call time, such as .where(total > 100).pick(name), sent as data, never as query text. How does an op allow one?
asks.suggest: op x refinable = ..., allowing filter and pick on its outputs only. It can only narrow what the op already returns; off stays the default because each refinement is a new query shape.

asks.text: filled marks a call parameter the client fills itself, like $today: date filled, since ops may not read the clock. Allow it only on date and datetime?
asks.suggest: Yes, date and datetime only. Those are the values a client can produce alone; on any other type there is nothing to fill, so a clear error beats a silent no-op.

asks.text: Parameters choose what an op answers; refinement only filters its returned rows and fields. With no way to widen, and costly ones refused, drop the off switch?
asks.suggest: Yes, no off switch. Refinement can only narrow the op's own outputs, guards still apply, and the cost gate refuses an expensive one, so there is no case that needs it off.

where: Built 2026-10-04: commits 96157e5, 5326bba, ae6094f, 1533961 (see checklist 27aj, 27ag). Findings: examples/syntax/README.md. Owed: bare duration, a check that walks a ref, blob .mime/.size. Open: asks 4 and 5.

name: An upload during a bucket detach or replace can be stranded
sub: Each stored file records its bucket
explain:
Found by the Fable audit of the bucket detach.

  • An upload finishing during a detach lands in the old bucket.
  • Other servers keep sending uploads there for up to 30 seconds.
  • That file is then unreadable, and the storage sweep cannot reach it.
  • Replace has the same window.

asks.text: Should an upload re-check the tenant's bucket just before it commits, and refuse with a retryable error if the bucket changed?
asks.suggest: Yes. It closes both the check-then-delete gap and the 30 second cache window, and the caller simply retries into the right bucket.

asks.text: No check per upload, then. Instead, each stored file records which bucket it went to, so reads and the sweep follow it after a detach?
asks.suggest: Yes. Nothing is checked or refused at upload; a file written during a detach stays readable and collectable where it landed.

where: commit 0a36ef7: $blobref and $blobtomb "store" (crates/ordo-crypto/src/blobref.rs), StoreResolver::named (crates/ordo-blob/src/lib.rs). Tests crates/ordo-host/tests/blob_door.rs: an_upload_that_lands_during_a_detach_stays_readable, the_sweep_collects_an_upload_from_the_bucket_it_landed_in, an_interrupted_upload_during_a_detach_is_collected_from_the_bucket_it_landed_in, a_replace_moves_new_uploads_and_the_file_written_during_it_stays_where_it_landed.

name: The audit of 27ao, 25ab and 27ap: two decisions
explain:
A Fable audit of sealed reads, key-release recording and the one-way gap fixes found no security hole. It fixed one defect and added one missing test.

  • Fixed: a key or signature sent with no destination ended the attestation witness; now refused.
  • Added: a moved sealed value refuses to open.

asks.text: Setting an attestation destination needs the owner key's signature; removing it needs role and a fresh sign-in. Require the signature to remove too?
asks.suggest: No. The signature binds the destination address, and a removal has none; role plus a fresh sign-in is the authority that chose it.

asks.text: Now that sealed reads are served, should sealed_unsupported answer 422 instead of 501 (not implemented)?
asks.suggest: Yes, 422. What is left are op shapes the app developer fixes, such as a missing take, not a feature that is unbuilt.

asks.text: Attestation sends a tenant's signed history checkpoints to an outside address the owner picks, as proof. Need a signature to stop it?
asks.suggest: No. The signature proves the owner chose that address; stopping has no address to prove. A fresh sign-in by the owner is the right check.

where: 422: commit f73052a, crates/ordo-api/src/error.rs, test sealed_unsupported_answers_422_as_an_op_the_app_developer_fixes; ordo-react refusal.ts. Attestation stop: no change, docs/corpus-rulings.md 2026-10-05.

name: Changing a money or decimal field's places is invisible to migrations
sub: Refused unless stated; --places rescale|keep
explain:
money(0) to money(2) passes migrations unseen, and every stored amount then reads 100 times smaller.

  • Every money(p) is the same database type.
  • The type compare ignores what is in brackets.
  • Found by the one-way gap review, confirmed in code.

asks.text: money(2) stores $29.99 as 2999; money(0) reads 2999 as 2999. Changing places rereads every stored amount 100x off, unseen. Refuse the change?
asks.suggest: Refuse it, unless the change says whether to rescale the stored amounts. A developer fixing bare money to money(2) means the amounts were dollars all along; only they know which.

where: commits 5c8200b, a685c73: diff B11 and the load gate (crates/ordo-schema/src/diff.rs), --places and the rescale (crates/ordo-host/src/schema_apply.rs), $places table. Tests crates/ordo-host/tests/money_places.rs (8), crates/ordo-cli/tests/plan_places.rs (2). A revert past a rescale: revert-past-rescale (25ad).

name: A revert past a places rescale writes old-scale amounts
explain:
Since 25aa, a stated rescale rewrites stored amounts. The history keeps the old ones.

  • A revert re-applies a before-image from the history
  • One taken before the rescale holds 2999 meaning $2,999, now read as $29.99
  • Nothing checks for this today (crates/ordo-exec/src/undo.rs)

Found 2026-10-05 by the 25aa agent, confirmed by the lead: undo.rs has no check for a schema change between the group and now. Changing an int field to money has the same question of what the stored number means, and is noted here. Rows written between the plan and the apply are checked for lost digits at apply time, which covers them.

asks.text: When a revert reaches back past a rescale of a field it touches, should Ordo convert the old amount to the new places as it applies it?
asks.suggest: Yes, convert, and refuse only if it would lose digits. The rescale is recorded with its factor, so the revert can apply it; refusing would make every pre-rescale change unrevertable.

where: commit c3dbba2a: $places records from_places, money and each space's chain head; crates/ordo-exec/src/undo.rs converts by the net rescale; RevertPolicy rounding default Refuse, half-even when allowed. Tests crates/ordo-host/tests/revert_past_rescale.rs (4). Filed: export carries no $places, so add places.jsonl to the bundle (docs/audit-2026-10-06.md finding 4); no program spelling for the rounding setting.

name: A person can leave: decline, leave a tenant, delete an account
sub: Decline built; leave and account delete built (27aq)
explain:
The one-way gap review found three ways a person cannot get out.

  • An invitation or a share cannot be declined; it sits live until it expires.
  • A member cannot leave a tenant; only an owner can remove them.
  • A person who signed up alone can never delete their account.

asks.text: May an invitee decline an invitation, and a guest decline a share ticket, before it expires?
asks.suggest: Yes, on the peek route: a decline spends the ticket and is recorded. A refused ticket should not sit live for days; the tenant sees the decline in its stream.

asks.text: May a member leave a tenant on their own, without an owner removing them?
asks.suggest: Yes: /auth/share/leave for role holders too, refused for the last owner. The identity is the person's and the membership is the tenant's; leaving should not need the tenant's act.

asks.text: May a person with an independent identity delete their own account, and what happens to their memberships?
asks.suggest: Yes, step-up gated: credential, links and passkeys go, memberships are removed, a last owner is refused. The language promises erasure; today only a tenant can be erased.

asks.text: A program with no release line: are its members locked in (only an owner can release them) or free to leave?
asks.suggest: Locked. Leaving is the app's choice, so it should be stated; ordo check says when a program has no release line.

asks.text: Should the release rule live in the program, with open, locked or rule also a setting a tenant can change when the app allows?
asks.suggest: Yes, both. The rule is the app's logic; the mode is a layered setting like every other limit.

asks.text: When a member leaves, do rows that point at them stay, pointing at a former-member seat, rather than block the leave?
asks.suggest: Stay. Their work stays the tenant's; access rows and grants go, and the history keeps who did what.

asks.text: May a tenant owner release a member past a locked rule, but not past the app's own conditions?
asks.suggest: Locked yes, conditions no. The owner can grant a special request; an app condition such as an unpaid invoice still holds unless the app adds an owner clause.

asks.text: When someone deletes their account while memberships remain, refuse and list each tenant with what stands in the way?
asks.suggest: Yes. They can see exactly what to resolve, and nothing is half-deleted.

asks.text: May the deployment owner delete an account for someone who cannot sign in, as a recovery-style case with evidence?
asks.suggest: Yes, after the first deployment. It is the special-request path you described, and it needs a recorded case.

asks.text: After deletion, the history keeps a random user id with nothing linking it to the person. Is that the erasure promised?
asks.suggest: Yes. The history must never be rewritten, and an id with no record behind it identifies no one.

asks.text: Ordo keeps one name per member (displayName, from sign-in). Should the app developer choose whether it is kept, and should a leave erase it from history?
asks.suggest: Yes to both. A setting: keep the sign-in name (default), a name the person enters, or none; on leave, history keeps the id only. The id alone still proves who did what.

asks.text: If the app developer changes how long deleted accounts are kept, should accounts already deleted follow the new setting?
asks.suggest: Yes, follow the current setting. Removal is the app developer's choice; a shorter time or "now" should apply to everyone waiting, and "never" already stops all removal.

where: Built: 8c8b4b5 0f01907 e2087cc 401197d 8c97b7e a406073; 2026-10-06: eb2c0b0f, 3136921e (a leaver keeps their name; a deleted account is kept; ORDO_MEMBER_LEFT_NAME, ORDO_ACCOUNT_REMOVAL); f7c0aae8, 125ac47f (audit fixes); bdf500d1 (removal follows the setting in force at each sweep, ask 12). Tests crates/ordo-host/tests/member_release.rs (29) incl. shortening_the_days_removes_an_account_that_is_now_past_due, changing_to_never_removes_no_one. Remains: R5 waits on 24a; R7 after first deployment.

name: A tenant owner cannot detach its own storage bucket
explain: A bucket can be attached and replaced, but never detached back to platform storage. Found by the one-way gap review.

asks.text: May a tenant owner detach its own bucket and return to platform custody, under the same refusal as a change while objects are held?
asks.suggest: Yes, as std.space.detachBucket: owner only, step-up gated, refused while objects are held. A detach that is consented, gated and logged is as loud as the attach.

where: std.space.detachBucket (77b6145); docs/howto-byo-custody.md (12900dc); tests only_the_owner_with_presence_may_detach_a_bucket, a_detach_returns_the_tenant_to_platform_custody_and_is_recorded, detaching_a_space_that_holds_objects_is_allowed (ruled 2026-10-06)

name: Attestation: the destination cannot be switched off or read, and dead letters reach nobody
explain:
Found by the one-way gap review.

  • attestTo sets a destination; nothing removes it or shows it.
  • Failed deliveries are kept as dead letters; only a count is visible.

asks.text: May a tenant owner switch off its attestation destination, and read back which one is set?
asks.suggest: Yes: attestTo with no destination removes it, and a read op shows it. The owner who chose a witness must be able to see it and end it.

asks.text: Should webhook dead letters be readable by the tenant owner and the deployment owner, with a retry?
asks.suggest: Yes: a read op per tenant and the entries on the overview; no retry yet. The checklist promises them on the ops surface; retry waits for a case that needs it.

where: a038156: std.space.attestTo with no destination, std.space.attestation, std.space.attestationDeadLetters, /health/deep; tests the_owner_switches_the_destination_off_and_reads_it_back, dead_letters_are_read_by_the_tenant_owner_and_the_deployment_owner

name: A tenant cannot be paused, only deleted
sub: Pause and resume built; nopause ops; space_paused
explain:
A whole tenant can be paused and resumed. Plan: docs/plan-tenant-pause.md.

  • Its people still sign in at the deployment level and see why.
  • Export, resume and delete still answer.
  • Workers that keep records keep running.

asks.text: May a tenant owner pause their own tenant, with the app able to switch that off?
asks.suggest: Yes, setting pause.byOwner, default on. The owner may need to stop everything at once; an app that bills by tenant may prefer only the deployment pauses.

asks.text: Paused calls are refused, except ops the app marks to keep answering, e.g. op billing whenpaused = ... Is a word on the op the right way?
asks.suggest: Yes, one op flag, like unguarded. It is greppable, in the manifest, and the app decides which screens a paused tenant still reaches; export and resume stay open regardless.

asks.text: Is the layer outside a paused tenant the deployment's own space, so nothing new has to be built for it?
asks.suggest: Yes. Sign-in is already deployment-wide, and notices, billing or contact pages are the app's deployment entities.

asks.text: The door already lets the app decide who calls its ops (roles, profiles, allowlists). Should platform ops like pause use the same, with defaults?
asks.suggest: Yes. Pause stays a deployment op by default, and an app grants it to tenant owners through the same rules it uses for its own ops; who may lift a pause is then the app's grant too.

asks.text: Scheduled work due during a pause: run it on resume, or skip it and record that it was skipped?
asks.suggest: Skip and record. A month of missed jobs firing at once on resume is worse than a gap that is written down.

asks.text: May a tenant owner write a free-text notice that members see while paused?
asks.suggest: Yes, as setting pause.notice, never written into the security record. The people affected deserve a reason in the owner's words.

asks.text: Which word marks an op that keeps answering while its tenant is paused: nopause, lockfree, freespace or homespace?
asks.suggest: nopause. It says exactly what it does where it sits (op billing nopause = ...), like unguarded and unbounded; the others need explaining.

asks.text: A paused tenant refuses most calls with space_paused. Should it answer 423 (Locked)?
asks.suggest: Yes, 423. Waiting never lifts a pause, so 503 would make clients retry forever; the caller holds the permission, so 403 is wrong too.

where: Built: f987ecf, 4c0ff93, 9dea00e; per-reason answers eaab5633 (ORDO_TENANT_PAUSE_ANSWERS, status 4xx or 503 and message per reason word, class always space_paused). Tests crates/ordo-host/tests/tenant_pause.rs (20) incl. a_billing_pause_answers_the_status_and_message_the_app_developer_set. Owed: P5 live close and onPaused; P6.

name: Maintenance mode: pause every tenant at once
sub: Asked by the owner, 2026-10-05
explain:
A deployment-wide pause for maintenance.

  • Every tenant answers paused; what still answers is decided as for one tenant.
  • The deployment's own space stays reachable, so people can see why.
  • Builds on tenant-pause (27ar) and is planned with it.
where: To plan with docs/plan-tenant-pause.md. Checklist 27as.

name: Two things that can be set but not seen
explain:
Found by the one-way gap review.

  • A guest share is revoked by a seat id that nothing lists.
  • Self-serve mode and the claim code can be set but not read back.

asks.text: Should a tenant owner be able to list its outgoing guest shares, as it lists links and invitations?
asks.suggest: Yes, std.space.shares: one row per live seat with its ops and expiry. Revocation takes a seat id that nothing shows after the share answer.

asks.text: Should the deployment's self-serve mode and claim code setting be readable after they are set?
asks.suggest: Yes, on the deployment status: the mode, and whether a code is set, never the code. A setting with a writer and no reader can only be checked by trying it.

where: std.space.shares (25a2fb3), /health/deep self-serve and claim code (06bb1bd); tests a_tenant_lists_its_live_shares_by_seat_and_a_revoked_one_leaves_the_list, deep_health_reads_back_self_serve_and_whether_a_claim_code_is_set

name: Serve reads that return a sealed field
explain:
An app can store sealed fields but cannot read them back: every read whose result holds a sealed value is a 501 naming no field.

  • An indexed sealed field can filter only when left out of the result.
  • Decrypting, key leases and records are built; reads never reach them.
  • A page is at most 50 rows.

asks.text: Build this next: per page of up to 50 rows, release the tenant's read key once and decrypt, naming the field in the refusal until then?
asks.suggest: Yes, next. Sealed fields are write-only to an app today; one key release per page keeps the work bounded and every decrypt recorded.

where: crates/ordo-exec/src/lib.rs (Executor::venue, open_sealed per page), commits 612cf27, 0657485, ad3aaaa9 (declared blind-index ops compile); tests crates/ordo-exec/tests/sealed_reads.rs, crates/ordo-host/tests/sealed_reads.rs

name: The audit of 2026-10-05: two decisions
sub: Built 2026-10-05; all 3 asks ruled
explain:
A Fable audit of the 9 commits of 2026-10-05 fixed 1 thing and left 2 choices.

  • Fixed: * through a filtered join offered extra fields.
  • Filed: filtered-term-reach (25v).

asks.text: Should a group or reduce over a sealed field count as plain SQL, since nothing sealed survives the fold and no key is used?
asks.suggest: Yes. Today it demands unbounded, lists a key release, and takes a read lease it never uses; nothing sealed reaches the output after a fold.

asks.text: Should a sweep pass that deleted nothing because storage refused still write a security entry, with deleted=0?
asks.suggest: Yes. A tenant should see that storage due to shrink did not; today only a metric and a log line say so.

asks.text: Should a tenant whose storage could not be reached at all also get a sweep security entry, with counts unknown?
asks.suggest: No. The entry records what a pass did to objects; an unreachable store is a fault of the deployment, already a metric and a log line, and its counts were never computed.

where: Commits 928f798, 2a517ec (checklist 27an). Third audit (2026-10-05): no defect in 8f0c549, 928f798, 2a517ec, be6a10d; tests 3099721 (the prune changes no result across eleven shapes, against Postgres), c7111dc (venue gate test seeds its database). Open: ask 3.

name: Refinement on by default for every read
sub: Built 2026-10-05, R1 to R8
explain:
Code calling an op can filter and trim its result without a new op. #1 on the list. Plan: docs/plan-refinement.md.

  • Built: the server envelope, the cost gate, the device engine.
  • Missing: every op refuses it, the executor ignores it, no SDK builder.
  • 8 increments, R1 to R8.

asks.text: Should conditions on open and blind-index fields compile into the plan, so pages come back full, instead of filtering after the page window?
asks.suggest: Yes, compile them in. They are plain SQL predicates, the same cost as an op with a parameter; only sealed host-side conditions would need the after-window rule, and those cannot run today.

asks.text: Should a sync accept where but refuse pick, since the device stores whole rows keyed by id?
asks.suggest: Yes. A picked row would overwrite a whole row another sync of the same entity holds, and the device already applies pick locally for free.

asks.text: Until host-side sealed filtering is built, should the door refuse a sealed unindexed condition, naming the field?
asks.suggest: Yes, refuse at the door. Today it passes the cost gate, then fails in the executor with a message that names no field and no fix.

asks.text: ordo check would add one line per read, e.g. "refinable: status, due (any operator); email (equality only); memo (refused)". Print that?
asks.suggest: Yes, print it. A developer sees what callers can filter before a refusal surprises them, without the compiler guessing indexes it cannot know.

asks.text: Should count over a filtered list (std.E.count with list's conditions) be built in this round, or after?
asks.suggest: After. It is the one refinement that changes the order of work and has no code yet; a screen can call count and list separately meanwhile.

asks.text: Should a refinement's size be a setting with defaults, such as at most 16 conditions and 200 values in one in?
asks.suggest: Yes, a setting with those defaults. An unbounded in is a scan the cost gate cannot see; a deployment owner can raise it where a screen needs more.

where: Plan with commit table: docs/plan-refinement.md. Guide: docs/howto-cost.md. Audit suite: crates/ordo-host/tests/refine_audit.rs. Checklist 27am.

name: The audit of 2026-10-04: eight decisions
explain:
A Fable audit of today's 26 build commits fixed 11 things and left 8 choices.

  • Fixed: 2 security defects (25t, 25u), live stream settings and gate, device money order.
  • These asks are the rest.

asks.text: Should the playground show money as the door does ("29.99") instead of stored cents (2999)?
asks.suggest: Yes. People learn the wire from the playground; the corpus decoder keeps stored units for its own checks.

asks.text: Should two outputs with one name in a join (a[note] b[note]) be refused now, before host-side opening is built?
asks.suggest: Yes, as projection_unknown_field. Matching by name could open the wrong column once host opening lands; refusing costs nothing today.

asks.text: Should the artifact's cost class use the schema, so a join with take 3 reads bounded-host as the door already says?
asks.suggest: Yes. The artifact disagrees with the door and the venue gate, and it is what a consent page shows. Goldens move.

asks.text: Should the storage sweep record its deletions in the security stream?
asks.suggest: Yes, one entry per pass per tenant, not per object. Deleting stored files is worth an audit trail, without flooding it.

asks.text: Should money(0) * money(0) be refused like money(2) * money(2), typed decimal instead?
asks.suggest: Yes. One rule for every places value; today places 0 slips through a check the others meet.

asks.text: Is 12 places the right ceiling for money(p) and decimal(p)?
asks.suggest: Yes, as a language fact in the reference, not a setting. It is the division scale, so widening never rounds.

asks.text: Should ordo dev keep refusing a reset when a table that is not Ordo's depends on one of Ordo's?
asks.suggest: Yes. Refusing keeps the foreign table intact; dropping the dependency silently is the data loss 27p fixed.

asks.text: When 27m lands, should one setting decide who may delete owned rows, for both a delete and an undo?
asks.suggest: Yes. Two settings for one question would let an undo do what a delete may not.

where: Commits 65c6ff7, d7dc60f, 2fd23f1, b3d5d06, 6afa5ef, bd9be06 (checklist 27al). Asks 7 and 8 need no build; 8 binds 27m.

name: Money declares its places; a storable decimal(p)
sub: Built 2026-10-04 except allocate wiring; bare money default put to the owner
explain:
Money stays whole minor units, and each field says how many places its currency has.

  • price: money(2); source writes 29.99 and the compiler converts.
  • A new decimal(p) field holds rates and unit prices at any precision.
  • decimal becomes money only by an explicit round.

asks.text: Bare money (no places) was built as money(0), so existing programs keep their meaning. Keep that, or require places on every money field?
asks.suggest: Keep money(0) for now, and warn on bare money in new code. Defaulting to 2 would silently multiply every existing literal by 100, the same kind of bug the old shortcut caused.

where: Commits 3933a89 to a1c0efb; bare-money warning 9cdf5b4 (checklist 27ak). Owed: allocate wired when each lands.

name: Dev, staging and production as things Ordo supports
sub: Ruled 2026-10-01, all five asks
decided: I want to make sure that there will actually be a served point for the environments.
explain:
ordo dev exists; staging and promotion do not. The spec is plan-environments.md.

  • dev: made by applying, same shape as production, no real data
  • staging: the program against a clone of named production tenants
  • production: moves tenant by tenant
  • Config travels with the program through settings-in-code (18ac)

GitHub integration and a data generation module are filed as future items (github-apply, data-generation). Destructive commands naming their environment is part of the rollout build (27h).

asks.text: Should ordo apply default to dev, and refuse staging until dev runs the version, and production until staging does?
asks.suggest: Yes. It is your proposal. A test that compiling is byte-stable across machines comes first, since the check is by hash.

asks.text: Should a dev branch be a tenant in the dev deployment, removed only by an explicit command?
asks.suggest: Yes. Schema is per tenant, so a branch costs one tenant database. A merge never deletes it, which avoids the Supabase UAT loss.

asks.text: When staging clones production tenants, should personal data be masked on the way in?
asks.suggest: Masked by default, the deployment owner may turn it off. The clone is re-sealed under staging's keys either way, but masking keeps real people out of a test system.

asks.text: Should per-tenant rollout (all at once, canary, or manual) be a setting in the program?
asks.suggest: Yes, default all at once. That is today's behaviour, and canary and manual give you blue/green per tenant without a second copy of anything.

asks.text: Should staging be treated as production for access, since it holds cloned data?
asks.suggest: Yes. Its data came from real tenants, so only deployment owners reach it, with its own keys.

asks.text: A branch tenant runs its own version; a deployment serves one today. Build multi-version serving with branches, or a dev deployment per branch?
asks.suggest: Multi-version serving, scoped to dev first. It is needed for branch promotion later anyway, and per-branch deployments add servers to clean up, which is the mess we want to avoid.

where: Spec: docs/plan-environments.md. Owed: 27e to 27h, 27v. Ruled 2026-10-08: multi-version serving for dev first (ask 6), and dev and staging each served at a real address (comment). Branch promotion: tenant-builds (27t).

name: Tables another system owns in the same database
sub: Ruled 2026-10-01, all four asks. Not deferred
decided: no - theyre independent. If there is an issue at first-apply ordo will error and will also show existing untracked tables as well.
explain:
Ordo leaves other systems' tables alone but cannot use them, does not notice them, and can collide with their names. The spec is plan-external-entities.md.

  • An external entity: a generated, read-only translation of a foreign table
  • Ordo sees it as an ordinary entity
  • Each apply lists what is present but not Ordo's

Your ruling on outside writes (g27) is recorded: direct database access is discouraged and handled by access control, so Ordo's role is the only one with write access. Detecting outside writes waits for a customer who needs it.

asks.text: Should Ordo read other systems' tables as external entities: generated, read-only translations that look like ordinary entities?
asks.suggest: Yes. It is your projection idea. Read-only first, because writing would bypass the other system's own rules.

asks.text: Should each tenant database put Ordo's tables in a random schema name instead of public?
asks.suggest: Yes. It is your prefix rule at schema grain. Other systems keep public, and a name clash becomes near impossible.

asks.text: Should other systems read Ordo through the door only, or also through read-only SQL views you grant?
asks.suggest: The door only, to begin with. Views would expose plaintext outside the guards. Add them if a customer needs SQL access.

asks.text: Should external entities wait until after the first deployment?
asks.suggest: Yes, except the random schema name and the audit. Those two change where tables live, which is cheapest before anything is deployed.

where: Spec: docs/plan-external-entities.md (rulings in place). Owed: 27i to 27k; 27l is deploy-schema-audit; 27u views, not planned.

name: Offline writes, and totals on the device
sub: Ruled 2026-10-01: all six recommendations. A library: the app developer decides what is shown
decided: All six recommendations accepted: queue by default (off per operation), 24 hours as a setting, show only what was typed marked pending, device counts for a fixed set with a parity test, counts before offline writes, last server total labelled with its time as a setting. Comment: a reminder this is all a library so app dev decides what information they display; we make that information available.
explain:
The offline plan is written: docs/plan-offline.md. Filed for after the first deployment.

  • Offline writes wait on the device and send on reconnect, with conflicts shown to the person.
  • Counts and totals can be answered on the device when it holds every row.
  • A queued write can wait 24 hours, the server's retry window.

Three parts: offline writes for ordinary tenants (6 steps), offline writes for client-first tenants through F7 (5 steps), and counts and grouped results on the device (6 steps).

Nothing is merged silently. A pending write shows exactly what the person typed.

asks.text: Queue offline writes by default wherever the device copy is on?
asks.suggest: Yes, and the app developer can turn it off per operation. Refusing by default would surprise people in exactly the case offline exists for.

asks.text: How long may a queued write wait before it is dropped and the person told?
asks.suggest: 24 hours by default, as a setting. That is the server's retry window; longer would turn a retry into a new request.

asks.text: What does a pending write show before the server accepts it?
asks.suggest: Only what the person typed, marked pending. The device cannot compute what the server would add, so it shows nothing derived.

asks.text: Compute counts and totals on the device, with a test proving they match the server?
asks.suggest: Yes, for a small fixed set of calculations. The full client-side database only comes with client-first tenants.

asks.text: Build counts on the device before offline writes?
asks.suggest: Yes. Counts change what the server describes, which is cheapest before anything is deployed.

asks.text: Offline, show the last total the server gave, labelled with its time?
asks.suggest: Yes, labelled, as the app developer's setting. It bends the never-older rule, but a total marked "as of 2:14 pm" is honest and better than a blank.

where: Plan docs/plan-offline.md, §0 'Where it stands' added 2026-10-10. Built under it: the device copy (5g-pre), device refinement (C6, db6e1ca), purge on revocation (C7, d4e756a), conflict state. Not built: §1 offline writes in server-managed spaces (needs only a go, not the vault), §2 client-first offline writes (waits on F7), §3 device counts. Checklist 18ad.

name: Offline writes in ordinary tenants
explain: Queue a write while offline, send it on reconnect, show conflicts to the person. Ruled in docs/plan-offline.md §1; needs no vault. Today a write with no network is refused, never queued. Ellanor (server-managed) gets offline through this alone.
where: docs/plan-offline.md §1 and §0

name: Counts and totals on the device
explain: Answer counts, sums and grouped reads from the device copy when it holds every row, instead of the network. Ruled in docs/plan-offline.md §3. No code.
where: docs/plan-offline.md §3

name: The same SQL on the device (Postgres in the browser)
explain: Run the server's own SQL on the device with Postgres compiled to WebAssembly (PGlite), so a device answers new questions exactly as the server would. Recommended by the vault plan (f7-vault-plan.md Q10). Waits on F7. A multi-megabyte download and a slower first load.
where: f7-vault-plan.md Q10; plan-client-cache.md §8 level 3; replica-engine

name: Shared rate windows across nodes
sub: Post-deploy, 2026-10-03 (public-path-design ask 12)
explain:
In v1 a per-address rate window counts on each node, so 3 nodes admit up to 3 times a limit.

  • A shared count makes the number exact.
  • Only matters once a limit is set: the default is unlimited.
where: docs/design-public-path.md §5; checklist 18ae

name: Recovery: five details
sub: From the recovery build, 2026-09-29. Five asks
decided: Answered in conversation 2026-09-29. 1: "thats fine": a recovery the deployment owner runs on the server skips the one-day wait (built). 2: a tenant manager may recover a member "if the app dev sets it that way"; a single-person tenant is an exception, and the sign-in method matters: a person who signs in through a third-party provider is recovered there, not by Ordo. 3: no, recovery does not cancel the person's grants. 4: the deployment owns this; there is no enforceable objection, it becomes the app developer's contract with their customer. 5: the same as 4.
explain:
Recovery is built. Five details are still yours. One was built on my recommendation as a setting, so either answer is one line.

  • The plan is docs/plan-passkey-recovery.md, section 11.

Numbers the build chose, all settings with minimums:

  • One day before a deployment owner's recovery takes effect.
  • Three days in which the lost passkey can cancel a recovery.
  • One day after any recovery before the account can export, delete or deploy.
  • One hour is the lowest any of these can be set.

asks.text: A recovery the deployment owner runs on the server itself: skip the one-day wait?
asks.suggest: Yes, skip it. Whoever runs the server already holds the database and the keys. Built this way as a setting; tell me if you want the wait.

asks.text: May a tenant manager, not only the owner, recover a member the tenant created?

name: Keys for the easy deployment
sub: For the conversation you asked for, 2026-09-29
decided: Agreed 2026-09-29, in conversation: "Agree with this setup - set bao for post deploy." The easy deployment is docker-compose first, then a small Kubernetes cluster. It uses the sealed key file (A) by default, a cloud key service (C) when the machine runs in GCP or AWS, and OpenBao in the same compose file (B) as an option after the first deployment.
explain:
You want to talk through which key design the easy deployment uses. Here is the choice as I see it.

  • The catch: a key service beside the server must unlock itself on restart. So it needs a key too, kept on the same machine.
  • On one small box, that protects less than it sounds. A cloud key service outside the box protects more.

Three options for the easy deployment

  • A. The sealed key file (built today). One file plus a passphrase. Restarts on its own. Anyone who takes the machine has both.
  • B. OpenBao or Vault in the same compose file. The server's key moves into it. OpenBao must unlock after each restart: by hand, which stops unattended restarts, or automatically, which needs a key on the same machine again.
  • C. A cloud key service, when the machine runs in that cloud. GCP or AWS unlocks by the machine's own identity. The key never sits on the disk. Needs a cloud account.

The plan is docs/plan-key-service.md. Nothing here is built yet except A.

asks.text: What is the easy deployment: one docker-compose command on any machine, or also a small Kubernetes cluster?
asks.suggest: Both, with compose first. Compose is the smallest thing that runs. A small cluster is where it goes next.

asks.text: Which key design should the easy deployment use by default?
asks.suggest: A by default, C offered when the machine runs in GCP or AWS. A restarts on its own with nothing else to run. B on the same machine adds a service without moving the risk off the box.

asks.text: Should the easy deployment offer B, OpenBao in the same compose file, as an option?
asks.suggest: Yes, as an option, not the default. It suits someone who already runs OpenBao, or who wants to unlock by hand after each restart.

where: A is built (the sealed key file). C and B are in docs/plan-key-service.md, checklist 18y, after the first deployment.

name: A key service for the master key
sub: Planned 2026-09-29 for after the first deployment. Not built
decided: Answered 2026-09-29. 1: both designs, leaning on the recommendation (B). 2: GCP KMS, AWS KMS, Cloudflare if it offers one, and HashiCorp Vault; also any other large one and a popular self-hosted one, remembering most deployments will be a small Kubernetes cluster or docker-compose. 3: the recommendation, five minutes, adjustable.
explain:
You asked me to check whether a key service is already built. It is not.

  • The place it plugs in exists. Only the built-in key handling uses it.
  • I told you the key would never leave the service. That is only true of one design. Both are below.
  • The plan is docs/plan-key-service.md.

Design A: the service wraps the master key.

  • The server unwraps it once at boot.
  • The key is off the disk. It is still in memory.
  • A taken-over server still has every key.

Design B: the service wraps each space's key.

  • The master key never leaves the service.
  • A taken-over server holds only the keys of spaces used in the last few minutes.
  • Access can be cut off, and the service logs every use.

The easy deployment, a key from a file, stays in both.

asks.text: Which design: A, B, or both?
asks.suggest: B. A does not fix the problem you raised: the key would still be in the server's memory. B costs one call per space every few minutes, not one per field.

asks.text: Which key service first?
asks.suggest: AWS KMS, since you named it. The first three steps need no cloud account, so the choice can wait until step 4.

asks.text: How long may a space's key stay in memory before the server must ask again?
asks.suggest: Five minutes, adjustable. Shorter limits what a taken-over server holds. Longer survives a brief outage of the key service.

where: Plan: docs/plan-key-service.md, updated to the answers. Post-deployment, checklist 18y.

name: Sign-in: four details before the build
sub: From the sign-in plans, 2026-09-29. Four asks
decided: Answered 2026-09-29, all five. 1: a sign-up no tenant admits is kept 90 days by default, configurable. 2: a person may see the list of their own tenants. 3: mail through SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Brevo and Mailjet, with SES after. 4: passkeys may be used on more than one address, so passkey addresses are their own setting. 5: not ours to decide; it is the developer's. Comment: "We do not enforce an app developer's choices but we can have it as default."
explain:
Passkey sign-in and enrolment start soon. Four details need you.

  • Ask 4 is needed before passkey sign-in reaches step S2.
  • Asks 1 and 2 are needed before enrolment's later steps.
  • Ask 3 is needed only for emailed codes, which come later.

The plans are docs/plan-passkey-signin.md, docs/plan-enrolment.md and docs/plan-auth-federated.md.

Smaller questions stay in the plans, under "Open for the owner". None blocks the first builds.

asks.text: How long is a sign-up kept if no tenant admits the person?
asks.suggest: 7 days, adjustable. Long enough for an invitation to arrive. Short enough that abandoned sign-ups do not pile up.

asks.text: May a person see the list of tenants they belong to?
asks.suggest: Yes, their own list only. Nobody else, including a tenant, sees which other tenants a person is in.

asks.text: Which five mail services, besides Resend?
asks.suggest: SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Brevo, Mailjet. Amazon SES after, since it needs its own signing.

asks.text: The addresses allowed to use passkeys: a separate setting from CORS, or the same one?
asks.suggest: Separate. CORS says which pages may call the server. Passkeys say which pages may sign people in. Joining them would widen one to change the other.

asks.text: An owner who signs in with a password cannot manage members; that needs a passkey. Keep that?
asks.suggest: Keep it. Managing members is an owner act, like deploying. It needs a passkey so a stolen password cannot hand the tenant to somebody else.

where: Passkey addresses: ORDO_AUTH_ORIGINS and ORDO_AUTH_RELATED_ORIGINS (4a7b123). Presence setting: ORDO_STEP_UP_EXEMPT_OPS, default every platform op asks (docs/security-logging-design.md 2.3). 90-day sign-ups, own tenants list: 12d8acc. Mail: built with emailed codes ([[mail-relay-gaps]], docs/howto-sign-in.md sections 9 and 10).

name: Backup codes, and a second factor with a hardware token
sub: T1 to T7 built 2026-09-29
decided: Answered 2026-09-29, all five. 1: 24-character codes. 2: a second step is available to anyone by default. 3: a reset or recovery removes every second factor, but only after the reset completes. 4: after a passkey, a second step only when a person or tenant turns it on. 5: 20 wrong codes in a row locks a factor by default, configurable.
explain:
The second factor and backup codes are planned. Built after recovery.

  • Backup codes follow NIST SP 800-63B. A code is used after the password, in place of the lost second step. Never alone.
  • One exception, already ruled: a person with only a passkey can use a code alone to start a recovery, with its day's block.

The plan is docs/plan-second-factor.md.

One rule the plan adds: a second factor never proves a person is present. Otherwise a stolen password plus the thief's own key would pass the checks for deploying and deleting.

The codes: 10 codes, 24 characters each, shown once, each usable once. Stored so a database copy alone cannot check a guess.

Sources: NIST SP 800-63B look-up secrets (rev 3 section 5.1.2, rev 4 section 3.1.2), and how GitHub and Google use backup codes.

asks.text: Backup codes: 24 characters, or 16 characters stored with a slow hash?
asks.suggest: 24 characters. At that length NIST allows a simple keyed hash, and a copied database cannot be used to guess codes. The 16-character form needs a slow hash on every use.

asks.text: The deployment's default for a second step: available to anyone who wants it, or off?
asks.suggest: Available. A person turns it on for themselves; nobody is forced. A tenant or the app developer can still require it.

asks.text: When a password is reset or an account recovered, remove every second factor?
asks.suggest: Yes, and record it. A reset or recovery means the old way in is not trusted. The person adds a factor again.

asks.text: A second step after a passkey sign-in: only when a person or tenant turns it on, off by default?
asks.suggest: Yes. A passkey already needs the device plus a fingerprint or PIN. This is how I read your word "optionally".

asks.text: How many wrong codes in a row before a factor is locked?
asks.suggest: 20. NIST allows up to 100. 20 stops guessing and rarely locks out a real person.

where: Merge 65a49f6: second_step.rs, totp.rs, second_factors.rs, second_factor_store.rs, auth/factors.rs, auth/second_step.rs; SDK auth/second-step.ts. Settings: ORDO_AUTH_SECOND_FACTOR and five more (docs/deploying.md). Plan: docs/plan-second-factor.md, Built.

name: Does every tenant get a bucket of its own, the way it now gets a database?
sub: Ruled 2026-09-25: one tenant one bucket, same principle, where a bucket may be shared and the tenant's folder inside it is the separation
decided: one tenant one bucket. Same principal. / 1 bucket can have folders so 1 bucket defined per - but it could be the same and bucketname/tenant would be the option. The deployment can also have its own bucket defined
explain:
The answer was none of the options as posed, because the question put the two tiers one level apart. A bucket answers to a cluster, and a folder answers to a database. Every tenant has a bucket defined for it, and that bucket may be the same physical bucket another tenant uses, with bucketname/tenant separating them, exactly as tenants share a Postgres cluster and never a database.

The layout already did this. ordo_blob::object_key keys every object <space>/<handle>, so two tenants in one bucket could never have collided whatever prefix either stated. The separation described here is what the code has always done.

Four levels, as on the database side: the console's own bucket, the deployment's own, a default bucket for tenants, and a per-tenant bucket, each defaulting to the one above and all of them possibly the same bucket.
suggest: What changed in the build. U6 shipped a refusal turning a second tenant away from a bucket whatever prefix they stated. That is reversed. What survives is D-S8, which you ruled “agreed” and which asks a different question: a bucket declared as one tenant’s own perimeter is theirs, and the platform may not put somebody else inside it. A folder does not answer that, because it is a disclosure rather than a collision. The op now refuses in that case and in that case alone, in both directions.

asks.text: Nothing open. The quota concern in my recommendation was answering a question nobody asked, and it is recorded rather than deleted because it is the shape of the mistake: the tiers were lined up one level apart, so a bucket was being treated as a database.

where: The ruling needed one code change, 99fe624: bucket_ops.rs stops refusing a second tenant in a shared bucket and keeps only the D-S8 own-perimeter refusal (tests/attach_bucket.rs). Folder separation was already ordo_blob::object_key keying <space>/<handle>. Ruling in corpus-rulings.md 2026-09-25.

name: CI runs Postgres at 100 connections and one suite alone needs 99
sub: Closed 2026-09-25 without touching CI. Your question found the real cause: PoolConfig::from_env never read ORDO_PG_POOL_SIZE, so every test that built a pool directly dialled eight whatever the environment said
decided: Why are we testing that many connections? Is it for stress testing?  We do not need to stress test everytime.
explain:
Measured, not guessed. crates/ordo-host/tests/runtime.rs peaks at 99 client backends on its own, against Postgres's default max_connections = 100. Cargo runs test binaries one at a time, so this is one suite against the ceiling rather than many overlapping: its ~22 tests run in parallel and each stand up a real deployment with several pools.

Sitting exactly on the ceiling is what made runtime and spaces fail a different subset almost every run for weeks, and why --test-threads=1 always passed. That flakiness had been attributed to leaked test servers (17ad); leaked servers make it worse and are not the cause. scripts/conformance-pg.sh now starts at 300 and the whole workspace is clean.

Why CI is not fixed with it. A GitHub Actions service container takes no command:, and max_connections needs a restart rather than a reload. Changing it means dropping the services: block and starting Postgres from a step instead, which on the self-hosted runner still means Docker: the pod runs a privileged docker:27-dind sidecar, which is the only reason service containers work there at all, and containers it starts share the pod's network namespace so a published port stays reachable at localhost. Nothing about it becomes a k3s object.
suggest:
The recommendation below was wrong, and is kept because the mistake is the point. PoolConfig::from_env() read six environment variables and computed the seventh as min(cores, 8), ignoring ORDO_PG_POOL_SIZE entirely. ordo_host::runtime read that variable separately, so a booting deployment honoured it and every test building a pool directly did not — which is why sizing the spawned servers down worked while setting the same variable for the whole run did nothing. Raising the limit to 300 would have worked and would have left the defect in place with the ceiling moved. Explained in full, with diagrams, in docs/pooling-explained.html.

Superseded: Restructure it. One suite needing 99 of 100 is not margin, and the failure surfaces as whichever suite happened to dial last, which reads as a bug in that suite and is not one. The change is contained to ci.yml and the runner already has the Docker daemon it needs. Held rather than done only because it changes how the job gets its database on a runner that has just moved.

asks.text: Nothing open, and nothing was restructured. Measured on a 10-core machine: tests/runtime.rs peaked at 99 and the whole workspace at 81; after the fix the whole workspace peaks at 25 against a stock limit of 100. The conformance cluster is back to stock and CI needs no change.

where: 669d3ed: PoolConfig::from_env in crates/ordo-exec/src/lib.rs now reads ORDO_PG_POOL_SIZE, and the keystore, credential store and principal directory share one connection. Explained in docs/pooling-explained.html. CI left unchanged.

name: Every tenant gets a database, and the setting picks the cluster
sub: Closed 2026-09-25. Built, and the migration question is moot: nothing has deployed, so there are no existing tenants to leave or move
decided: left alone or moved under what circumstance? Nothing has deployed in terms of ordo so we make - expectation of recoverability for anything at the moment
explain:
What has to change. T8 shipped $db as name the database this tenant's rows go in, with $dbHost, $dbUser, $dbCredential and $dbOwnPerimeter beside it, and refused the call unless every one was given. The ruling says the database is not optional and is not the caller's to name. So the parameter becomes which cluster: absent means the deployment's default tenant cluster, present means a cluster the deployment holds for that tenant. The database name is minted, the way the space id already is.

Four clusters, not two (clarified 2026-09-25): “It doesnt neccesarily need to be the control plane database. The console has its own it can define, the deplyment can define its own, it can define one as a default for tenants, and it can define individually per tenant.”

  1. The console's own database, which belongs to the console rather than to any deployment it manages (18o puts the console and the operator outside the deployment).
  2. The deployment's own, which is the control plane: identity, grants, $artifacts, $spacedb, the witness.
  3. A default cluster for tenants, where a tenant's database is created when nothing else is said.
  4. A per-tenant cluster, which is the BYO case.

These are configuration levels, not necessarily separate servers (2026-09-25): “someone deploying could use the same cluster for all 3 if they chose.” So each level defaults to the one above it rather than being required, and a deployment that configures nothing runs console, control plane and every tenant database on one cluster. That is the ordinary small deployment and it must stay a no-op to set up.

It also settles how this interacts with the ControlDatabase refusal and with D-D's “database/schema not cluster”: what may be shared is the cluster, what may not is the database. The existing check already compares host, port and database, so a tenant database beside the control database on one server passes and the control database itself is refused. Nothing there needs to change.

3 is the one the build does not have. runtime.rs hands TenantOps a PoolConfig::from_env() template, which is the control database's own connection, so today a tenant with no cluster named lands on the control plane's cluster by inheritance rather than by configuration. Under this it needs a setting of its own, and the ControlDatabase refusal stops being the thing that separates tenants from the control plane and goes back to being the backstop it was meant to be.

What stays exactly as built. One tenant per database (DatabaseOccupied), the control database refused as a target, the host allowlist, the routing lock, the fleet view and the custody record. None of that depends on who chose the name.

What gets more load-bearing. A thousand trial tenants becomes a thousand databases before any of them writes a row, so the reaper and the usage ledger stop being background concerns. They belong in this increment rather than after it.
suggest:
(a). Moving a tenant's rows from one database to another is exactly what 18e is for, and it is out of scope by your own routing-migration ruling. Doing it as a side effect of an upgrade would make an unbuilt mechanism's first outing an unattended one, on live data. A deployment that wants its old tenants separated can create new ones and use the export and import doors, which already exist and are tested.

Built 2026-09-25, except the migration. $db is gone; the database name is minted from the space id. ORDO_PG_TENANT_HOST, _PORT, _USER and _CREDENTIAL are level 3, each falling back per field to the deployment's own, so configuring nothing still gives every tenant a database on the deployment's own server. The reserved credential label $deployment is what makes that work with no credential directory installed. A cluster the operator configured is allowed without an allowlist entry, per D-S6 — without that, an unset ORDO_PG_ATTACH_HOSTS would have refused a deployment its own cluster and no tenant could ever have been created.

One thing this surfaced. Turning it on immediately broke the test that checks a new tenant's owner can reach their space, because the founding member row is now in the tenant's own database and the door had been reading memberships from the control one. That is §9.3's D-2 landmine, described in the plan as “the kind of defect that looks like an authorisation bug for a day”. runtime.rs already routes through directory::routed_engine and was correct; the test was reading a path production does not take, and now reads the same way the deployment does.

(a) for the remaining question, and say so in the release note rather than in a migration. Moving a tenant's rows between databases is 18e's whole subject and it is out of scope by your own routing-migration ruling; doing it as a side effect of an upgrade would be the riskiest possible first outing for a mechanism that has not been built. A deployment that wants its old tenants separated can create new ones and export-import, which are doors that already exist.

asks.text:
Nothing open. The question was moot and I should have established that before asking it. It assumed deployments in the field with tenants already in their control databases. There are none, so there is nothing to leave alone and nothing to move, and no migration is owed. The general form of this is its own entry in corpus-rulings.md: until something deploys, a change of shape owes no recovery path.

Superseded, kept because the rewrite was needed twice:

Rewritten, because the first version did not land. Here it is concretely.

Before today, a tenant created on a running deployment had its rows put in the control database, in shared tables, separated only by a $space column. From today every new tenant gets a database of its own instead.

So: if a deployment has been running and already has, say, five tenants sitting in its control database, and you upgrade it to this build — what should happen to those five?

(a) Leave them. They keep working exactly as they do now, and only tenants created after the upgrade get their own database.

(b) Move them, copying each one's rows out of the control database into a new database of its own.

If no deployment has ever run long enough to have tenants in it — which may well be the case, since nothing has shipped — then the answer is (a) by default and this row closes.

name: If one tenant means one database, what happens to tenants created without one?
sub: Ruled 2026-09-25, and it reframes the question: every tenant gets a database, and the routing setting picks which cluster that database is created in
decided: okay lets reframe this - there exist a default cluster which databases are created in. 1 tenant one database - in addition a tenant COULD have their own BYO DB. But the settings are simply to decide what DB cluster to store the database in. Either whatever the deployment provides as default, or what the deployment provides for that tenant.
explain:
What your ruling changed, and what it did not reach. “1 tenant 1 database” is now enforced wherever a tenant is given a database: std.space.create with $db refuses any database that already holds a tenant, whatever the custody. Built and tested 2026-09-25.

The other path still shares. A tenant created without $db goes into the control database alongside every other such tenant, separated by the $space column. That is what every tenant did before 18d and what they still do. Under the ruling read literally, it is non-conforming.

Why it was not just changed. Ending it means every tenant gets a provisioned database at creation, which touches provisioning, the cost model (the 18o row's own note is that a deployment’s cost is its database, not its pod), the usage ledger, T9 and T10, and the reason the $space column exists at all. It is an increment, not an edit, and it is the kind that should not start from an inference about what you meant.
suggest:
What the reframe fixes that the question got wrong. T8 built $db as name the database this tenant's rows go in, with host, user and credential beside it, and refused the call unless all of them were given. Under the ruling that is backwards: the database is not optional and is not the caller's to name, so what the parameters should carry is which cluster, and nothing else. A tenant with no cluster named lands on the deployment's default cluster, in its own database, with a name the platform mints.

The cost is real and is now a deliberate choice rather than a side effect. A thousand trial tenants is a thousand databases before any of them writes a row, so the reaper and the usage ledger matter more than they did. That belongs in the increment rather than after it.

asks.text:
Nothing open. The answer was neither (a) nor (b) as posed: the question had the wrong shape. It assumed a tenant might or might not be given a database. Every tenant has one; what the setting chooses is the cluster it is created in.

The build increment this creates is db-always-a-database below.
