name: The erasure receipt, and a credential that survives rotation
sub: Ruled 2026-10-01: build it alongside the attach work
decided: Take recommendation (build it alongside the attach work).
explain:
The receipt. Ordo cannot prove bytes are gone, and neither can anyone else, because absence is not observable from outside the store that holds them. What it can prove is unopenability, which is the claim cryptographic erasure actually makes, and it can prove it without being trusted: the chain records the destroyed epoch as a custody action, the checkpoint signer signs the chain, and the offline verifier checks a proof against a published key with no access to the deployment. The receipt carries the signed entry, the epoch destroyed, and the count and location of whatever was left. The application hands it to its user; the user verifies it without asking either of you to be honest.

The negative test is the strongest half and costs nothing: a user holding a sealed value tries to open it after the erasure and fails. They run that themselves, against the running system.

The same shape answers the bucket match: a one-for-one migration produces a manifest of every reference and the digest the target returned, signed into the chain, so both sides have the same verifiable set without anyone listing the bucket.

Rotation. The pool reads its password once at boot, so a rotated credential is an outage until a restart. Reading through the provider, invalidating on an authentication failure and retrying once makes a rotation cost at most one failed request.
suggest: Worth building alongside the attach work rather than after it, because the manifest the attach needs and the receipt the erasure needs are the same mechanism pointed at two moments.
where: Owed: the erasure receipt and a credential read through the provider that survives rotation, both specified in checklist 17ab (open) and corpus-rulings.md 2026-09-21 (9ea4dcf). No code for either exists in crates/.

name: Per-tenant object storage, alongside per-tenant databases
sub: Requirements delivered 2026-09-21 as plan-tenant-storage.md (18p). U0 and U1 built 2026-09-21, in lockstep with the database side
decided: While we're doing this we need to make sure the same per tenant / deployment S3 configuration exists.
explain:
U0 and U1 are built. U0 pinned three properties that held by accident, each proved first against deliberately broken code: a store error never reaches the caller, the object key is the space and the handle and nothing else, and two spaces on different stores do not share keys. The second moved out of a unit test into the shared contract suite so both bindings run it, and that turned up something the plan’s file list missed — the suite asserts how many cases ran, so without bumping that count the promoted case would have been added and never executed, which is the exact failure promoting it was meant to prevent.

U1 closed the credential leak (the attach response no longer returns the label) and added path_style and key_prefix to the attachment, with NULL and empty meaning today’s behaviour so no stored row changes meaning. The test that mattered most writes a row naming only the original eight columns, never mentioning the new two even as NULL, so it exercises a genuinely old row rather than a new one with the fields unset.

Object storage is in the same state the databases were: $spacebucket exists, the custody model and its disclosure exist, and std.space.attachBucket exists and is registered as unavailable, with the reason written into the startup log: no resolver reads an attached bucket, so every space resolves to the one configured store. The binary wires SingleStore, exactly as it wires SinglePool for databases.

Where storage genuinely differs, and where the requirements are told to answer rather than copy: S3 credentials carry more than a password (a region, an endpoint, a path style, possibly a role); the bytes and their references separate, since bytes live in the store and the sealed references live in the database, so a tenant with its own bucket and a shared database is a real configuration; the garbage sweep must reach every attached store and must never touch another tenant’s objects; key rotation writes a new object and leaves the old one until the sweep, which on a tenant’s own bucket is their storage bill and their deletion; export and import both move bytes; and bytes stored is a measured quantity, so the gap-not-zero ruling applies.

The increments must say which of them ship with a database increment rather than after it, because a tenant attaching both at once is the case that will actually happen.
suggest: Built together with the database increments where they overlap (the credential provider, the quarantine shape, the attach op, the operator surfaces), so the platform grows one mechanism for “this tenant keeps its things somewhere else” rather than two that drift.

asks.text: Nothing yet. Decisions will come back with the requirements.

where: U0 to U6 of docs/plan-tenant-storage.md are built: 408c5ad (U0, U1), 6a1c891 (U2), 5762f44 (U3), 52c32d5 (U4), e06f69b (U5), 6e15764 (U6, tests/attach_bucket.rs). Still owed under 18p: U7 failure modes (did not ship with T5), U8 sweep runner, U9 usage, U10 the record.

name: The first deployment is live
sub: Server up since 2026-09-20. Notes ran once about 2026-10-05; its page is not served today
explain:
Running in the cluster, synced by Argo from smg_infrastructure/ordo: the server, its own postgres:17 on a volume, the tunnel hostname, and configuration from Secret Manager. Readiness answers with the five checks that matter (database reachable, custody open, configuration present, workers running, schema creatable) and reports program_active: false as a fact rather than as a failure.

Four things it found that no test had. The deployment died on a timer, because serving was wrapped in a timeout meant for the shutdown drain. The binary could not create its own custody table on an empty database. The pods sat on a stale image, because a moving tag is not re-pulled. And the first release failed after every binary had built, on a provenance step that needs a GitHub plan this organisation does not have.

What is still needed before an app runs on it: a program deployed to it (ordo apply --host works now), a tenant with custody, and authentication switched on. Import is the remaining piece, and it goes over the wire next.

The instance is yours to poke at; it sits behind Cloudflare Access, so a browser works and a bare curl gets the login redirect.
suggest: Worth deploying a small real program to it next, because every serious defect this week came from running the thing rather than reading it.
where: The instance runs at ordo.inf.smg.icu from the external smg_infrastructure/ordo repo, v0.1.0 is tagged, and docs/deploying.md and docs/go-live.html describe it. Owed: a program deployed to it, a tenant with custody and authentication switched on (docs/go-live.html, 17ae).

name: Testing whether a human can actually use it
sub: Planned 2026-09-20 after a survey found no usability testing of any kind, and the one informal pass found a wall in the first five minutes
decided: Take recomendation.
explain:
A survey of what Ordo tests found deep coverage of behaviour and none at all of use: about 496 unit tests, a 100-case language corpus executed against real Postgres, 295 integration tests that spawn the real binary, and mocked tests for the JavaScript clients. Nothing measures whether a person can get through the path.

The evidence that this matters is recent. The quickstart was written on 2026-09-20 by an agent that ran every command rather than recalling them, and it hit a wall immediately: ordo dev handed the developer no usable token, so they could not call the op they had just written. The first five minutes of the product, invisible to 1,231 tests.

The plan has two halves. An automated walk of the documented path from a clean machine, asserting at each step that what a human needs is actually on screen: the command exists, the output names the next step, the token printed works, the error on the wrong path is legible. And a protocol a person runs with a real developer in under an hour, recording task success, time, assists, where they left the documented path and what they said, with a shortened Cognitive Dimensions questionnaire, which is the established framework for developer-tool usability rather than general interface usability.

Six increments, A to F: three need no participants, three need real people. The first target is a number for the first five minutes, from an empty directory to a callable op.
suggest: Build increments A and B (the automated walk) next, because they are cheap, repeatable and would have caught the token wall. The participant sessions are worth more per hour but cost scheduling, so they suit a moment when the path is stable rather than now, while it is changing daily.

asks.text: Two things worth your view when the first increments land: the first-five-minutes target (the plan proposes 90 seconds on CI hardware), and whether you want to sit in on the first participant session or read the transcripts.

where: The plan is written, docs/plan-usability-testing.md (737a219, 8f44c6c), and the owner took the recommendation. None of it is built: no automated quickstart walk exists under crates/*/tests and no sessions are recorded. Checklist 17x open.

name: One tenant can no longer take every connection
sub: Built 2026-09-20: a per-space share of the pool, a statement time bound, and metrics that name who is consuming it. Three named limits keep the item open
explain:
The audit’s heaviest finding, and true until today: one connection pool shared by every space, no time limit on a statement, and nothing in the metrics saying which tenant was responsible. One slow scan could hold every connection and hand everyone else a saturation error.

A share per space. A space can now take at most the pool minus a reserve, so some capacity is always left for everyone else. The starvation test was written first and run against the old pool, where one space took all four connections and another’s SELECT 1 was refused. That run is kept as a test arm, so the old behaviour stays visible rather than being deleted with the bug.

A statement bound (30 seconds by default, configurable, zero for none) refuses rather than hanging, with its own wire class at 503 instead of surfacing as a driver failure.

Attribution names the space in two counters, deliberately readable with per-space metrics switched off, because their population is the spaces that were refused rather than every space you have.

Found on the merge: the apply lock also waited 30 seconds, equal to the new statement bound, so which one fired was a coin flip and the losing side reported a driver failure instead of “an apply is already running”. Fixed by exempting that transaction from the bound.

Three limits are recorded: there is no fair queue, so several spaces at their caps can still reach the pool’s own bound; the cost gate still ignores indexes; and a tenant promoted to its own database is bounded but not yet attributed.
suggest: The reserve defaults to a quarter of the pool, which is the smallest thing that makes starvation impossible rather than unlikely. Revisit with a fair queue if a deployment ever runs enough tenants for the caps themselves to collide.
where: Built 2026-09-20 (930be66, 150a2af): per-space pool share and statement bound in crates/ordo-exec/src/lib.rs, attribution in crates/ordo-host/src/metrics.rs, tests/noisy_neighbour.rs, docs/deploying.md 2a. Owed under 20a: a fair queue across tenants, an index-aware cost gate, and the observer on AttachedPools.

name: Loading an existing application's data in
sub: v1 built 2026-09-20; the files leg and the door both landed 2026-09-26, so a customer can now get their data back IN through the deployment itself
explain:
Until today rows could only enter a space one call at a time, with nothing driving that, which a review called the single biggest obstacle to migrating a real application. v1 loads an export bundle through the ordinary write path, so every row gets its seals, its blind indexes, its guards and its place in the audit chain. Nothing bypasses the protocol, because rows written around it are rows the platform cannot read, verify or revert.

Batching is what makes it bearable: 199 rows a second one at a time, 3,705 a second in batches of a thousand, so a million rows is about four and a half minutes. It refuses rather than guesses on thirteen named conditions, including a bundle whose digest does not match, a field the schema does not have, a reference to a row that is not there, and a space that is not empty.

Two live defects it found on the way, both in code nothing had executed before, and both now fixed: creating a row in an entity with no key was refused every time, and a negative number could not be passed as a call argument at all. The negative-number fix went into the binder, where the read and write paths meet, so the workaround the write path carried is gone rather than duplicated. Each fix has its own test file.

Attachments come back too, 2026-09-26. Export has carried the actual files since the blob work landed, and import refused them in three places, so a space with a single attachment could be exported and could not be loaded, which is half a promise rather than a whole one. It now round-trips: the rows go in first, then each file is uploaded into the destination through the ordinary upload path a customer's own file takes, so it is re-encrypted under the destination space's own key, the row is version-bumped, and the upload is in the audit chain and can be reverted like any other write. The test exports a space with a file, loads it into an empty one, reads the file back out and checks byte for byte that it is the same file, with the same content digest recorded under a different key.

Nothing invents a second way to store a file. The importer asks the same door; that was a ruling, and three tests read the source code to keep it true.

One thing the bundle had to start recording: a file's type (“this is a PDF”). It was encrypted and stored beside the file, so a reader could not see it, and an import would have had to label every file “unknown binary”, a value the customer never chose. The bundle now names it, and only where the bundle actually holds the readable file, so an encrypted-only export still discloses nothing.

Refused rather than guessed: a bundle with files but no file storage wired, a file naming a row or a field that does not exist, bytes that do not match the digest the bundle recorded, and the three file kinds the upload door itself cannot serve (client-encrypted, stored-in-the-row, and encrypted-handle). A re-run after an interruption does not upload the same file twice.

Three follow-ups are filed: summarised import groups (cheaper chain for a large import), a CSV path for data from a system that is not Ordo (waits on the mapping file), and the separate question below about rows that point at people.
suggest:
What landed 2026-09-26. Until then the loader had no caller anywhere outside a test: reaching it needed a key, and the command-line tool has none and should never have one. So the import now runs on the deployment, which does hold the keys, and ordo import asks it to. An operator stages a bundle in the destination tenant's own directory and names it; the path is never supplied by the caller, because one staging area serves every tenant and each tenant's owner passes every check this operation has.

The bug the tests were written for is the quiet one. Sealing has to happen under the destination's keys, and the obvious way to wire it covers every read while leaving every write sealed under a key that is a constant in this repository. Nothing looks wrong: the rows are there, the audit chain is intact, and the sealed values cannot be opened by the tenant that now owns them. Breaking that line on purpose produces exactly that failure, which is why the line is now covered.

Still owed: getting a bundle to a hosted deployment at all, since staging one means filesystem access a tenant does not have, and the separate question filed beside this one about rows that point at people.

The bundle was the right input for v1: it already carries load order, per-entity encodings, row counts and digests, so export and import are inverses and a round trip is checkable. CSV needs a mapping file before it means anything.
where: Engine crates/ordo-exec/src/import.rs (v1 2026-09-20), blob leg 2fd819b (tests/import_blobs.rs), door std.space.import and ordo import d8e941c (tests/import_op.rs), people map 40645ac. Owed under 11-10a: delivering a bundle to a hosted deployment, and the foreign-system mapping file.

name: What happens to rows that point at people when a space is loaded
sub: Found by the attachment work 2026-09-26 and closed the same day: you took the recommendation, so an import now takes a people map the operator supplies and refuses any name it does not cover
decided: continue with - Platform refs
explain:
Almost every real application has rows that name a person: owner, assignee, author. Those columns point at the platform's own membership list, and the importer deliberately does not load membership, because a bundle that could create members would be a bundle that grants itself access to the space it is being loaded into. So the rows arrive, find no person to point at, and the whole import is refused by name on the first one.

That is the correct refusal and the wrong end state. It means the import path works today for reference data and for anything owned by nobody, and not for the ordinary case of a real application's data. It was found while building the attachment leg, is not an attachment problem, and is not something a mechanism can settle by itself: the honest answers all involve deciding who the people in the destination are.

The three candidates. (a) A people map supplied with the import. The operator says “this source person is that destination member”, the importer refuses any name it was not given. Honest, auditable, and real work for the operator. (b) Point everything at one member, named by the operator, usually the destination's founding owner. One line of work, and it silently rewrites authorship: every document in the imported space looks like it was created by the same person. (c) Create the missing people as members of the destination. Convenient and the one I would refuse outright: it lets a file decide who has access to a space.
suggest:
Built as recommended. An operator stages a small file beside the bundle saying which person in the old system is which person in the new one. Rows that name somebody land on the person named in that file; anybody the file does not cover stops the import with their name in the refusal, before a single row is written.

Two things it will not do, and both were the point. It cannot add people to the destination: naming somebody who is not already a member is refused, so a file can never hand out access. And it will not merge two old accounts into one person, because every reference to either would then point at the same person with nothing to show it happened. Merging is a decision to make in the old data where it is visible.

What an import decided is answerable later. The mapping is stored in the destination under the import's name, so months afterwards somebody can ask who a document was attributed to and why. Re-running with a different file is refused rather than applied, since half the rows would already be attributed the old way.

Still owed: group memberships do not survive an import and should not, for the same reason the map cannot add people, so they are rebuilt in the destination; and the file is per import, where a deployment-wide directory of known people would be the next step and needs its own decision.

(a), the supplied map, and refuse any name it does not cover. Authorship is part of the data, and an import that quietly reassigns it produces a space whose audit history is wrong in a way nobody can see afterwards. The operator already knows the mapping in every real migration, because they are the ones who onboarded those people into the destination. Until it is ruled, the refusal stays as it is: loud, by name, and blocking, which is better than any of the silent options.

asks.text: How should an imported row that names a person resolve: a supplied people map (a), everything onto one named member (b), or something else? (c), where the bundle creates the members, I would refuse whatever the convenience, because it makes a file a grant of access.

where: 40645ac: the people map in crates/ordo-exec/src/import.rs and crates/ordo-host/src/exit_ops.rs, tested in crates/ordo-host/tests/import_op.rs, documented in docs/plan-import.md section 12 and docs/migration.md.

name: Credentials and sessions survive a restart
sub: Built 2026-09-20: credentials, sessions and the directory all survive a restart, and the unsafe flag that stood in for the gap is gone
decided: Keep Both Agreed. Should be configurable to some degree - different info sec has different levels of compliance.
explain:
Enrolments used to live in memory, so every credential vanished on restart. They are now in the database, on the same pattern as key custody, and a store that cannot open refuses the boot rather than falling back to memory. Sessions gained the rest of their life: logout (a token stops working before it expires), refresh (a session continues without signing in again), and a revocation check the door consults on every request, costing a lock read and a set lookup rather than a query.

It also closed a timing oracle nobody had noticed: an unknown username did less work than a wrong password, which is measurable from outside. A decoy hash makes both cost the same, and the test that proves it was observed failing first.

The gap is closed, the same day. The directory is durable too, in two tables: one holding each identity once, one holding which login names which identity. Splitting them makes a duplicate identity a database constraint rather than a hope. Principal ids are now 128 random bits rather than a counter, so a restart cannot re-mint one that exists, and the store refuses a draw that collides rather than trusting the odds. The unsafe flag is deleted from the code, the boot census and both guides. Proved by tests that actually restart: an enrolled login still maps to its principal, and onboarding twice across a restart yields one identity, not two.
suggest: Keep both. Rotation buys stolen-token detection and costs a durable write per refresh plus a record of what superseded what, which is the session table this design deliberately does not have, and it turns a retry or a second browser tab into a surprise logout. Revisit if a compliance regime asks for it. An application still builds signup, password reset and email verification itself, and that is written down for whoever builds the first one.

asks.text: Two calls, both defaulted and configurable: a session of 1 hour with a 12 hour ceiling, and refresh that does not rotate the token. Keep both?

where: fbe002c and b53dad6: PgDirectoryStore in crates/ordo-host/src/principal_directory.rs, durable credentials and revocations in credentials.rs, tested by crates/ordo-host/tests/auth_durability.rs; ORDO_AUTH_UNSAFE_MEMORY_DIRECTORY removed. Recorded in corpus-rulings.md and 20b.

name: Schema evolution
sub: Increment 2 built 2026-09-20 and the apply belongs to the service: a first apply creates the schema, later applies send safe additive changes, and everything else is refused by name. Increments 3 to 5 (backfills, constraints, destructive) remain
decided: Approve I think that the audit line should split and a summary should be created - the idea is that the data integrity is guaranteed so data before = data now in a different structure.
explain:
Increment 1 landed, finished and audited after the original agent died. Both defects are fixed and proved: a schema-only change now moves deploy identity (the artifact carries defaults, normalize, enum values, composite uniques and indexes, and the version hashes the DDL too — so the next omission moves the version anyway), and the drift gate now sees constraints, including the NULLS NOT DISTINCT half down to its consequence. ordo plan --against prints the classified report with probes and freeze estimates, and refuses (exit 1) when any probe is non-empty. The finishing review found four defects in the inherited code — the sharpest: a sealed indexed field losing only indexed left its blind-index column live and invisible to every future report. Your audit-line answer is NOT yet recorded anywhere, and the plan still contradicts it — see the separate Backfill audit encoding question below, which is the thing blocking increment 3. Increments 2+ are checklist §13b–13e.

ddl_for emits CREATE TABLE from scratch. No diff, no ALTER beyond creation-time constraints, no backfill anywhere. DL §9 settles it; the write barrier is settled; neither is built. The shape gate makes it bite — it refuses any boot whose database disagrees with its compiler.

A 767-line build plan now exists (plan-schema-evolution.md). It recommends expand-contract in place, not blue/green: the audit chain would fork, there is no per-space table so a copy is a whole-deployment copy, and live_drift is already deliberately one-way — extra columns are not drift — which is the property expand-contract needs.

Planning found two defects: a schema-only change is a silent no-op deploy (the artifact carries no unique_keys, indexes, defaults, normalize or enum_values, so adding unique (a,b) yields identical bytes and is discarded while the operator is told “already present”); and live_drift reads only columns, so every constraint change is invisible to the gate.
suggest:
Approve it. The two defects must be fixed first regardless — the no-op deploy is dangerous on its own.

On the backfill question: full images for now. It must be settled before increment 3, because the barrier and cursor work against either answer, but the group encoding cannot change afterwards without moving every chain hash it wrote.

asks.text:
Approve the expand-contract shape and start increment 1 (the read-only ordo plan --against <db>, plus fixing the two defects)?

Separately: what does a transforming backfill write into the audit spine? Full per-row images are correct and revertible but produce a log larger than the data. Summarised groups are settled only for creates — a backfill is all converges, whose before image is the only record of what the value was.

name: Triggers & routines
sub: Routines built; each-> bodies and the producers owed
explain:
A routine runs ops on a schedule or when data changes, in every tenant, recorded as its own actor.

  • routine name { trigger every 15m run(...): writes }
  • Or trigger when shop.orders.created
  • Paused tenants are skipped unless the routine says nopause
suggest:
Wire them now, behind an explicit flag on ordo serve, defaulting to on for a single-node deployment. The reasoning is the same one that put the authorization bound in with the mechanism: a subsystem that is fully built and never runs decays silently — nobody notices a regression in code no deployment executes, and the tests that cover each step in isolation will keep passing while the composition rots.

The flag matters because clock leadership is an advisory lock and a multi-pod operator may want the loops on a dedicated pod. But the default should be that a trigger you wrote fires, because the alternative is a feature that is documented, tested, shipped and inert — which is worse than one that is absent, since only the absent one is honest.

asks.suggest: Yes, next. Most real jobs (expire leases, send reminders) read rows and act on each; ellanor's approval and automation sweeps need it.

asks.text: When a routine is first deployed into a tenant with history, should it act on past changes or only new ones?
asks.suggest: Only new ones, the default as built. Replaying history surprises people; an app developer can backfill once with a one-off op if they want the past handled.

name: Retiring a listener leaves a cursor that pins the log forever
sub: Built 2026-09-30: ordo triggers ls and ordo triggers deregister
decided: Take Recommendation
explain:
The mechanism, and why it is right. Every trigger listener a deployment serves gets a cursor row in $logconsumers, and that cursor pins the pruning floor: the command log cannot be trimmed past the oldest thing any listener has not yet read. That is at-least-once delivery seen from the other side, and the cursor kind is deliberately non-evictable, because evicting one and resuming it at the current floor would silently turn at-least-once into zero-times.

The consequence. A deploy that renames or deletes a listener leaves an immortal cursor pinning a log nobody will ever read. The log stops shrinking, and the reason is a listener that no longer exists.

What is built. The supervisor reports and does not act: orphaned cursors — registered, non-evictable, and not present in the live program — are listed on /health/deep with their positions and how long they have been idle, and ordo prune’s floor report already names the holder. The obvious fix is ruled out and stays ruled out: a supervisor that deregistered cursors on swap would, during a rolling deploy, have a replica on the new version silently reset the guarantee of a listener a replica on the old version is still serving.

What is missing is the spelling of the operator act. Removing a cursor today means prune::deregister_consumer, which is a Rust function with no command in front of it, so the honest instruction to an operator is “read prune.rs”.
suggest:
My recommendation: yes, and route it through the door like every other act that changes a deployment (your 2026-09-20 ruling), with the database path as named break-glass.

Two reasons it is worth the command rather than leaving it at the function. First, the act is destructive to a guarantee, not to data: it says “stop promising at-least-once for this listener”, and an act like that should be impossible to perform without recording who performed it — which is exactly what --as is for and what a bare function call cannot give. Second, the alternative in practice is not “an operator reads prune.rs”; it is an operator whose log will not shrink writes raw SQL against $logconsumers, which removes the row with no record and no refusal if they name the wrong one.

It is small: the report, the refusal (a listener that is in the live program is not an orphan and must be refused by name) and the attribution all exist. I have not built it, because §3.7 marks it [proposed] and the corresponding row is here rather than in the code. Say the word and it is one increment.

asks.text: Add ordo triggers deregister <listener> --as <who>, so the one act that removes a floor-pinning cursor has a name and an attribution?

name: Conformance corpus
sub: Your go recorded: GC007 fixed in code, GC048 edited to follow GC080, GC083 left
decided: Implement the fix - I will take your suggestion.
explain:
The central assurance mechanism: cases transcribed from the specs, executed against real Postgres with rows asserted. The document is the authority and the test transcribes it — a test written from the implementation agrees with whatever the code does, including whatever it does wrong.

A divergence is where document and implementation disagree, asserted as the implementation behaves so the entry fails the moment anyone fixes it. I wrote docs/corpus.md describing all of this; it did not exist.
suggest: Fix GC007 in code — guard stacking on a dot-path is genuinely unimplemented and the fixture hides it. GC048 needs your ruling; the two documents cannot both be right. Leave GC083 — same facts, different words, and forcing it churns the manifest for nothing.

asks.text: You said: implement the fix, taking my suggestion. Recorded as: fix GC007 in code (a dot-path target’s read guard must inline; the fixture hid that it does not); settle GC048 by editing the case, since the engine already follows GC080’s post-pruning rule and the document has to stop listing level among cardList’s guard reads; leave GC083 as vocabulary. Small, self-contained, and suitable for a cheaper agent; it is first in the queue below the runtime because it needs no process to run in.

name: Effective cost class
sub: Closed as 11-8 — but no refinement can reach the door in a real deployment
decided: Execute.
explain:
Landed as 11-8, both halves, proved against real Postgres. One cost model extended rather than a second one invented: CostClass::join, refine_field_class and refine_candidate_bound. That last function is the whole finding in one place — row_bound answers what a plan RETURNS, and a refinement is applied to what it EXAMINES. For a row-shaped op the two agree; for a keyless reduce they do not, and that gap is the exploit: count returns one row, registers with no acknowledgment, and refines before the reduce over the entire space. refinement_unbounded came off the “specified but not built” list, which is now empty.

Ops are gated at registration for cost. A refinement is a per-request narrowing a caller supplies, and it can raise an op's cost past what it was registered for — so the request's effective class must be recomputed. Before this: two documents settled that it must be, and nothing computed it.
suggest:
Add the marker — it is one declaration keyword and it is the difference between a shipped feature and a shipped simulation of one. Everything downstream is built: the tier check, the manifest validation, all three sealed rules, the cost join, the refusal class, and now the interface descriptor which stamps outputs[].refinable so a generated client can see which fields accept a condition.

The reason to do it now rather than later is the artifact: adding a declaration moves every op version and kills every capability grant pinned to them — 14a just spent that cost, and spending it twice for two markers is worse than spending it once.

Do not build host-side filtering with it. Write the disclosure rule first. A refinement the executor applies host-side reads rows the caller never asked for, and the whole point of the cost class is that examining is not returning.

asks.text:
The gate is built and nothing can reach it. There is no op-level refinable marker in the language, so every op registers RefineTier::None and every refinement in a real deployment is refused before the cost model is consulted. “Nothing is refinable that the op author didn’t ship” is honoured by shipping nothing.

Two more from the same item: the effective class is computed, enforced and not traced (there is no tracing substrate to hang ordo.cost_class on), and the executor ignores $refine entirely — the envelope is validated, priced, and handed to an executor that does not apply it. That last is 5c's host-side filtering, deliberately unbuilt because it would examine rows the caller never asked for and needs a disclosure rule nobody has written.

Add the op-level marker to the language, or leave refinement dormant?

where: Checklist 11-8 closed: crates/ordo-plan/src/cost.rs (refine_candidate_bound); refinement is served by crates/ordo-host/src/refine_call.rs (27am); tests crates/ordo-plan/tests/refine_cost.rs, crates/ordo-host/tests/cost_class.rs. Corrected by audit-2026-10-09 finding 23

name: Security event stream
sub: 7d(a) and (b) built 2026-09-26: the verifier, the owner-facing read surface, and the signer on its own cadence. Found that retention had been signing unverified heads, which let a prune launder a tamper. Still owed: (c) the dashboard explorer
decided: Execute your suggested rollout.
explain:
Landed. The stream now drains to storage on a background task wired into the deployment assembly, so the door’s own denials land in $secevents. Unreachable store: drop, bounded, and declare the drop inside the record — a hashed EventsDropped link, because a counter in a process about to restart is not visibility, while a gap declared inside the artifact a reviewer audits is. Cost: ~1.0 µs per denial, no I/O on the request path; growth is per collapsed window, not per request, so a scanner firing 100k times costs one entry. Quiet deployment ~20 MB/month; denial-heavy ~200 MB/month. Two real defects found: a per-request O(n) scan under the recorder mutex that was dearest under a denial storm, and a fully-pruned stream that would have verified green from genesis.

Records every authorization decision — denials, step-ups, token failures — with correlation back to the command. Chain, verifier, store and deny-volume alert monitor all shipped.
suggest:
The verifier is built, 2026-09-26, and it is one command with two answers. ordo verify --space <spc> walks both artifacts and prints the stream as its own paragraph with its own VERIFIED/FAILED line; ordo verify --deployment walks the deployment scope, which belongs to no space and has no command chain beside it. Neither half short-circuits the other, and the direction that matters is the unobvious one: a broken command chain must not stop the stream being checked, because the stream exists to be the thing you can still believe after the domain record is in doubt.

Four checks, and the fourth is the one a chain walk structurally cannot do. Nothing was pruned to nothing; the anchor is genesis or a signed checkpoint at exactly the base; the stored suffix recomputes; and nothing was removed from the end — because deleting the last N entries leaves a perfectly self-consistent chain, and only a marker signed at a higher position knows they were ever there.

A run with no key is a narrower claim and now says so rather than printing a bare green line. It also needed a new variable: the command chain has published its verifying key separately from its signing seed since the beginning, and this stream had only the seed — so there was no way to name the key without also handing over the ability to forge, which is a small part of why nothing ever verified it.

Two defects found on the way, neither in the stream itself. The store’s verify_from bridges through block_on, so calling it from async — the obvious way to write this — would have panicked on the first stream with an entry in it. And a corrupt entry was reported as index 0: the read fails the whole 512-entry window and its error carries no position. The command chain deliberately does better, and a second artifact with a worse diagnostic is one nobody can act on. Both fixed.

I said here that nothing in production signed a stream checkpoint. That was wrong, and the truth was worse. Step 1 of the retention pass signed one, reachable whenever the security key is set. So three things were wrong rather than one missing: the marker’s cadence was retention’s (six hours, a storage sweep setting an evidence window), its enabling condition was retention’s (retain: false, an ordinary “keep everything” choice, silently switched truncation detection off), and it signed a head nothing had verified.

That last one is the serious one. A checkpoint is the only lawful cut point, and check_prune is handed the head at the cut point — it never walks the prefix it destroys. So an unverified signature at the head licenses the next retention pass to delete the very entries that prove the stream was edited: the prefix goes, the survivors chain cleanly from a marker carrying the deployment’s own signature, and ordo verify reports VERIFIED. Retention laundering a tamper, on schedule, as designed. Closed below.

The read surface is built too, 2026-09-26 — your rollout’s step 2. GET /security/events?space=&from=&limit=, on its own reserved name, and the gate is the whole of it: every other route on that router authorizes against the deployment’s own space because every other route is an operator surface, and reusing that would have produced a route that returns data, passes a naive test, and still leaves an owner unable to read their own denials. It binds the space the caller named, so a tenant owner reads their own space and nothing else. A deployment operator does not thereby gain read of every tenant’s stream, which follows §6.1’s split.

It also routes, and that is not a convenience. S4 sends each space’s entries to that space’s own database, so reading a routed tenant’s stream from the control pool finds nothing — and for a security surface “nothing” renders as your space has recorded no denials. A clean bill of health for a stream nobody looked at is the worst answer it could give, so an unwired process refuses instead of answering an empty page.

A break failed to fail and that is the useful part. Deleting the refusal of the reserved $deployment key left the test passing, because the access check refuses it anyway — nobody holds a membership in a space by that name. So the test was proving the refusal, not the guard. A membership row is a row, though, and if one ever named that key the access check would allow and the explicit refusal is all that stands between a tenant and the cross-space sweep. The test now grants exactly that membership and requires the route to refuse anyway.

The signer is built too, 2026-09-26. secevent.checkpoint: its own schedule row, its own one hour (the attestation cadence’s number and argument, not the checkpoint month’s — this artifact has no second series beside it to close the gap), leader-only so a fleet signs once per period, and gated on the key alone so a retention choice can no longer switch it off. It verifies first and signs the pair the walk itself arrived at, which is a stronger promise than the command chain’s own signer makes and needs no append lock to make it: the signed head is the walk’s last observation, so nothing can commit between verifying and signing. Retention’s step 1 now delegates to it, and a refusal there stops the cut as well as the signature. Five named refusals, each a state where a signature makes matters worse.

ordo checkpoint --security (--space | --deployment) is the operator’s door; refusals exit 3, the verification-failed code, because you asked to sign and were handed a verification finding. ordo verify now catches entries deleted from the end of a stream end to end, with no hand-built marker.

Still owed: (c) the dashboard explorer, which consumes the read surface. Two follow-ups this surfaced are on the board as secevent-key-rotation.

Original recommendation:

Do the verifier first, and make it one command with two answers. ordo verify should walk both chains and report them separately — a merged verdict hides which artifact moved, and which one moved is the whole diagnosis. It is a small piece of work against machinery that is entirely built; the only reason it was missed is that §7 closed on the drainer and the cost audit, which were the loud halves.

Then the read surface, space-scoped and gated on its own reserved op name the way /security/alerts already is. Naming a suspect is a different disclosure from publishing a counter, and that distinction was already made once here — it should be made the same way again.

The dashboard explorer waits on the read surface and is not urgent: it is a nicer view of something nobody can see yet.

asks.text:
A coverage audit on 2026-09-07 found two things this row was calling done, and they are the two that make the artifact worth having.

1. Nothing verifies the stream. ordo-secevent has verify_stream and verify_stream_from; the stream is hash-chained, checkpointed, and signed under its own key with its own domain tag. And ordo-cli does not mention the security stream anywhere — ordo verify walks the command chain only. So the verifier exists and no command, route or job has ever called it. The argument for the second key was that one key would mean “compromising the attestation key is also the ability to forge the record of the compromise”; that argument only pays out if something checks.

2. No owner can read their own space’s security events. §6.1’s members-only routing rule exists precisely so that a space owner sees the denials in their space. The only route is /security/alerts, which serves the deny-volume monitor’s firings — not the stream. There is no read surface at all.

Both are now checklist 7d. Confirm the priority?

where: 7d(a) verifier ecddae6, 7d(b) route /security/events 9b07bd6 (crates/ordo-host/src/serve.rs), signer 65cdc7c (crates/ordo-exec/src/secevent.rs). Owed: 7d(c) the dashboard explorer; 17m open.

name: F7 client-first vault
sub: Future roadmap, the pinnacle: client-first as an option, to compete with Jazz (owner 2026-10-10)
decided: Okay continue and execute including the enforcement required. At the end of the day the app developer will chose how he wants to handle the specific thing but we should build a scaffold they can use.
explain:
Where this actually stands, so the pill is not read as progress. Your reasoning is recorded as f7-vault-plan.md §5.3, RULED — schema migration under client-first custody is settled. Not one line of F7 is built (checklist 5g, planned, not started): nine phases, 26–36 agent sessions plus 8–12 of prerequisites, and phase 4 — the deterministic evaluator — is a third of the work and carries all the schedule risk. Twelve open protocol questions each carry a recommendation, and Q7 is a defect in the spec: the snapshot state_digest is defined over sealed bytes while seals use a fresh random nonce, so two devices with identical state produce different digests — the field cannot do the job it exists for.

Client-first custody: the server holds ciphertext it cannot read. The most architecturally invasive item outstanding, because it changes what the server can referee — with client-first custody the server cannot evaluate a guard over a sealed value, so it stops being the referee for that part of the model.
suggest:
Proceeding as you directed. Here is what I will build and the three things I will not let stay implicit.

Caveat 1 — the migration script is code the server hands the client, and the whole point of a client-first vault is not trusting the server. This is the one that actually matters. A compromised server could ship a “migration” that re-encrypts under an attacker key, or copies a sealed field into an open one, and the client would run it because migrations are supposed to be routine. My recommendation: the migration must be expressed in Ordo’s own closed expression grammar, not arbitrary code. We are unusually well placed for this — the grammar already has no I/O, no loops and no way to name a destination, so a client can read the migration and verify what it does before running it. A migration that cannot be expressed in that grammar is refused rather than escalated to something more powerful. This is the same instinct behind refusing a check we cannot lower honestly.

Caveat 2 — not every migration is content-free, and the exception is uniqueness. Adding unique (a, b) requires knowing that no two rows collide, which is a fact about values. But we already have the tool: a blind index is an HMAC over the sealed value, and the server can compare those for equality without reading either one. So equality-uniqueness is checkable server-side — provided the field carries a blind index, which becomes a precondition on that migration class. Ordering constraints (a range check, a < comparison) remain uncheckable, and should be refused rather than approximated.

Caveat 3 — “other clients MUST update” needs teeth, or it is a wish. A client that never returns leaves rows on the old shape forever, and a client running old code against a new shape writes rows that are wrong in a way nobody notices. The mechanism I would build is a schema floor: the space records the minimum shape version it accepts, and the server refuses writes from any client below it, by class, naming the version. An old client then fails loudly instead of corrupting quietly — the same reason the deploy path refuses rather than degrades. Reads can stay permissive longer than writes; it is writes that do damage.

What I have started. The schema-evolution agent now carries an instruction to add a section naming the client-first case and your reasoning for it, so the two plans agree rather than each assuming the other. Device sync for client-first vaults is a genuine gap in f7-vault-plan.md and I am recording it as its own item rather than letting it hide inside “migration” — it is a distinct problem (getting a key and a shape version to a device that is not here) from transforming rows.

asks.text:
Your reasoning, and my assessment of it. You made three claims. Two are right and one needs a mechanism that does not exist yet.

1. “Schema change is not content specific it is schema specific.” Correct, and it is the sentence that unblocks this. I had been treating vault migration as impossible because the server cannot read values. But a schema migration is a transformation authored against the shape, and the shape is public — the server knows every entity, field and type, because the developer declared them. Adding a field, widening a type, renaming, splitting one field into two: none of these need to know what any particular row says. So the server can compute the transformation and hand it over without ever opening a payload. That is the right shape and I was wrong to file it as blocked.

2. “The schema is changed by the dev not the tenant.” Right, and it is why this is tractable at all. There is exactly one authority for the shape, versioned, and every client can be told which version it is on. That is already how deploy identity works.

3. “They already would have it synced to their other devices.” This one does not hold yet. You asked me to check, so I did: f7-vault-plan.md mentions multi-device only in passing (“every enrolled device holds the space key”), and §5 Migration covers migration along the custody dial — managed ↔ client-first, chunked re-encryption with per-chunk checkpoints — not schema migration under client-first custody, and not device sync at all. Every enrolled device can decrypt, but nothing pushes a change to the others. So “other clients MUST update” is a requirement with no enforcement behind it, and that is the piece to build.

where: Owed: all of F7, nine phases in docs/f7-vault-plan.md (26 to 36 agent sessions plus 8 to 12 of prerequisites; Phase 4, the deterministic evaluator, a third of the work and most of the risk; twelve protocol questions open). Checklist 5g planned, not started. The client cache (5g-pre) is built. Status summary in docs/plan-offline.md §0.

name: Multi-device sync for vault spaces
sub: Your go recorded: form 2 through the oplog, plus the content-blind broadcast for liveness
decided: Okay execute form 2 as per your suggestion.
explain:
In a client-first vault the server holds ciphertext it cannot read, so every change has to be applied by a client that holds the key. f7-vault-plan.md §3.2 enrolls each device with the space key, so any of them can decrypt. But nothing pushes anything to a device that is not currently present — there is no mechanism by which your laptop learns that your phone changed something, or that the schema moved.

This surfaced only because you assumed it existed. Your answer on the vault said “they already would have it synced to their other devices”, and you asked me to check. I did, and it does not — §5 Migration covers the custody dial (managed ↔ vault) and device sync appears nowhere. I have recorded it as §5.4 rather than letting it stay an assumption.
suggest:
My recommendation: form 2, via the oplog the plan already has — plus exactly the broadcast you described for liveness.

“Live” features are not dead. Your instinct at the end is the right mechanism: a device that appends to the oplog triggers a content-blind notification — “space X advanced to sequence N”, nothing more — over the invalidation bus we already run. Connected devices hear it, pull the new segments, decrypt locally, update the UI. That is precisely what Jazz-style sync is under the hood: notify-then-pull over an encrypted log. The server learns nothing it did not already know (it assigned the sequence number itself), and latency is one round trip worse than plaintext live — imperceptible.

Form 1 still has one honest job: device enrollment — getting the space key to a new device — genuinely needs either a device-to-device ceremony or the recovery phrase, and §3.2 already covers that. Data sync never needs both devices online; key handoff does, once per device.

On tenant choice: agreed it is tenant-scoped — but as policy on one mechanism (how long the server retains segments, whether live notify is on), not as two mechanisms. Two sync paths means two consistency stories and double the verification surface, for no capability form 2 lacks.

If this reads right to you, I will fold it into f7-vault-plan.md §5.4 as the settled sync design — oplog pull + content-blind notify, enrollment as the only device-to-device moment, retention as the tenant dial.

asks.text:
Your two forms, taken seriously:

Form 1 — state check + server-brokered device-to-device sync. The server holds only a schema/state hash; when a device is behind, the server opens a connection between devices and they sync directly. You named its own flaw: “let us keep a state and have both devices online” — a phone in a drawer can never catch up from a laptop that is asleep. Rendezvous sync dies on the empty intersection of online windows, which for personal devices is most of the day.

Form 2 — an E2E copy that gets blasted as it changes. Here is the good news: this is already the F7 architecture. The vault design’s oplog IS a sequence of end-to-end-encrypted, signed records that the server stores and orders without being able to read them (“content-blind sequencing”, Phase 3). Sync is not a second mechanism — it is a device pulling the oplog segments it has not seen and replaying them locally. And your overhead worry dissolves: there is no duplicate full copy, because the encrypted oplog is not a copy of the primary — it IS the primary. The server was going to hold exactly these bytes anyway.

where: Owed: form 2 sync through the F7 oplog (f7-vault-plan.md §5.4). Waits on the vault (5g). No mechanism tells one device that another changed something. docs/plan-offline.md §0.

name: CI & image pipeline
sub: Green, and the gates are proved: a drill broke each one on purpose on 2026-09-20 and all twelve failed as they should. Owed: the first v* release run
decided: Fix and execute what is required.
explain:
The plan you asked for is written (docs/plan-ci-images.md) with the workflow files and Dockerfiles committed as proposals — manual-trigger only, so they appear in the Actions tab and run on a button press, never otherwise. Shape: a CI workflow (fmt, clippy, full suite against a postgres:17 service, the corpus’s executed-case assertion tightened, the inventory checks as separately named steps so a red direction is legible); an images workflow (three images — host and cli on distroless, playground on slim because it shells out to the psql binary — cargo-chef layer caching, multi-arch, GHCR, content digest as the identity rhyming with deploy identity); a release workflow (CLI tarballs, checksums, provenance). No secrets needed — GHCR uses the built-in token.

The smoke gate is the good part: the built image boots against Postgres before anything publishes, and the host check distinguishes three meanings — 403 on /health/deep = mounted and gated (pass), 404 = router never mounted, 200 = the gate is missing and an anonymous caller just read custody identity out of the image.
suggest: Recommended order: (1) the ordo-host binary (0a); (2) commit Cargo.lock; (3) flip ci-proposed.yml to replace the live ci.yml (five improvements including the executed-case fix — the current assertion would stay green if the case it names were deleted); (4) enable the images workflow. Ruled out with reasons in the plan: images on every PR, conformance inside the image build (“a cached RUN cargo test is a test result nobody ran”), CD, a Helm chart before the key providers exist.

asks.text:
One real blocker surfaced: there is no deployable server binary. ordo-host is a library returning an axum Router — no main.rs, no [[bin]]; the only thing in the workspace that binds a port is the playground. So “image building” found that the product ships no server to put in an image. The plan’s increment 0a is writing that binary (config from env, the Router mounted, graceful shutdown). Approve building it? It is small and everything else in the pipeline waits behind it.

Two more findings worth your eyes: Cargo.lock is gitignored — without it, image digests are not reproducible and dependency drift lands silently (recommendation: commit it; it is a binary-producing workspace, the ecosystem convention agrees); and ordo-conformance compiles into the deployable (it is a normal dependency of ordo-host/ordo-exec, so the test harness and its psql shell-out ship in the server) — recorded as a finding, unscheduled.
