name: The runtime: binary, keys, supervisor
sub: R1–R4 done 2026-09-19: the binary, custody, the supervisor, platform ops, and CI images that boot-test it on every push. The image smoke found one last binary bug (a fresh database), now fixed
decided: GO with everything needed. But if it is just a library how are we handling the storage and such?Something needs to execute things, triggers, key rotation all of that must exist on some backend.
explain:
State on 2026-09-18. An agent built R2a, R2c, R1 and R2b on 2026-09-07 and died partway into R3; its branch sat unmerged until today. It is now on main, resolved toward the multi-space host main built in the meantime (one shared space resolver for the op path and the blob door). 846 tests pass across the seven affected crates, including 7 that spawn the real binary. This also closes a defect on main: the served write path had been sealing under the test key published in this repository while reads used the real provider; R2a makes loading install the operator’s custody and asserts it. The R3 review (2026-09-18) found most of the worker set built and one serious gap: leadership is claimed once at boot and never retried, so if the leader replica dies, no other replica takes over its clock, checkpoint, attestation and prune work. Also missing: the security-event retention worker, the security drain as a supervised worker, the orphaned-cursor report, and tests for quarantine and for the door staying live through a panic. All five were built the same day and each has a test: two supervisors on one database hand leadership over when the leader stops or its lock session is killed; the retention worker claims its schedule once per period; orphaned cursors and dead letters are listed on /health/deep; a worker quarantined after ten failures shows enabled: false while /health/live keeps answering 200 over a real socket. The failover test also found a startup bug (leader-only workers idled 5s at boot), now fixed. Re-audited 2026-09-26. The re-seal and usage slots are filled (K1, M1); per-worker tick overrides (ORDO_WORKER_<NAME>_TICK_MS) are now read, and an unreadable one refuses the boot rather than defaulting silently. The audit also found two defects nobody had a test for, both of them a supervisor doing nothing without saying so: the shutdown path never ran (it needed sole ownership of a handle /health/deep also holds, so every worker kept running through shutdown, no final act fired, and the usage rollup dropped its partial period on every restart), and the tenant reconciler was registered behind a trigger-listener condition no deployment meets, so it ran nowhere and the census named it neither running nor disabled. A provision that died half way therefore stayed provisioning instead of turning failed and appearing in the operator's troubled pane. Both fixed. Still open inside R3: a real run handler (12a). Platform ops, 2026-09-18: the binary now serves std.space.callersOf (owner only, proved against the spawned process), the exit ops when ORDO_EXIT_BUNDLE_DIR is set, and the attestation ops when the checkpoint key is. They read the live access engine, so a swap no longer leaves them answering from a stale copy, and a swap that would shadow a reserved name is refused. std.space.attachBucket stays unregistered until something reads attached buckets. Remaining: serve the platform ops from the binary, then R4 (CI images).

The single biggest BaaS gap: there is no server. ordo-host is a library; nothing binds a port; the only key provider is a test constant — and the plan’s survey found sealing ignores the provider it is handed (hardcoded at program load), so custody-into-loading (R2a) is the first increment, before the binary itself. docs/plan-runtime.md (1,915 lines) covers it: R2a custody injection → R2c the Postgres key store → R1 the binary (env config, graceful shutdown, health) → R2b the sealed-file master + ceremony → R3 the worker supervisor (the loops for triggers, clock, secevents, prune — all built, nothing calls them) → R4 CI flipped live.
suggest: Recommended as the next build after the in-flight items (attestation, blob) land — the blob store and attestation worker both want R3’s supervisor to ride on, so the sequencing is natural.

asks.text:
You said: go with everything needed. And: if it is just a library, how are we handling storage and such? Something needs to execute things: triggers, key rotation, all of that must exist on some backend.

That is exactly what this plan builds, and your question is its table of contents. Today ordo-host is a library that returns a router, and nothing in the workspace binds a socket to it. R1 makes it a process: the ordo serve binary that reads its configuration from the environment, authenticates the pool to Postgres, loads the active program, and serves the door. Storage is Postgres for everything the chain and the rows hold, reached through that pool, plus the object store for blob bytes (the blob-store row above is one of R1’s variables). R2 gives that process a production key provider instead of the constant test key. R3 is the backend you are asking about: the worker supervisor, long-running tasks inside the same process that drain the trigger queue, fire clocks, run key rotation (17i), reference GC, the attestation outbox and the security stream, with clock leadership as an advisory lock so a multi-pod deployment runs each loop once. R4 wires CI so the image job stops probing for a binary that does not exist.

Not started yet. This is the largest build on the board and it is several heavy agents in sequence (R1, then R2 and R3, then R4). I have not launched it from a decisions-file read alone; say “start the runtime” and R1 begins.

where: crates/ordo-host/src/supervisor.rs, crates/ordo-exec/src/keystore.rs, crates/ordo-host/tests/runtime.rs; checklist 17a, 17c, 17d closed (5dad4ed, 76226fe).

name: Sharing: guests, windows and share links
sub: Guests and share links built 2026-09-29. Guest writes are after deployment (18ab)
decided: Answered in conversation 2026-09-29. 1: yes, a guest's acceptance is recorded in the sharer's log and the deployment's security log. 2: share links on by default with 7 days as the default expiry, and no maximum: "not enforced by us". 3: a guest writing is planned for after the first deployment; shares are read-only until then.
explain:
Sharing is planned. A window and membership in several tenants turn out to be one mechanism with different defaults.

  • Default: a guest. They read what the sharer shared, through a window. Nothing is copied.
  • Household finances: both people are members of one tenant.
  • Share links open without an account, read only, and expire.

The plan is docs/plan-sharing.md.

One seat, two kinds of authority. A person has one seat in the sharer's tenant. As a guest, the seat reaches only what was shared. As a member, it reaches what the role allows. Changing the role turns a guest into a member.

One thing it overturns: today a seat with no role is treated as a viewer and can read everything a viewer can. The plan makes it a guest, who reads only what was shared. This is the first step of the build.

A share link can never: write, act as anyone, reach another tenant, share onward, or outlive its expiry. It works as a guest seat nobody owns.

Guests first, then links. Feeds (copies) stay later: they need triggers and routines that do not exist yet.
suggest: Recommendation unchanged: Option A, grant-shaped, no syntax — it closes four spec silences for free (expiry, either-side revocation, expansion-kills-share, one consent prompt) and its enforcement half already passes real-Postgres tests; only registration is missing. Say “A” (or B/C) and the build starts.

asks.text: Where is a guest's acceptance recorded: the sharer's log plus the deployment's security log?
asks.suggest: Yes, both. The guest may have no tenant of their own, so their tenant's log cannot always hold it.

asks.text: Share links for people with no account: on by default, 7 days by default, 30 days at most?
asks.suggest: Yes, and the app developer can change all three. A link is a bearer secret, so it must always expire.

asks.text: May a sharer let a guest write, not only read?
asks.suggest: Yes, when the sharer chooses it, and only through ops that check guards. Never for an open link. Until you answer, shares are read-only.

where: share_ops.rs, share_accept.rs, share_links.rs; routes /auth/share/*, /auth/window, /auth/link; the blob door runs the token gate; SDK auth/share.ts (openLink). Plan: docs/plan-sharing.md. Owed: 18ab.

name: Export & space deletion
sub: Built; your emphasis on dynamic export is how it was built: the bundle is derived from the schema, so it changes with the data
decided: Yes plan and build it - put extra emphasis on making sure it is dynamic and flexible and the code can change with the flexibility of the data it is exporting otherwise we'll have to modify the export code for every change - it should be dynamic. (at least from how I'm viewing this ask)
explain:
Landed, and dynamic the way you demanded — enforced in four places, not promised: one function is the single answer to “which columns does this table have”, the bundle’s schema and artifact are the deployment’s own stored bytes, value encoding is an exhaustive match with no wildcard arm (a new field flows through free; a new scalar type in the language fails the build until someone decides its JSON), and a test exports, adds an entity + field, exports again — asserting the new data appears AND the untouched entities are byte-identical. The bundle: manifest, schema.sql, artifact.json, per-entity JSONL, and the command log with both chain hashes per group so anyone can re-verify the chain without us. Deletion destroys the SMK as well as the DEKs — DEKs alone would leave “was the value X?” answerable through surviving blind indexes. Sealed fields follow migration.md §6: owner-authorized open mode or declared-ciphertext mode; an unopenable value refuses rather than nulls. Blob bytes wait on blob custody, declared machine-readably in the manifest. Five finds on the way — the sharpest: a pooled connection leaked its search_path, which in production would have made an unrelated later query read from an empty shadow schema, correctly typed, no error anywhere.

Full space export and space deletion — owner-only, step-up gated, command-logged. Settled in migration.md §6, which is the one settled section in an otherwise proposed document.

licensing.md makes this leg one of a three-leg trust argument: the case for trusting the platform rests partly on being able to leave it. Before this: no row, no code.
suggest:
Put the BYO-DB sentence on the consent page before the next remainder is built. It costs a paragraph and it is the difference between a disclosed limit and a false claim — and this one has a legal shape, because “we deleted your data” is the sentence customers repeat to their regulators. Proposed wording: on a database you operate, deletion removes the rows and destroys the keys; sealed columns in your own backups become unopenable, and plaintext columns in your own backups remain yours to erase.

Then bundle delivery, because it is the one that decides whether a hosted tenant can exercise the right at all — everything else is a self-hoster’s convenience. Legal hold I would leave alone: policy compliance is [lean], and building a hold nothing can set is exactly the producer-less class this project keeps deleting.

asks.text:
Six remainders are named in checklist 11-10. Five are ordinary work. One is a disclosure you owe a customer, and it is the one I want a ruling on.

The BYO-DB consent gap. Crypto-erasure works because the DEKs are ours: destroying them makes even a customer’s own backup of their own sealed columns unopenable. But a BYO-DB space stores plaintext columns in a database the customer runs and backs up themselves — and no op we could ever write reaches those backups. So “delete my space” means something materially weaker on BYO-DB than on managed, and nothing tells anyone that.

The other five, for context: bundle delivery (the op writes to a configured directory and returns a path, so a self-hoster has the bytes and a hosted tenant does not); blob bytes (waiting on blob custody); the confirmation window (needs pending-deletion state and a job); legal hold (no producer anywhere, so deletion cannot respect one); and PlatformExecutor dropping the durable ReplayLease (safe here only because both exit ops are idempotent by construction).

where: crates/ordo-exec/src/export.rs with crates/ordo-exec/tests/export.rs and erase.rs; commits c2e2d47, c65a373, af84981 (door ops, owner-only, step-up).

name: Delegation grants
sub: Increment 2 and the consent ceremony (11-4b) built; worker credentials after the first deployment
explain:
A worker or server function acts in a tenant for a person, within limits, and every act is recorded with both names.

  • Core grant and door built (11-4)
  • Increment 2 building: $caller becomes the person; the worker is recorded beside it
  • Deletes closed to workers by default; the app developer opens chosen ops
suggest:
Yes — rebind it, and do it before the ceremony, the consent page or MCP. Those three are polish on a feature that otherwise returns empty results, and shipping them first would produce a delegation surface a builder can complete end to end and get nothing back from.

The reason it is safe is the reason the door was built first: the two consents already intersect, so a delegated call can never exceed the delegator's own live reach. Rebinding $caller at the row layer moves the executor toward the bound the door already enforces rather than past it — the current state is the one that disagrees with itself.

The “not one row more” half is the test that matters, and it needs a guard-conformance case, not just a unit test: the risk is not that the delegator's rows are missing, it is that some third party's rows arrive with them.

asks.text: Separate cache keys per worker cost nothing extra: same lookups, just more entries. Keep each worker's replay cache separate from the person's?
asks.suggest: Yes. It is a longer key, not more work, and it stops one worker being handed another worker's cached answer.

asks.text: A worker (a backend function, a job, a script acting for a person) cannot delete rows unless you list the op. Close bulk updates by default too?
asks.suggest: No, deletes only. Closing every bulk update would break ordinary jobs; you can still close more ops with the same setting.

asks.text: Platform writes (leave, membership, removal) stay closed to workers until they can record the worker. Build that recording next?
asks.suggest: Yes, after this increment. Then the app developer can open chosen platform ops to workers, and the record still names both.

asks.text: Nothing creates a worker credential yet. Add an app-developer command and op to grant a worker access to a tenant, before the consent screen?
asks.suggest: Yes. It is what ellanor's worker and denizens' functions need; the grant is recorded and revocable. The person-facing consent screen (11-4b) follows later.

asks.text: No door call lets a person grant an assistant delegation yet (11-4b, the consent ceremony); the example uses a dev tool. Build it before the first deployment?
asks.suggest: Yes. Without it no real app can let a person hand an assistant or AI agent their rights; the rest of delegation is built.

where: Consent ceremony 27be5047, da698621, 4e7d8b7e, 7d1f39d9: POST /auth/delegation/request and /redeem, std.delegation.review/approve/decline/mine/revoke; settings ORDO_DELEGATION_AGENTS, ORDO_DELEGATION_MAX_HOURS (8), ORDO_DELEGATION_REQUEST_SECS (600), ORDO_DELEGATION_MAX_OPS (10); tests delegation_consent.rs (12), assistant_app the_manager_lends_through_the_consent_ceremony

name: Blob / content custody
sub: Landed, B1–B5: fourteen commits merged to main. Three rulings below are yours.
decided: Okay then do what is required to finish the implementation.
explain:
Landed in full and merged to main. The store trait with S3 (hand-rolled SigV4, pinned to AWS’s published vectors) and filesystem bindings; blob/uri through the whole language with all seventeen ratchets decided; chunked STREAM sealing (a published construction, taken rather than invented); the blob door sharing the op door’s access checker with zero new refusal classes; reference GC floored at the undo horizon; BYO bucket as an owner-only step-up op; export’s unbuilt list emptied; eight stale doc claims corrected. The sweep proved a rule worth remembering: every first real traversal of a layer produced a defect, four for four, and unit tests saw none of them. The sharpest: every blob GET answered access_denied for everyone until the pseudo-op was granted.

The session that built this broke before it could finish this page. Audited on 2026-09-07: nothing was lost. All fourteen commits (d8cbd5c through e4e38b1) are reachable from main through three merges; the worktree directory is gone but its branch was fully merged first. The full workspace suite was re-run on main to confirm: 135 suites, 1,320 tests, 0 failed (more than the worktree’s 1,247 because main also carries the attestation merges). The only unfinished work was this page, and that is what this regeneration completes.

What is honestly not done, and belongs to the three rows below: a blob upload writes nothing into the command chain (plan-blob §8.1); the integrity digest is computed and sealed but not carried in any image (§8.2); and no deployment constructs a StoreResolver, so the door is proven but served by nothing (17g’s remainder). plan-blob.md §8.3 lists what must not be built until §8.1 is ruled: triggers on file arrival, un-attach in undo, history views of file changes, log replay for blob references.
suggest: Nothing further on this row. Answer the three rows that follow; each is a separate decision with a separate status, so you can rule one and defer another.
where: crates/ordo-blob (contract.rs, fs.rs, s3.rs, pipeline.rs) with tests crates/ordo-blob/tests/contract.rs and pipeline.rs; checklist 17g closed, docs/plan-blob.md.

name: Blob uploads through the write protocol
sub: Built 2026-09-09 to 2026-09-21. C1 to C8 all landed
decided: Okay then lets do C - but before we do - verification is comparing audit log hash against what exists - that is proof of what was and what is
explain:
Built. The blob door seals the bytes, mints a PinnedUpload that carries its own target row and its own $blobref INSERT, and hands it to the write protocol. An upload is now an ordinary converge: it appends a command group, moves rev, fires converged and written, and is revertible. ordo_exec::blob::attach is deleted, and with it the only entity-row write in the tree that appended nothing.

A revert compares the digest the chain recorded against the object that exists, which is your definition. Mismatch refuses before any write; an absent or unreachable object restores and raises a security event; the undo horizon keeps its own refusal; an image with no digest restores and the skip rides the group.
suggest:
Six increments landed, four defects fixed along the way. C1: the revert applier addressed rows by id alone in seven statements, not the four the plan predicted, while ids collide across spaces by construction. C2: the two full-row image builders became one, licensed by a byte-for-byte comparison over 102 rows before either was deleted. C3: blob sealed refused at the door, since a sweep over such a schema errored on bytea = text. C4: the ruling itself. C5: the digest in the image. C6: verification, plus a streaming fix, since verify buffered whole objects.

Remaining: C7 (ordo verify --objects) and C8 (the record). Both small.

asks.text: Say the word and C7 and C8 finish it.

where: C1 to C6 per docs/plan-blob-chain.md; C7 and C8 closed in f62be1c (ordo verify --objects). Checklist 17g′ closed.

name: The digest in the chain
sub: Built 2026-09-09 as C5. Sealed, never plaintext.
decided: Waiting on 8.1
explain:
Built. A blob column's image carries "{field}$digest" beside the handle: a SealedRef into $sealedpayload holding the verbatim $blobref.integrity envelope, copied rather than re-sealed, because it is already AAD-bound to (entity, field) and the payload row records both.

Never plaintext. A hex digest in the plaintext chain would be an unsalted permanent equality index over file content, answering “did these two rows ever hold the same file” forever and surviving crypto-erasure. The test asserts over the chain's own encoded bytes, and also asserts the handle IS present, so it cannot pass by encoding nothing.
suggest: One consequence worth knowing: every chain hash for a group with a blob column differs from here on. Groups already appended keep the bytes they were appended with, and verification recomputes over those, so nothing existing breaks.
where: C5, ba6dccf (merged 654078c): the image carries {field}$digest, per docs/plan-blob-chain.md.

name: Where a deployment's default blob store comes from
sub: Decided 2026-09-09: yes, that answers it. Goes to R1.
decided: Yes the deployment requires an actual setup - it is a part of the whole ecosystem - this as a "BAAS" system. if you start the deployment you point it at an S3 gate of some sort. Later we may add an internal s3 that just saves to where it is running (possibly just handle through k8s pvs is an example) but for now point to s3 that needs to be configured. Does that answer the question? By default that is what is required - then tenants can have their own or use what the system provides.
explain: It does answer it. A deployment is pointed at an S3-compatible endpoint configured at start, which is what ORDO_BLOB_S3_* already reads and what production_ready already refuses a deployment for lacking. Tenants either bring their own bucket or use the one the system provides. A store that writes to wherever the process is running, a mounted volume rather than a bucket, is a later addition and never the default, because a default that silently works on one node is the failure mode this refusal exists to prevent.
suggest: Goes into R1 with the runtime: the binary refuses to serve blobs with no store configured, and says which variable is missing.
where: The default store is the configured S3 endpoint: ORDO_BLOB_S3_* read in crates/ordo-blob/src/s3.rs, and BlobStore::production_ready refuses a deployment without one (crates/ordo-host/src/runtime.rs).

name: Attestation layers 2–4
sub: Built: egress kernel, webhook, chainProof, offline verifier. Four witness formats owed.
decided: Execute this.
explain:
Landed, per your “execute this”. The egress kernel (ordo-egress) ships §7b’s six pins as types rather than checks, as the first increment of its first consumer, since the attestation webhook is an outbound POST. Layer 2: $attestsinks with an owner-signed destination re-verified before every send, std.space.attestTo (owner-only, step-up gated), an at-least-once outbox with backoff and dead letters on the ops surface, and the published payload schema ordo.attestation/1. Layer 3’s generic mechanism: the signed-checkpoint POST, which is what §7 means by “witnesses are wherever the owner points that webhook”. Layer 4: std.space.chainProof($from, $to) emitting ordo.chainproof/1, and ordo-verify-proof, a binary that links the command-log crate and a JSON parser and nothing else. ordo verify --proof calls the same routine. The public transparency log stays declined, as this row recommended.

Four rulings became mechanisms. Pin 5 (“egress holds nothing”) is a dependency edge: the egress crate depends on no other Ordo crate, and a test parses the manifest to keep it that way. Pin 2 is a move: a pinned destination is minted once and consumed by value, so re-resolution before each send is the only shape the API has. The delivery MAC and the checkpoint key are two keys, so the key that authors this deployment’s claims never sits inside the egress identity. A chain proof carries digests, not bodies, which is why it discloses no space content and can be manager-reachable.

What the build found. Three SSRF bypasses a correct IPv4 range check never sees (::ffff:127.0.0.1, the NAT64 prefix, 0.0.0.0/8): every address is now canonicalised before any predicate runs. §7b’s fd00::/8 was the wrong half of fc00::/7, widened and recorded. And a health counter only the loop incremented, so a caller driving a pass directly read zero after a delivery that landed. Full record in corpus-rulings.md, “Attestation layers 2–4” (2026-09-08).
suggest:
Owed, and named rather than implied, in the order I would build them. (1) The WORM / object-lock bucket format is nearest: a request builder on the same pinned client with the SigV4 the blob work already hand-rolled. It is not shipped because “the request has the right headers” is not the property; “S3 accepts it and applies object lock” is, and proving that needs a real bucket in CI, which is 15a’s territory. (2) Rekor second, because its Merkle inclusion proof generalises the offline verifier rather than special-casing it. (3) OpenTimestamps has the weakest verification story (honest checking wants a Bitcoin node) and git-over-HTTPS is the most code for the least property; both wait. Also owed: a proof over more than MAX_LINKS stays two proofs against two anchors, by design; setup guides per target once their formats exist; and a multi-sink allowlist table, which belongs to 17k.

My read: queue the witness formats behind the runtime and CI work rather than start them now. Every one of them is proven only against a real external service, and the CI pipeline that can hold one does not exist yet.

asks.text: Confirm the sequencing. The four witness formats wait for CI to be able to hold a real bucket (15a), and WORM then Rekor is the order. If you want a witness format sooner, say which, and it goes ahead of 15a with a manual verification step in place of the CI proof.

where: Layers 2 to 4 built: crates/ordo-egress, crates/ordo-verify-proof, chainProof; one witness format shipped. Owed: four witness formats, checklist 11-12 is [~].

name: Space provisioning lifecycle
sub: Started 2026-09-25. The state machine, row-first ordering, std.space.reap, the reconciler, phase 0 with dryRun and item 44 are built. Ruled 2026-09-26: this item stays open until its blockers complete
decided: Even though provisioning should be fast - this makes sense and would need persistence probably through cache or something - or a value within the space.
explain:
Found by the 2026-09-07 coverage audit: no row anywhere.

bootstrap.md §1–§4 are settled and describe a great deal more than one op: a seven-phase model, a 46-item input inventory, the genesis command group at chain position 0, a provisioning → active | failed → reaped state machine, a bootstrapTimeout reconciler, a per-resource compensation table, and std.space.reap.

In crates/, reap, reconciler and bootstrap_timeout match nothing at all. What exists is the op name.

Why it matters more than it sounds. Creating a space is not one write — it mints custody keys, provisions a database or a schema, writes the genesis group, and registers the owner. Any of those can fail halfway. The compensation table is the document that says which resources to hand back for each failure point, and the reconciler is the thing that notices a space stuck in provisioning and runs it. Without them, a half-created space holds keys and storage that nobody will ever reclaim, and nothing reports it.
suggest:
Built 2026-09-25, and your “a value within the space” is what it is. $spaces now carries state (provisioning → active | failed → reaped), phase, target, state_at and note. No cache: the registry row is the persistence, exactly as you said.

The leak was real and is closed. The row used to be written last, after the custody keys and the database, so a crash in between left both with nothing naming them — §4.4’s “every orphan is reachable from one table” was false. It is now reserved first, the target is recorded before the database is created, and activation is the last write. A failure marks the row failed rather than deleting it, because deleting it would be the same leak arriving through the tidy-up path.

std.space.reap is built and refuses anything active, per §4.5: cleaning up a failed provision and destroying a customer’s world are different buttons with different callers. It releases the attachment, drops the database, forgets the fleet row and destroys the custody keys — keys last, because keys destroyed before the rows they seal leave unreadable data standing. A tenant on its own perimeter has its database reported and left standing: the platform never drops one it did not create.

The reconciler is built too (ORDO_BOOTSTRAP_TIMEOUT_SECS, default the plan’s 15 minutes). It marks and does not release: a stale provisioning row becomes failed, which is what puts it in the troubled list, and releasing the resources stays std.space.reap, which a person calls. A process that destroyed databases with nobody asking would eventually destroy the wrong one.

Phase 0 is now a phase, and it closed a smaller leak of a different kind. bootstrap.md §1.2 says “preflight is the whole product” and that every decidable failure is refused before the registry row exists. It was not: every check — a host the deployment may not dial, the control database, a database another tenant already sits on — ran after the row was reserved. So an operator who mistyped a host was told so and left a failed tenant behind, sitting in the troubled list, which is the deployment’s one place to look for provisions that need a human. A typo is not a stuck provision, and a detection pane that reports typos is one people learn to scroll past. Those checks now run first, and the refusal leaves nothing.

Preflight also dials the target now, which §2 item 26 asks for in those words: “connects and runs a probe transaction; it does not merely parse”. A wrong port or password used to be discovered by CREATE DATABASE — after the row and after the custody key — so the commonest configuration mistake in the whole op was the one that cost the most to recover from.

dryRun (item 45) is built on top of it: it runs phase 0 and answers with the plan — which cluster your parameters resolved to, the database that would be minted, the schema version it would receive, whether that database is already standing — and reserves nothing, so two dry runs in a row both succeed. Item 45 calls this “the surface agents and operators should call first”.

Item 44 is built, 2026-09-26: Idempotency-Key is required on std.space.create and on no other op. The header is optional on every other write because the cost of omitting it is bounded there — a retry repeats an insert and the row’s own key or a rev CAS catches it. That bound does not hold for an op whose effect is outside the database it writes to: a retry mints a second KMS key and a second database, answers with the second tenant’s id, and leaves the first for somebody to find by reading the cluster. Both rows are active and correct, and nothing reconciles them.

ordo space create mints a key per invocation and prints it when the call dies in transport, with --idempotency-key to pin one — which is the case the requirement is actually for. A transport failure leaves you unable to tell “the door never saw it” from “a tenant was built and the answer was lost”, and those need opposite next steps. Re-running with the same key settles it rather than risking a second tenant.

Item 22 is built too, 2026-09-26. Preflight asks whether custody can be opened at all and refuses before the registry row exists, which item 22 calls “the check that keeps phase 2’s non-transactionality from mattering in the common case” — the common cases being a provider that is down and a process holding the wrong master key. It is the same question /health/deep already asked, now one function so the two cannot drift, and the choice of question is the substance: current_epoch and release unwrap nothing, so a mistyped master passes both and then fails every read of every sealed field. It does not claim to catch a provider that can be read and will not create — that still lands in phase 2 — and a test requires that path to stay reachable, because a probe that appeared to close it would be worse than none.

Still to build: the rest of the 46-item inventory and the three entry paths, each closing as its blocker completes. Most of the remaining items name subsystems that do not exist yet (domain packages and their bootstrap blocks, access-profile templates, jurisdiction and compliance packs, the client registry, notification channels, genesis import), so they are not one increment and are proposed as a split in the bootstrap-inventory-split row.

Original recommendation: Your instinct lands exactly on the plan’s shape: the reconciler needs durable progress, and “a value within the space” is the right home — the genesis writes a compensation record as its own first row, so a half-created space carries the evidence of how far creation got, and the reconciler (a §17d supervisor worker) either completes or reaps from it. No cache needed: the space’s own storage is the persistence, and a space too broken to hold the record is by definition reapable. Queued behind the supervisor (17d); I’ll bring it as a build item then.

asks.text:
Your words: provisioning should be fast, but the lifecycle makes sense and needs persistence, through a cache or a value within the space.

Reflected: bootstrap.md §1–§4 already put the phase (provisioning → active | failed → reaped) on the space record itself, which is the “value within the space” form, and the genesis command group at chain position 0 is what makes it durable without a cache. The row stays queued (17l) with that reading. Still open from before: the whole lifecycle, or the minimum that stops a failure leaking resources?

where: Built: state machine and std.space.reap c0c8e11, reconciler 65435ab, phase 0 04fd5e1, item 44 b962dfb, item 22 bbd43fb (crates/ordo-host/src/tenants.rs, crates/ordo-exec/src/spacedb.rs). Owed: the remaining docs/bootstrap.md inventory items; 11-15 open.

name: Rotating the security key makes ordo verify report tampering
sub: Found and ruled 2026-09-26: the verifier takes several keys and selects by the marker’s own key id. Old markers are never re-signed
decided: take reccomendaton and document
explain:
The gap. audit_stream’s fourth check — nothing was removed from the end of the stream — verifies the newest checkpoint under the key the verifier was handed. Rotate the security key, and every marker signed before the rotation fails under the new one, so ordo verify reports the security stream as FAILED. Not “unverifiable”, not “anchored earlier” — tampered.

The command chain does not have this problem in the same way: a checkpoint’s signature is time-independent and receivers hold published keys per key id, so an auditor can bring the key that matches the marker. Here there is no key-discovery story at all for this artifact, and the verifier takes exactly one key on the command line.

Why it matters more than a routine ergonomics bug. Key rotation is something a deployment does because it suspects a compromise. So the moment you most need this artifact to be readable is the moment it starts reporting tampering, and an operator who has just rotated cannot tell that finding apart from the real thing. A security record that cries wolf after a rotation is a record people learn to dismiss.

The smaller one beside it. $seccheckpoints is keyed (scope, upto) and put_security_checkpoint is ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, so a hand-written row at the position the signer would sign makes a genuine insert return success and store nothing — checkpointing stops at that position and the only symptom is a counter that does not move. The signer now refuses loudly when it meets a marker it did not sign (ForeignMarker), which surfaces it; the vector itself is still there.
suggest:
RULED and built 2026-09-26. --security-key-id and --security-public-key repeat and pair up in order; the verifier selects the key by the marker’s own key_id and reports what it could and could not check. A marker signed by a key you did not bring is now unreadable, not failed — a narrower answer rather than a wrong one — and that distinction is the whole fix: before it, the day after a rotation ordo verify said the security stream had been tampered with.

Selected by id rather than tried in turn, which keeps StreamCheckpoint::verify’s binding intact: a marker is checked against the key it claims, so “some key we hold verifies this” is never mistaken for “the key it names verifies this”. Falsified both ways — treating an unreadable marker as a failure, and accepting any key that happens to work.

A mismatched pair is a usage error, exit 2, not a verification failure: passing the flags wrong and the record being wrong are opposite findings, and an operator’s scripts watch for the second.

Old markers are not re-signed, as recommended. A rotation that could restate the past would make the new key retroactive authority over the old record — precisely the property the separate key exists to deny.

The suppression vector is left as it was, also as recommended: the signer refuses loudly when it meets a marker it did not sign, and widening $seccheckpoints’s key would let a real marker sit beside a bogus one at one position, where try_latest_checkpoint’s ORDER BY upto DESC LIMIT 1 would choose between them arbitrarily. A published key-discovery document is still the right end state and is not built.

The recommendation, as put:

Accept several keys, and say which one verified. The smallest change that fixes the false alarm: --security-key-id/--security-public-key become repeatable, the verifier tries each against the marker’s own key_id, and the report names the key that verified beside the anchor it chose. An operator who has rotated passes both keys during the overlap and reads a green line that says which key backs which claim. StreamCheckpoint::verify already binds key_id to the verifier, so the matching is not new logic.

Do not re-sign old markers. Re-signing history under a new key is the one option that destroys the property the second key exists for: if a rotation can restate the past, then compromising the new key is retroactive authority over the old record, which is the failure the separate key was chosen to avoid in the first place.

A published key-discovery document is right and is bigger. It is what the command chain’s receivers already have and where this should end up, but it is a surface with its own hosting and cache questions, and the false alarm wants closing before that lands.

On the suppression vector, my recommendation is to leave the key alone and keep the refusal. Widening it to (scope, upto, head) the way $checkpoints did would let a real marker sit beside a bogus one at one position, and try_latest_checkpoint’s ORDER BY upto DESC LIMIT 1 would then choose between them arbitrarily — a verifier picking the forged marker silently is worse than an insert that refuses loudly. Take the rotation half first.

asks.text: How should a verifier find the right key for a marker — a published key-discovery document per key id, several --security-public-key pairs accepted at once, or markers re-signed under the new key at rotation?

name: A dot-path reads its target entity unguarded, and fixing it is a semantics choice
sub: Found 2026-09-26 chasing GC007. RULED the same day: the guard goes in the join’s ON clause, so the field nulls and the row stays. Build is GC007’s
decided: take reccomendaton on dotpath - document it
explain:
The gap, confirmed in the code rather than inferred. When an op reads through a dot-path — task.project.name — the target entity’s own read guard is never evaluated. ordo-sema’s entity_source pushes the base entity’s guard into the query’s filters; walk_refs, which handles each dot-path hop, pushes a bare Join and the Join IR has no field for a guard at all. So tasks’ guard runs and projects’ does not.

guards-conformance.md R-G6 says the opposite in as many words: “every entity the flattened plan reads contributes its read guard as a conjunctive semi-join, dot-path targets included”. This is the corpus doing its job — GC007 has recorded the divergence since the beginning, and the conformance fixture hides it because the test caller happens to satisfy both guards.

Why this is yours and not mine. The obvious fix — push the target’s guard into WHERE like the base entity’s — silently changes what a row is. A dot-path is a LEFT JOIN, so a guard in WHERE turns it into an inner join in effect: a task whose project you may not see disappears from the result entirely. Put the same condition in the join’s ON clause instead and the task stays with a null project name. Both are defensible and they are different products:

  • ON (null the field): you see all your tasks; the ones pointing at projects you cannot read show a blank project name. Nothing vanishes, and the blank is itself a small disclosure — it says something is there that you may not see.
  • WHERE (drop the row): you see only tasks whose whole dot-path you may read. Nothing leaks, not even existence, and a task can go missing from a list with no indication why — which users report as data loss.

Whichever you pick also changes taskSheet’s scope manifest, because projects.owner becomes a genuine guard read, and it needs a conformance case with a caller who satisfies the task guard and not the project guard — the case the current fixture cannot express.
suggest:
RULED 2026-09-26: null the field. The guard goes in the join’s ON clause, so a task whose project you may not read keeps its place in the list with a blank project name. Recorded in full in corpus-rulings.md, with the five things implementing it owes — the Join IR gaining a guard, taskSheet’s scope manifest changing, and above all the falsifying case the fixture has never had: a caller who satisfies the task guard and fails the project guard. Without that case the fix is unverified, which is the state GC007 is a record of. The build itself stays GC007’s, under the corpus row.

The recommendation, as put:

Null the field — the guard goes in the ON clause.

The rule it keeps is the one the rest of Ordo already follows: a guard decides what you may read, not whether the row you already may read exists. The caller passed tasks’ guard; that task is theirs to see. A guard on a different entity reaching back to delete it from their list is that entity’s guard deciding something outside its own scope.

It is also the answer that fails visibly. A blank field is a question a user asks support about; a row that silently is not there is a bug report about lost data, and the support cost lands on the application author who did nothing wrong.

The counter-argument, stated fairly: a null is an existence disclosure. Blank-project-name tells the caller a project is there that they cannot see, and with a sharp enough query that is countable. That is real, and it is the same disclosure the platform already accepts everywhere else — a space id is treated as leakable, which is why grants are space-bound, and $spaces discloses that other tenants exist. Existence is not the secret; contents are.

Either way this should not ship quietly. Whichever you choose, the manifest changes and the catalog should say which entities a dot-path pulls a guard from, so an author reading their own op can see that taskSheet now depends on projects’ guard. And it wants the falsifying conformance case first: a caller who satisfies one guard and not the other, which is exactly what the fixture has never had.

asks.text: When a dot-path crosses into an entity whose read guard the caller fails: does the row vanish (guard in WHERE) or does the field come back null (guard in ON)?

where: a77cf1a: the guard is rendered in the join's ON clause; tests crates/ordo-conformance/tests/guards_compiler_joins.rs. Ruling in docs/corpus-rulings.md (GC007, 2026-09-26).

name: What is left of the 46-item bootstrap inventory, and where it should live
sub: Asked 2026-09-25, answered 2026-09-26: items stay open and close after their blockers complete. 11-15 does not close at the lifecycle
decided: They’ll close after their blockers complete.
explain:
Where 11-15 stands. The lifecycle half is built: the state machine, row-first ordering, std.space.reap, the bootstrapTimeout reconciler, and now phase 0 with dryRun. What the checklist still carries under the same item is bootstrap.md’s 46-item input inventory, the seven-phase model and the three entry paths.

The problem with leaving them as one item is that they are not one piece of work. Going through the 46 against what exists, they fall into four groups. Built or structurally settled today (about 12): the minted id, the fixed owner role, derived attribution, the placement/cluster inputs, the BYO database target, credential handles as labels never secrets, dryRun, and the refusals that are refusals by construction. Buildable now, small (about 6): Idempotency-Key made mandatory on this one op, the owner-principal existence check, the step-up assertion per path, the perPrincipalLimit quota. Blocked on a subsystem that does not exist (about 20): domains[] and package bootstrap blocks, access-profile templates, bootstrapRows, jurisdiction and the compliance pack, retention floors, the client registry, notification channels and routes, seed and genesis import, the custody acknowledgement tokens. Refused, and already refused (about 8): caller-supplied ids, grants, per-member overrides, outbound sinks, auth methods, issuer.

The third group is the whole of the remaining weight, and each of those items is small once its subsystem exists and unbuildable before. Holding 11-15 open until all of them land means one roadmap item that cannot close for months and whose state nobody can read at a glance.
suggest:
RULED 2026-09-26, against the recommendation: the items stay open and close after their blockers complete. So 11-15 does not close at the lifecycle — it stays open until the 46-item inventory and the three entry paths are genuinely built, and each blocked item closes as the subsystem it waits on lands. The roadmap keeps one item that tells the truth about what bootstrap still owes, rather than a closed item and a scattering of pointers.

What that changes about how I work it: the blocked items are not re-filed and not forgotten; each names the item it waits on, and 11-15’s entry carries that list so a reader can see what is left without re-deriving it. The two that are not blocked still get built next under this row — item 44 (Idempotency-Key required on std.space.create, without which a retried create mints a second tenant with a second database and a second key) and item 22 (a health question on KeyProvider, so an unhealthy provider is refused in preflight rather than failing in phase 2 and leaving a reserved row).

The recommendation, as put, and not taken:

Close 11-15 at the lifecycle, and let the inventory ride with its subsystems. Three reasons, and the third is the one that matters.

An item nobody can close stops being read. 11-15 would sit open across every other increment, and its checklist entry would grow into a second copy of bootstrap.md that drifts from the first.

The dependency is real, not a sequencing preference. bootstrapRows cannot be validated before packages declare a bootstrap block; profile cannot be instantiated before templates exist. Building either early means building a parameter that is parsed and ignored, which is the failure mode std.space.create’s own routing parameters were written to avoid.

And the part that is genuinely at risk of being lost is small enough to name now. Two things in the inventory are not blocked and are easy to forget once the item closes: item 44, Idempotency-Key required on this op and no other — without it a retry after a network failure mints a second tenant, with a second database and a second key, and the caller never learns the first one exists; and item 22, a health question on KeyProvider so an unhealthy provider is refused in preflight instead of failing in phase 2 and leaving a reserved row. I would build both as the last piece of 11-15 rather than let them ride, and then close it.

If you would rather keep one tracking item, the alternative that works is closing 11-15 and opening a thin bootstrap-inventory row that only lists which of the 46 are outstanding and which item each waits on — a checklist of pointers rather than a work item.

asks.text: Does 11-15 close when the lifecycle and phase 0 are done, with each blocked inventory item riding with the subsystem that owns it — or does it stay open as the one place the whole of bootstrap.md is tracked?

name: The client and its local cache
sub: Built 2026-09-17, C1 through C7 plus C4d and C4e. 110 of 165 ops are not yet syncable
decided: Local cacheing is a staple of this system to be able to have the benefits and reconcile trade-offs from Jazz. It’s not a question.
explain:
Recorded, and I had this wrong. I offered three positions including “no local caching story”, which contradicts the architecture: local caching is what buys the local-first benefits, and it is the thing the Jazz comparison in this session was measuring against. It is a staple.

What the check turned up is still the useful part: nothing in the tree is a client. No indexeddb, no opfs, no localstorage in any crate. ordo-wasm compiles the compiler for the browser and ordo-playground writes pipelines; neither holds a replica. f7-vault-plan.md names the embedded engine among F7’s prerequisites, prices it at another 8 to 12 agent sessions, and says “not counted below”. Filed as 5g-pre, because a staple with no row is a staple nobody schedules.

Built through C5, 2026-09-15. C1 to C3 gave a read a chain position and the device a sealed replica keyed by entity and id. C4 added the sync feed: the server sends a synced op’s guarded result as paced load pages, then upserts and deletes at their positions, and a guard change reaches the device as deletes of the rows it hid. C5 is the manager: it declares the ops a device syncs, reopens a feed that ends, and publishes one position, the lowest any live op has reached, which never decreases. So a screen never mixes one op’s newer rows with another’s older ones, and a reconnect cannot move a row or a screen backwards. A refusal the door names stops that op instead of being asked again.

What building C5 found, and it is worth your notice: @ordo/sdk read the class of every refusal from a field named class, and the door has never written that field. It writes code, which is what api-engine-design.md §4 documents and what @ordo/react reads. So every refusal the door ever sent this package decoded as internal, keeping its message, which is why nothing looked broken. Three of the package’s own tests had been written to the invented shape and passed against it. The manager is what made it bite, since it retries internal and stops on everything else. Fixed.

C6 followed the same day. The device answers its own questions now: refineOp filters, picks and sorts the rows a synced op holds, with the Tier-0 operators Ordo already defines, so a filter keystroke asks the server for nothing. Values compare by the type the executor gave them, so money and ints compare as numbers rather than as text (“250” > “12000” as text is the trap that pins).

And it turned up something worth your notice: Tier-0 refinement is specified, validated, cost-gated and served by nothing. Every op ships refine.tier: “none”, so the door refuses $refine catalog-wide; @ordo/react builds envelopes it can never send; and ordo-host’s executor takes a validated refinement and ignores it, which its own test states. So C6 is the first working Tier 0 in the system and it runs on the device. Whether that stands is the refine-tier-local row.
suggest:
What is genuinely open is scope and order, not whether. The local cache is the substrate for three things that currently assume it: offline reads, the client-first vault (5g), and revocable local caching (5g-rev). Its first version does not need the vault’s deterministic evaluator, which is a third of F7 and carries all its schedule risk. A client that holds a sealed replica and reads from it is much smaller than a client that can evaluate writes deterministically offline.

So the sequencing question is whether the cache ships ahead of F7 as its own thing, or inside it. Ahead looks right: it unblocks offline reads and 5g-rev without paying for Phase 4.

asks.text: Cache first as its own increment, or only as part of F7?

name: Backend functions: custom code the deployment runs
sub: Increment 1 on main (f9835982), all green. Left: SDK call + notes v2 button, ordo fn runs, engine cache
explain:
Plan: docs/plan-backend-functions.md. The app developer's own code runs inside the deployment, beside ops and routines.

  • One JS file per function, run as WebAssembly
  • It may call out, use a secret by name, call listed ops, and log
  • Woken by the page, a routine, or a webhook

asks.text: The settled spec says "no foreign code in v1". Should Ordo now run the app developer's own code, as you asked on this task?
asks.suggest: Yes. It is what ellanor's 40 and denizens' 6 functions need, and your words on this task ask for it. The spec line is updated to match.

asks.text: Run functions as WebAssembly with a built-in JavaScript engine, so a function is one bundled JS file?
asks.suggest: Yes. It isolates each function from the server and from other tenants, and JS is what both apps' functions are written in. Other languages can follow.

asks.text: API keys for functions: sealed under the deployment's keys, set per environment, never readable back. Agreed?
asks.suggest: Yes. A function holds only a name; the server inserts the key into the outgoing request, only for the hosts that key is bound to. Keys never reach the history or logs.

asks.text: When the page calls a function, should it run as the signed-in person, through a one-call delegation?
asks.suggest: Yes. The function can then do only what that person may do, and everything it writes is recorded as the function acting for them.

asks.text: Build increments 1 (page-called), 2 (files in) and 4 (calling ops) first, the rest after?
asks.suggest: Yes. Those three move real functions: ellanor's classify-notes, extract-document and the Calendar proxy, and denizens' face-chat. Streaming, webhooks and schedules follow.

asks.text: Connected accounts (a user's Google or GitHub): built by the app with functions, or a platform feature with OAuth sign-in?
asks.suggest: Built by the app with functions, for now. It keeps sign-in small; a platform feature can come once two apps need the same thing.

asks.text: Run functions as WebAssembly inside Ordo (wasmtime with a JS engine), rather than V8 isolates like Cloudflare and Supabase?
asks.suggest: Yes, Wasm. Nothing beyond the Ordo binary, starts in microseconds, any language later. V8 ports Cloudflare code faster but ties Ordo to JS and a large C++ engine.

asks.text: Does every call get a fresh instance, with nothing kept between calls?
asks.suggest: Yes, fresh per call. A snapshot makes it nearly free, and no state can leak between people or tenants, unlike warm reused processes.

asks.text: May the program give a function its own grant, used instead of the caller's reach, recorded on every use?
asks.suggest: Yes, declared in the program. It covers passing grants along and public grants with no service key; the grant names its ops, so never wider than written.

asks.text: Does the SDK take a function inline and bundle it at synth, beside functions written in their own file?
asks.suggest: Yes, both. Both give the same function block and hashed file; an inline function may capture only imports, so it runs the same anywhere.

asks.text: A public function that only reads gets the public cache by default. One that writes (a form) is never cached. Agreed?
asks.suggest: Yes. Reads match public ops, cached by default. Caching a write would drop the second form sent, so writes always run.

asks.text: For services (long-running code), does Ordo first give identity, a route and the egress proxy, leaving running containers to the cluster?
asks.suggest: Yes, phase 1 first. Services get Ordo's promises (ops only, sealed secrets) with no scheduler to build; waking and sleeping comes in phase 2.

asks.text: A public function (a form) has no signed-in person. Does it run with the public grants plus its own grant from ask 9?
asks.suggest: Yes. The visitor gets only what public grants allow; the form's own grant lets it write just the ops it names, recorded as that function.

asks.text: Backend functions are v1 work now. Build increment 1 (page-called functions, secrets, fetch, wasmtime) next, before increments 2 and 4?
asks.suggest: Yes, after the repo goes public. Increment 1 is about 3 sessions and moves ellanor's first function. Going public does not wait on it, and the README will say functions are being built.

asks.text: Secrets are kept per deployment, so each environment is its own deployment. Should staging always be its own deployment, never inside production's?
asks.suggest: Yes. Then staging's secret can never be production's, with no --env flag. One deployment holding several environments would need secrets scoped per environment inside it.

asks.text: Functions are served at /fn/<name>, beside /op/<name>. The plan wrote /v1/fn/<name>. Keep /fn/?
asks.suggest: Yes, /fn/. It matches /op/, so a client builds both the same way. Versioning lives in each function's hash, as it does for ops.

asks.text: The JS engine is Boa (pure Rust, 3.6 MB, ~80 µs per fresh instance) instead of StarlingMonkey. Keep Boa for v1?
asks.suggest: Yes, for v1. StarlingMonkey needs Node, jco and a C toolchain at apply. Boa runs JS slower and lacks some APIs, which suits short glue code; swap later if needed.

asks.text: ordo-fn now allows one unsafe call, loading the cached engine from disk. The rest of Ordo still forbids unsafe code. Keep it?
asks.suggest: Yes. It loads only files Ordo wrote, owned by its user and writable by no one else. It cuts start from 1.2 s to 26 ms and each call from ~80 µs to ~8 µs on macOS.

asks.text: A function can't use a secret as an HMAC key, so it can't check a webhook's signature. Add a host-side HMAC keyed by a secret's name?
asks.suggest: Yes, before v1. The key stays in the host and never enters the function, as fetch does now. Webhooks are a main use of functions. Size S.

asks.text: If ops may read a person's own linked Discord id and name: only their own, every read recorded, sealed at rest, gone on unlink. Enough?
asks.suggest: Yes, with all four. The person can see who read it and when, nothing else can read it, and unlinking or deleting removes it.

asks.text: Once a deleted account's data is removed, may the same email or Discord sign up again as a new, empty person?
asks.suggest: Yes. Blocking it would mean keeping the very data the removal erased.

asks.text: When importing Supabase users who already have email and Discord on one account, keep them as one account?
asks.suggest: Yes. Supabase joined them by verified email; carrying that join over is not making a new one, and splitting them would lose people's data.

asks.text: A first Discord or password sign-in gets no tenant of its own, because self-serve asks for a passkey touch. Let self-serve run without it?

asks.text: Email code limits count per clock hour and clock day, so up to twice a limit can land across a boundary. Is that fine?
asks.suggest: Yes, keep clock windows. They are cheap and simple; the deployment-wide cap and optional Turnstile still bound abuse.

asks.text: Under invite-only, an invitation admits no newcomer by any method today (25ar). Fix it so an invitation lets a newcomer sign up with every method?
asks.suggest: Yes, every method. The guide already promises it for passkeys, and "a login method is a login method".

asks.text: A tenant can count a provider's two-step login as presence only if the app developer opened that provider to tenants. Keep that ceiling?
asks.suggest: Yes. The app developer sets the outer limit, as with admission; a tenant chooses within it. Your ruling let tenants decide, so this narrows it.

asks.text: When a provider's fresh two-step login is accepted, should it also skip Ordo's own second step at sign-in (plan §5.3)?
asks.suggest: Yes, same setting. Asking for a second factor twice is the nuisance you ruled out; it is not built yet.

asks.suggest: Yes. Same pattern as admission: the app developer opens the door, the tenant chooses inside it.

asks.text: Where does a tenant's client secret live? In the tenant's own database, sealed with the tenant's key, never shown back?
asks.suggest: Yes. It dies with the tenant, the deployment cannot read it in bulk, and a leak of one tenant's store exposes one provider.

asks.text: A tenant's provider may be at any address, but "loopback" (the Ordo server itself, localhost) is still refused. Keep refusing it?
asks.suggest: Yes. A provider is never on the Ordo server itself; allowing it would let a tenant reach ports only that machine should see.

name: One sign-in across an app's subdomains
explain:
Sign in once on a core site (login.example.com), return signed in to any subdomain.

  • Passkeys already work on every subdomain under ORDO_APEX_DOMAIN.
  • Missing: a hand-off back to the page you came from, with its own session.
  • Today every origin and return address is listed exactly.

asks.text: Build a hand-off: the core site signs in, then sends the person back with a one-time code the subdomain swaps for its own session?
asks.suggest: Yes. No shared cookie and no token in a URL: the code is single-use, short-lived, and bound to the page that asked.

asks.text: Return addresses are matched exactly today. Match by origin and allow any path on it, so a person lands back where they were?
asks.suggest: Yes, origin plus any path. Listing every path is unworkable; the origin is what keeps a code from leaking to another site.

asks.text: Allow a wildcard like *.example.com for origins and returns, off by default?
asks.suggest: Yes, opt-in only. Handy with many subdomains; exact names stay the default because one stray subdomain could then receive codes.

name: Losing a passkey: the plan, and what it needs you to decide
sub: R1 to R8 built 2026-09-29, with backup codes. Five details remain for you on recovery-details
decided: Answered 2026-09-29, all five. 1: a recovery code works at once. 2: a day's block on export after recovery, adjustable. 3: the deployment owner restores a tenant owner who lost their only passkey, and nobody inside the tenant does. 4: a recovered person is not locked out of each tenant. 5: email alone is not enough by default, and the option is documented well.
explain:
The problem: any way back in is weaker than the key, so it is also the easiest way to steal an account.

  • Four ways back, none compulsory: a second passkey, printed codes, a tenant administrator, the operator.
  • Three protections apply to all of them.
  • Recovering an account does not recover data whose keys lived on a lost device.

The three protections:

  • Every open session is ended.
  • For three days the old passkey can do one thing: cancel the recovery.
  • For a day the recovered account cannot export, delete or deploy.

What a tenant may do:

  • Suspend or remove a membership.
  • Recover a login only for somebody it created who belongs nowhere else.
  • It is never told which other tenants a person belongs to.

The plan is docs/plan-passkey-recovery.md, with four smaller questions and recommendations.

asks.text: Should a recovery code work at once, or after a wait?
asks.suggest: At once, with the block on export. Somebody who kept their codes did the careful thing.

asks.text: Is a day the right block on export after recovery?
asks.suggest: Yes, a day, and three days after recovery by the operator. Adjustable.

asks.text: A tenant's owner has lost their only passkey. May the deployment owner, the app developer who runs the service, restore them?
asks.suggest: Yes, the deployment owner, and nobody inside the tenant. By operator I meant the deployment owner. If a manager inside the tenant could restore an owner, reporting a lost key would be a way to become one.

asks.text: Should a recovered person be locked out of each tenant until that tenant lets them back in?
asks.suggest: No by default. It would make somebody in three tenants wait on three administrators because they dropped a phone. Available for a tenant that needs it.

asks.text: Should email ever be enough on its own to recover an account?
asks.suggest: No by default. A mailbox is the most commonly stolen thing a person has. Available to a deployment that chooses it knowingly, with the longest wait.

where: Merge 7a07f54: recovery.rs, recovery_codes.rs, identity_ops.rs, recovery_hold.rs, auth/authenticators.rs; SDK recovery.ts. Tests: tests/recovery.rs, recovery_ops.rs. Plan: docs/plan-passkey-recovery.md, Built.

name: Five things the enrolment plan needs you to decide
sub: E1 to E7 built 2026-09-29
decided: Answered 2026-09-29, all five. 1: agreed, a tenant resets a password only for a person it created who belongs nowhere else. 2: viewer by default, and the app developer may change it. 3: the first-person claim code is a setting, managed through the console, the API and the environment. 4: recommendation taken, a typed temporary password is a recorded option, off by default. 5: recommendation taken; people who came through a tenant's own registered provider are destroyed with the tenant, and platform sign-ins remain.
explain:
The enrolment plan is written. Five decisions are left.

  • Your two rulings pull against each other: a tenant may reset a password, and one password opens every tenant a person is in.
  • My proposal decides it by who created the person. Ask 1 is that rule.

If a tenant created the person, that tenant may reset their password for as long as it is the only place they belong.

Once they are admitted anywhere else, the first tenant keeps control of the membership and loses control of the password. That change is recorded.

Somebody who signed up by themselves is never resettable by a tenant.

The plan is docs/plan-enrolment.md.

asks.text: Password resets: may a tenant reset a person's password only if that tenant created them and is the only place they belong, with everyone else resettable only by themselves or the operator?
asks.suggest: Yes. A password unlocks every tenant a person is in, so one tenant resetting it would reach into the others.

asks.text: What role does a stranger get when an open tenant admits them?
asks.suggest: Viewer, with the tenant able to raise it, so making strangers editors is something a tenant has to choose.

asks.text: Should the first person to reach a public deployment need a code from its startup log?
asks.suggest: Optional, off by default, and switched on in the go-live guide. Between a deployment going up and its owner signing in, anybody who finds the address can be first.

asks.text: May an administrator type a temporary password by hand?
asks.suggest: Allowed as a recorded option, off by default. The normal path gives the person a one-time ticket and lets them choose their own password, so the administrator never knows it.

asks.text: When a tenant is deleted, what happens to the people it created?
asks.suggest: They become independent if they have ever signed in, and are removed if they never have. Deleting them outright could destroy their way into other tenants.

where: Merges e352209, 12d8acc, and 24e (tenant invitations: std.space.invite, invitations, revokeInvitation). Plan: docs/plan-enrolment.md, Built.

name: Nobody can sign in to a real deployment, and nobody could deploy to one if they did
sub: Passkey sign-in, enrolment, recovery and the second factor built 2026-09-29. Outside providers and emailed codes remain (federated plan)
decided: it does not make sense to enforce a particular flow. Service owns the credentialing we need auto-provisioning. First come first served in a single tenant deployment. Each new sign in is an enrollment unless they want to manually provision and invite.
explain:
What exists. Password sign-in is switched on and well made: sessions, signing out, surviving a restart. Passkey sign-in is fully written and tested as a checker, and the server refuses to start with it. Sign-in through an outside provider such as Google is a placeholder that contacts nothing. Three more methods are names on a list.

Why the one that is switched on cannot be used. There is no way to give anybody a password: the code that does it is only ever run by tests. So a deployment has a sign-in page and no one who can sign in.

And why it would not be enough even then. Deploying a program, creating a tenant, and loading or exporting data all require proof that a person is present, which a password cannot give by design. A passkey can. So those operations cannot be performed by any real sign-in today. The tests that show them working skip signing in and hand themselves the proof directly.

Two of our own guides told you otherwise, including the go-live page I made two days ago. Both corrected.
suggest:
You overruled me, and the reasoning is recorded. I proposed a one-time code as the way the first person gets in. You ruled that no flow should be compulsory, because a system that forces one ritual on everybody is hard to use.

Three plans are being written against your rulings: how a person gets a credential and is admitted to a tenant (written, plan-enrolment.md), sign-in through outside providers and by emailed code, and what happens when somebody loses their passkey. The last two are with separate planners and not back yet.

A one-time enrolment code, shown to the operator when a tenant is created. Creating a tenant already names its first owner. At that moment the system prints a code, valid once and for a short time. The owner opens the sign-in page, enters the code, and registers a passkey. From then on everybody else comes in by invitation from somebody who is already in, which is the same code mechanism.

This makes passkey sign-in the first thing to build twice over: it is what you chose for the notes app, and it is the only thing that lets anyone operate the deployment itself.

Passwords stay available as you ruled before, for deployments that want them, but they can never deploy a program or create a tenant, and the documents will say so.

asks.text: How does the very first person get their passkey registered, when nobody can sign in yet to let them in?

where: Merges 4a7b123, e352209, 12d8acc, 7a07f54, 65a49f6. Owed: docs/plan-auth-federated.md.

name: There is no way to add, suspend or remove a person in a running system
sub: Built 2026-09-29 as enrolment E3
decided: Invitation does make sense - but it should not stop signups from existing if a tenant chooses it or if they provision 3rd party auth systems that auto-provision. Also what about multi-tenant users.
explain:
When a tenant is created it gets one person, its owner. Nothing in the running system can add a second. Nothing can change somebody's role, suspend them, bring them back, or remove them. The specification describes the list of people and the rules about it, and names no operation for any of those five things.

This matters now because you chose a notes app with users who sign in. Signing in proves who somebody is. It does not make them a member of anything, and only members can read or write.
suggest:
Planned against your rulings in plan-enrolment.md. Each tenant chooses its own ways in: open sign-up, invitation, arrival through an outside provider, or first-comer for an empty tenant. Any combination, and none is compulsory. The deployment sets the outer limit on what a tenant may switch on.

Something I found while planning, which your question about people in several tenants exposed. The system keeps a person and their membership of a tenant as separate records, and never connects them when checking a request. So today one person could not belong to two tenants under one identity. Connecting them is the first thing the plan builds.

Both ways in, chosen per deployment, and invitation as the default. Automatic admission suits a public notes app where anyone may sign up and see only their own notes. Invitation suits everything where membership means something. Defaulting to invitation means a deployment that has not thought about it admits nobody by accident.

Owners and managers may suspend and remove; only owners may change roles, and the last owner of a tenant cannot be suspended or removed, since that would leave a tenant nobody can administer. Each of these is recorded in the audit history with who did it, and each tells every running process at once rather than waiting for the 30 seconds.

asks.text: How does a person become a member: invited by an owner, admitted automatically the first time they sign in, or both? And who may suspend or remove somebody?

name: CRITICAL: a permission rule is skipped whenever the compiler adds a table to a query by itself
sub: Fixed 2026-09-28 in three places. You asked whether it happened anywhere else: it did, once more
decided: Fix (see if there are any other places where a similar issue could come up (as it seems something similar was previously found already)
explain:
When a query names two tables that only connect through a third, the compiler adds the third automatically. It does not apply the third table's permission rule. The reviewer reproduced it live: a member saw which person was assigned to which place, where the assignment belonged to somebody else and their own rule forbade reading it.

It is the same defect as one we already knew about (following a link from one record to another), on a second path nobody had recorded. The description the system publishes about the operation says the rule is applied, which makes it worse: anyone auditing from that description would be told it was safe.
suggest:
Fixed, and looking for other places found a third. I checked every place a table can enter a query. Two were the ones the review found. The third was the whole-record read, which returns a record together with a short summary of each thing it points at: those summaries were read with no permission check, so reading an open record handed over the contents of a protected one it pointed at. Nothing serves that read yet, so it was waiting rather than live.

All three now use one shared check. A thing you may not read looks exactly like a link that is empty: the record stays, the field is blank.

Each test was broken on purpose and seen to fail, printing the secret it would have leaked.

Yes, and before anything with permission rules is deployed. The fix is small and already ruled: the rule goes into the join itself. What it needs first is test data able to show the defect, which the current test data cannot, as written up last week. Both paths get fixed together because they are one mistake in two places.

asks.text: Go to fix? The ruling already exists from the first case and covers both.

name: CRITICAL: suspending a member does nothing, and removing one takes effect only at the next restart
sub: Built 2026-09-28: a suspended or removed member is refused within 30 seconds and nothing restarts. Seen working on a running server. The command that suspends somebody does not exist yet
decided: I don't know what a member is here - but yes this should be fixed and meet to match spec. / We shouldnt be restarting delpoyments because someone got or lost access that would be nonsensical
explain:
What a member is. A member is a person who has been let into one tenant. Every tenant has a built-in list of them, which you never declare and cannot delete; it is the thing every permission rule compares against. When a rule says only the owner may read this, the owner is a member, and the person making the request is identified as a member.

Each member has a role (owner, manager, editor, viewer) and a status, which is either active or suspended.

You did not add suspension, and neither did I this week. It is in the language specification, in the table describing that built-in list: suspension is a command, not a delete. The idea is that you can cut somebody off at once without erasing them from history, so their past work still shows who did it. The specification has it, the permission engine has the code for it, and nothing connects the two.

The front door decides who may do what from a list it reads once, at startup, and rereads only when a new program is deployed. That list does not include whether a member is suspended, so every member is treated as active, and there is no operation that suspends anybody. The reviewer marked a member suspended in the database and they kept full access.

Removing a member does work, at the next restart or deploy. Until then they are still served.

Our own guide for operators said suspension was immediate by construction. It now says what is true and how to cut somebody off today: remove them and restart.
suggest:
Built, with no restart anywhere. Each running server process keeps the list of members in memory. It now re-reads that list from the database every 30 seconds and swaps the new one in. Nothing stops: a request in progress finishes, and the next one is checked against the new list.

Seen on a running server, the same process throughout: served; refused four seconds after being marked suspended; served again after being reinstated; refused after being removed.

What is still missing is the button. The system now obeys a suspension, and there is no operation that performs one, so today it takes somebody with database access. That is filed separately, because looking for it showed the gap is wider than suspension.

Make it real, and make it prompt without asking the database on every request. Read the status, add the operation that sets it, and have any change to membership tell every running copy to refresh, which is a channel that already exists for new tenants. Put a ceiling on how stale the list may ever be, so a lost message costs minutes and not the time until the next deploy.

The alternative is to leave it as it is and keep the documents honest. That is cheaper and I would not choose it: the moment you need to cut somebody off is the moment you cannot afford a restart.

asks.text: What should suspension and removal mean, and how quickly must they take effect?
