name: CRITICAL: encrypted values can be moved from one record to another without being detected
sub: Built 2026-09-29, B1 to B4. A moved sealed value now fails to open
decided: This sounds computationally expensive at run time / yes build it
explain:
The cost is close to nothing. Every protected value is already locked and unlocked by a cipher each time it is written or read. That cipher already takes a label saying which column the value belongs to. The fix makes the label slightly longer, by about thirty characters, so that it also says which record. No extra database query, no extra storage, no extra trip. I withdrew the one expensive part of my proposal, re-checking every stored file on every read, because once the label is right a swapped file simply fails to unlock.

It is not a database permission feature. Nothing runs inside the database. It happens in our own code at the moment of locking.

You are right that whoever controls the database controls a great deal. They can delete records, restore an old copy, or withhold everything, and nothing here stops that. What the design promises is narrower: they cannot read protected values, and they cannot rewrite history unnoticed. Moving a protected value from one record to another sits inside that promise and currently breaks it: they still cannot read a diagnosis or a salary, but they can put one person's on another person's record, and it opens with no error. With the fix the same move produces a loud failure to unlock.

Every protected value is locked in a way that records which column it belongs to. It does not record which row. So somebody with access to the database, who cannot read the value, can copy it onto a different record in the same column and it will open there as if it had always been there. The same is true of stored files: swap two in the file store and each opens as the other.

This is exactly the person the key design is meant to constrain: an operator who holds the database and not the keys. They still cannot read anything. They can rearrange it.

Not yet known: whether the audit history would reveal the move afterwards. Nobody has checked, and it is listed as an open question rather than assumed.
suggest:
A correction to what I told you. I said the cost was close to nothing. That holds when a write touches one record. It does not hold for a write that changes a protected field on many records at once: today that locks the value once and copies the result onto every record, and once each value is tied to its own record it has to be locked once per record. So that one kind of write costs in proportion to the records it touches. Creating, updating one record, and reading are unchanged.

It fixes something nobody had noticed. Because one locked value is copied onto many records today, anybody reading the table can see those records hold the same value without unlocking anything. Locking each separately ends that.

It is a bigger change than I implied: 65 places in the code, in four stages, written up in plan-row-bound-seals.md. Not started.

Yes to both, and now is the cheap moment. Nothing is deployed, so changing how values are locked costs no migration. After the first deployment it means re-locking every protected value in every tenant.

One complication worth knowing: reading part of a large file cannot check the whole file, so partial reads need their own answer. The honest options are to check in pieces or to say plainly that partial reads are unchecked.

asks.text: Bind each protected value to its own record, and check stored files every time one is read?

name: Loading data in: four weaknesses, one of them a decision
sub: Duplicates ruled Refuse and built 2026-09-28. Three mechanical fixes remain. The review had described one of these wrongly, and testing it showed how
decided: Refuse
explain:
I told you a changed bundle under a used name would be refused. That is only true if the record ids changed. If the ids are the same and the contents differ, a re-run carries on, keeps the old contents for what it had already loaded, takes the new contents for the rest, and reports success. Corrected in five places.

Two records sharing a unique key are quietly merged into one instead of being refused. The code says so in its own comments and had deferred it.

There is no size limit on anything it reads, so one oversized file can exhaust the machine before any refusal is reached. And it follows shortcuts in the staging folder, which weakens the rule that a tenant can only name bundles staged for them.
suggest:
Built as you ruled: a second record under a key already taken is refused, and says so.

Testing it corrected the review. The review said two records sharing a key were quietly merged. They were not. They were already being refused, by accident, because a merge produced an answer the loader did not expect, and the message named the wrong problem. So this was a confusing refusal and never silent data loss. It is now deliberate and readable.

Still to do, no decision needed: compare contents as well as ids when resuming, limit sizes, and stop following shortcuts in the staging folder.

Refuse. A loader for somebody else's data that cannot reject a duplicate is the wrong default, and merging silently is how a migration ends up with fewer records than it started with and nobody noticing. The other three are mechanical and need no ruling: compare contents as well as ids, put limits on sizes, and do not follow shortcuts.

asks.text: When a bundle contains two records with the same unique key: refuse the import, or merge them?

name: Ten old security findings: nine now traced, one is not
sub: Answered 2026-09-29. All ten findings now have an answer or a filed item
decided: Answered 2026-09-29, all five. SH-2 traced. SH-18 filed (18x). SH-7 checked, three parts owed (22m). SH-12 accepted. SH-11: a key service is wanted and is planned for after the first deployment (18y); the easy deployment stays.
explain:
SH-7 is checked. The copy in the browser is mostly protected.

  • Built: sealed on the device, one store per space and person, wiped on revocation.
  • Owed: passkey unlock, locking when idle, a limit on how long a copy is kept. Filed as 22m.
  • SH-18 is filed (18x). SH-12 is accepted and documented.

Where these are tracked

  • The findings themselves: docs/security-hardening-review.md.
  • What was traced to code: docs/audit-security-trace.md.
  • What review 6 found on each: docs/security-review-6.md, section 4.
  • Your answers: docs/corpus-rulings.md, 2026-09-29.

SH-7 in detail

  • Sealing: clients/ordo-sdk/src/replica/seal.ts. The keys stay on the device and cannot be exported.
  • Wipe on revocation: replica.ts, poison.
  • Permissions are never copied to the device: sync.ts, NEVER_MIRRORED.
  • The keys are not yet protected by a passkey, so opening the app opens the copy.

SH-2 in detail

  • The fingerprint key comes from the space's own master key: crates/ordo-crypto/src/custody.rs, blind_index.
  • Every space gets a random master key when it is created.
  • No test compares two spaces. Filed as 22l.

name: The board: is the database the store, or the files?
sub: Ruled 2026-09-29, left to Claude: the files stay the store, the database holds vectors and locking
decided: okay then proceed as you see fit
explain:
The board keeps its rows in two places: a SQLite database in ~/.board, and two files in the repo. Today the files are the real store. Every write rewrites both files in full, and the database is rebuilt from them whenever they differ. That makes the database a copy, which is why you asked what it is for.

Token cost is the same whichever way this goes. The saving comes from the command line touching one row at a time.
suggest:
Decided 2026-09-29, left to me: the files stay the store. This reverses what I first suggested here, which was to make the database the store.

Two things changed my mind. The database now has work of its own: it holds the embedding vectors that the question search uses, and it stops two writes at the same moment from clobbering each other. And making it the store would buy nothing measurable while adding one way to lose things: answers typed since the last commit would exist only in ~/.board.

As it stands every write lands in the files at once, git always has the current board, and deleting the database loses nothing but two minutes of re-embedding.

name: The tutorial teaches something the compiler refuses, and the refusal looks like a typo
sub: Found and fixed 2026-09-27. Both halves: the refusal now says the word is reserved and not built, and the four documents that teach it say so too
decided: Fix the finding(s)
explain:
Section 13 of the tutorial teaches a kind of declaration for scheduled and reactive rules, and spends a page on getting it right. The compiler cannot read that word at all. What it says back is that it expected one of three other things, which reads as you made a typo or your copy is out of date. Somebody who has followed twelve sections correctly now believes they mistyped something the page told them to write.

The feature being unbuilt is not the problem, and was a deliberate decision. Two of our own documents spell that declaration two different ways, so building either would have picked between them by accident. That still holds. What it missed was a pass over the pages that teach the spelling nobody picked.

Six documents teach it as if it works, and the tutorial carries no warning anywhere.
suggest:
Done, and the error message half covers eight more words than the one you were shown. Nine reserved-but-unbuilt declarations now refuse by name, each saying what it is and where it is specified, instead of listing the three that do work. The tutorial and three other documents carry a notice separating what is settled — the rules about what such a rule may see — from the spelling, which is what is actually waiting.

The fix found out why this was missed for so long. The first attempt was written in the wrong branch of the parser, and it compiled and looked correct and changed nothing, because the branch it should have been in produces an identical-looking message. Reading the output could never have told the two apart. A test caught it.

Both, and the error message is the one that matters. Marking the pages fixes six files. Making the refusal say this word is reserved and not implemented yet fixes every future case too: the same wall is waiting behind six other declarations we have reserved and not built, and each one will produce the same misleading message the first time somebody writes it.

This is the cheapest kind of fix there is, and it is the exact failure the original review kept finding: people are stopped by what the documents say, not by the language being hard.

asks.text: Nothing open. You said fix it, so both were done.

where: d832dcd: the refusal names the word reserved and unbuilt (crates/ordo-syntax/src/declparse.rs), and docs/tutorial.md, traps.md, modeling-guidance.md, syntax-examples.md say so. Checklist 17af closed.

name: A VS Code extension
sub: Yours, 2026-09-27. Filed for after the first deployment. Most of the pieces already exist, so a useful first version is packaging rather than new language work
decided: add vscode extension to post deploy roadmap
explain:
Three of the four pieces are already built. The syntax highlighting rules exist. The compiler already prints errors with a file, a line and a column, which is exactly what an editor needs to underline the right word. And the file that describes every operation, its parameters and its fields is already written on every save, which is what completion reads.

What is missing is the resident part — a process that stays running and answers questions about the code as you type, which is what go-to-definition and hover need. That is the real work, and a first version does not need it: highlight, underline errors when the file is saved, and complete from the description file.
suggest: The value is in the errors, not the autocomplete. This language refuses things for reasons that teach you the model: a permission clause with one half missing, an entity left open that reaches a protected one, a list with no ceiling. Today you learn that by saving and running. Seeing it under the word as you type is the difference between a rule you were told and a rule you understand, and it is worth more than any snippet library.

Something you actually use, and with real authorization in it. The toy in examples/first-app proves the whole path end to end and proves almost nothing else: one table, one field, no guard, one user. A program that deploys cleanly and never exercises who-may-see-which-row would leave the part of Ordo that the entire argument rests on untested in production, which is the opposite of what a first deployment is for.

name: No browser page can call a deployment unless it is served from the deployment's own origin
sub: Built 2026-09-29: ORDO_CORS_ORIGINS. Setting it from the console is owed
decided: Well it is extrememly likely that the ordo endpoint will not be the same as the webpage that it is being called from - for instance cloudflare pages  as the front with ordo as the baas -  Allowlist makes sense (confiugurable) but should be well documented so it is not missed and should be easily confiugurable in the console.
explain:
Verified against a running door rather than inferred. A cross-origin read answers 200 with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so the browser receives the body and throws it away. The preflight is the harder half: OPTIONS /op/listReadings answers 405, because no route method admits it.

And every Ordo call is preflighted. A call carries Authorization and X-Ordo-Space, which is what makes a browser ask permission first. So the 405 is the common path, not an edge case.

Whose problem it is first. @ordo/react is a browser runtime that reads /interface and calls /op/* at run time, and every app it exists for is a page on some origin. A bundler's dev proxy hides this locally by default, which is why it has stayed invisible for so long: the first app found it only because it was written without a bundler.
suggest:
Ruled: an allowlist. Your example is the ordinary case and the reason the default cannot be the only answer: a page hosted in one place calling the system hosted in another.

Two requirements you added, both recorded as part of the work: it must be documented prominently enough that nobody misses it, since the failure is a browser silently discarding a good answer; and it must be easy to set from the console. The console does not exist yet, so the first version is a setting on the deployment, built so the console can drive the same setting later.

Recommend: an allowlist the deployment states, with absence meaning same-origin only. One environment variable naming the origins that may call this deployment, the preflight answered by the same layer, and no wildcard accepted at all, since a wildcard plus credentials is the one combination browsers refuse anyway. Absence stays the safe default, so nothing changes for a deployment that has not thought about it.

The alternative is to say the door is same-origin forever and put a reverse proxy in front of both the app and the deployment. It costs nothing in crates/ and it is how the first app works today. It also means every customer must run that proxy before their first page loads, and the failure they hit if they do not is a body the browser silently discards, which reads as Ordo is broken rather than as a missing header.

name: A built-in link shortener
sub: Yours, 2026-09-23. Post-deploy. One ruling to make before it can be built
decided: add built in link shortener
explain:
Why the platform owes one rather than each application writing it. Every feature that mails somebody a link needs one, and each would otherwise mint its own table, id scheme, expiry, redirect route and scan surface, five times over with five different answers about how long a link lives and who may resolve it. It is also where 18s’s request links live, which need a stable short identifier that is deliberately not the authority.

Four questions, and the first is a ruling rather than an implementation choice. A short code is global by construction, so it cannot be per space the way a tenant’s data is: either the code carries the space, or the table is deployment-wide and resolving one discloses that it exists. Under your id ruling a code is minted and never chosen, and this is the one place a caller-chosen identifier would be tempting.

Then: resolution is an unauthenticated GET, which makes it the only enumeration surface in the platform, where length and alphabet are the whole defence and the rate limit on a miss matters more than the one on a hit. Expiry and single use are the same two properties 18s needs and should share one mechanism with. And whether a resolve is an audit event at all, since who clicked is a different question from who acted.
suggest: Deployment-wide with minted codes, and treat the existence disclosure as the cost. A code that carries its space is longer, leaks the tenant to anyone who reads the URL, and still does not stop enumeration.

name: An emailed link that is not a bearer credential
sub: Yours, 2026-09-23. A platform feature an application consumes: the link names the request, the authority comes from a proven session
decided: Basically we just want to make sure to provide as a feature the ability to send emails with action links that can be used by the application with some authority on authenticated users. Wire the alert API to your existing login using a server-verified authentication proof: the browser proves control of the signed-in account through a short-lived challenge, the server verifies that proof and checks workspace membership, it matches the verified account to the email link's intended recipient, and confirmation still validates expiration, request version, and single-use protection before applying the action.
explain:
A platform feature the application consumes, rather than a pattern each application reimplements. The application declares the action and names the recipient; Ordo mints the link, holds its expiry and single use, poses the challenge, verifies the proof, and checks the verified account is the one the link was addressed to. What reaches the application is an action it may apply, already attributed.

What this buys. A link in an email is normally a bearer credential: whoever holds it acts. That turns a forwarded mail, a leaked referrer, a corporate mail scanner pre-fetching URLs and a shared mailbox into grants of authority nobody issued. Here the link only names the request and the authority comes from a session the server proved separately, so a forwarded link does nothing for whoever receives it.

Ordo already has three of the four pieces. Step-up exists and is structurally human-only, so no capability token can satisfy it, which is exactly what the challenge step needs. Single use is idempotency’s. Expiry is the token tier’s.

What is missing is step 3, binding a verified account to the recipient a specific link was minted for. Membership alone is too coarse: it answers “may this person act here” and not “was this request addressed to them”.

The trap, named before anyone builds it. Steps 2 and 3 collapse into one check very easily, and collapsing them is the defect: workspace membership is not recipient identity, and a system that verified only membership would let any colleague action any colleague’s alert while looking correct in every log.

Your note names an existing product’s login as the example. Recorded generically, because what Ordo owes is the verifying half rather than any one identity provider.
suggest:
Make the safe shape the only shape. The value of putting this in the platform rather than in each application is that nobody can accidentally ship the bearer-token version where holding the URL is enough. If the surface offers a way to skip the proof, every application under deadline finds it, and the feature becomes a documentation problem rather than a guarantee. There should be no parameter meaning “just trust the link”.

Build it on 18r, and keep steps 2 and 3 as two separate checks in the code even though one call could answer both. The cost is a few lines; the benefit is that the dangerous collapse becomes a deletion somebody has to justify rather than a shortcut nobody notices.

name: A failing test leaks a server, and a leaked server is a false pass waiting to happen
sub: Found 2026-09-23 sweeping for orphans: one had been serving for 32 hours
explain:
An ordo-host process was still answering /health/live on a loopback port 32 hours after the test run that started it, parented to init. Killed.

It is not a missing cleanup. The suite spawns the real binary sixteen times and kills it sixteen times. Every kill is on the happy path, so an assertion that fails between the spawn and the kill unwinds straight past it. Given how often those suites failed while this week’s work was landing, that one is unlikely to have been the only leak; it is the one that lived long enough to be noticed.

Why it matters more than a wasted process. It holds a listening port, and the helper that picks a port for a test asks the OS for whatever is free. A later test handed a port a stale binary already owns would talk to that binary: a deployment from before three of this week’s increments, answering confidently. That is a false pass, and it reads as flakiness rather than as a bug. It cost no CPU and no database connections, which is exactly why it sat unnoticed for a day and a half.
suggest: A Drop guard on the spawn handle, so unwinding kills the child. Sixteen more explicit kills would be skipped by the next panicking assertion just as these were. A sweep at suite start is the weaker alternative: it cleans up after the damage rather than preventing it, and cannot tell one run’s leak from another’s.
where: Owed: a drop guard that kills the spawned server when a test fails; crates/ordo-host/tests/runtime.rs still kills only on the happy path. Checklist 17ad open.

name: A snapshot that restores into a later version
sub: Your idea, 2026-09-21. Most of it is already built; one deliberate refusal is in the way
decided: It may make sense to be able to create a snapshot the user can offload and keep somewhere. This will also require migration instructions - which should function cross-versions - but the concern is data destruction but that is no different than any migration where a schema change could invalidate or destroy data as part of that migration.
explain:
Most of this exists. std.space.export produces the bundle and import_space loads it back through the write protocol — not as an INSERT, so every row is re-sealed under the destination’s key, re-digested, re-chained. The loader is already the dynamic thing you asked for on the export row: “nothing here knows an entity name, a field name or a type”, built from the schema and the manifest, so a new field never means editing the loader.

One deliberate refusal is in the way. The import compares the bundle’s artifact version against the deployed one and refuses any difference. So a snapshot restores only into the exact program it was taken under — which is the version most likely to be gone by the time anyone reaches for the snapshot. A backup you can only restore into a deployment you no longer run is not a backup.

The fix is a real build, not wiring. The schema-diff engine already computes what changed between two versions and classifies each change; carrying a bundle forward is that computation applied to rows on the way in rather than to a live database. The refusal then narrows from any version difference to the changes the diff cannot carry, which is the honest boundary and the “migration instructions” you asked for.

You are right about the destruction risk and it is not a reason to stop. A cross-version restore can lose a dropped field’s values exactly as a live migration can. The asymmetry is in the snapshot’s favour: the bundle still exists afterwards, so the loss is confined to the restored space rather than being the only copy — which is what a migrated database’s dropped column is.
suggest: This is the better answer to the question you were weighing on D-B2. If the safety net for we need to go back is a bundle the customer holds, the deployment does not have to be the safety net by keeping several programs serving at once. Cheaper for you, worth more to them: their bundle outlives the deployment entirely.

Split out of 11-11 so that item stops implying key rotation covered it.

name: Refreshing the page signs you out
sub: Built 2026-10-22: reload and restart keep you signed in; session settings in 3 layers
explain:
Found testing notes v1 (2026-10-21). By design today, and a burden.

  • The session token lives in page memory only, so a reload drops it
  • Coming back costs one passkey touch every reload
  • Safe from a script reading a stored token, but most apps keep you signed in
  • Every app developer would have to solve this alone

How it would work: sign-in also sets the cookie. On load the page calls POST /auth/refresh with credentials, and the door returns a fresh token if the cookie is valid. The SDK does this in one call, so no app developer copies session.ts.

Limits: the cookie only works when the page and the door are on the same site (for example notes.inf.smg.icu and ordo.inf.smg.icu). A page on another site keeps today's behaviour, and the refusal names why.

Settings: the lifetime stays ORDO_SESSION_SECS and the 12-hour ceiling. A new setting turns it off for apps that want a touch on every reload.

asks.text: Should Ordo keep a person signed in across a reload by default?
asks.suggest: Yes, with a setting to turn it off. People expect it, and a reload that signs you out reads as a bug, as it did here.

asks.text: Should it use a renewal cookie scripts cannot read (HttpOnly, SameSite=Strict, sent only to /auth/refresh), with the token itself still in memory?
asks.suggest: Yes. A script on the page still cannot read or steal it. Sign-out and the 12-hour ceiling end it as they do today.

asks.text: How long should a person stay signed in on a device they have stopped using?
asks.suggest: 30 days, renewed by each use, as a setting. Common for consumer apps; sign-out, a passkey removal or account recovery ends it sooner.

asks.text: May a tenant set a session longer than the app developer's default, or only shorter?
asks.suggest: Within a range the app developer sets. The app developer names the minimum and maximum; a tenant picks anywhere inside it. Compliance usually shortens, but some tenants need longer.

asks.text: Should a remembered sign-in have an overall limit (sign in again after N days, however often used), and what default?
asks.suggest: A setting, default none, settable by app and tenant. Big consumer apps keep you in while you use them; a company with compliance rules sets e.g. 30 days.

asks.text: Should reading a tenant's session settings skip the passkey touch that every platform op asks for today?
asks.suggest: Yes, for this read only. It changes nothing, and a settings page that asks for a touch just to show values is a burden. Changing them still asks.

name: Ease what the SDK asks of app developers: 7 improvements
decided: 1 Yes. 2 We're basically working on v2 now so lets go ahead and plan this work out.
explain:
Fixing 2 defects showed 7 places where our SDK makes the app developer do hard work.

  • Small (S): 4 items, about 1 session together
  • Medium (M): 3 items, about 1 session each
  • Each one removes code every app would otherwise write

Small (S). 1. No polling timer. The notes page reloads every 30 s and on focus, because the server once missed tenants made after it started. That is fixed, so the SDK can reconnect on its own when the network returns and offer one nudge(). 2. A typed network error. Today a blocked cross-origin call, a server that is down and a slow server all look the same, so every app guesses. An OrdoNetworkError with kind timeout, unreachable or blocked, each naming the setting that fixes it. A timeout is reported as a timeout. 3. A device per space, handled for you. The app opens one device per shared space and must close old ones itself. ordo-react would keep them by space and close them with the provider. 4. Tabs do not overwrite each other. Two tabs on one device store can undo each other's bookkeeping. Each write takes a browser lock first (navigator.locks).

Medium (M). 5. A ready-made device. Today about 100 lines of app code (offline.ts) build the replica, the manager and a restart. The restart's order caused the filtered-list defect. openDevice() would return one ready to use. 6. Dropping unused syncs. Every tag a person clicks becomes a feed that stays open for good. The SDK would drop one shortly after the last screen using it closes. 7. One stream per tab. Browsers allow 6 connections per server, shared by all tabs. Each synced op uses one. Carrying them all on one stream removes the limit from the app developer's mind.

asks.text: Should I build the 4 small ones now: no polling timer, a typed network error, a device per space handled for you, and tabs not overwriting each other?
asks.suggest: Yes. Each removes a trap that caused or hid a defect this week, and together they are about 1 session.

asks.text: Should the 3 medium ones (a ready-made device, dropping unused syncs, one shared stream per tab) wait until notes v2 shows how much they matter?
asks.suggest: Yes, wait. Notes v2 will use more synced ops and shared spaces, which is where these start to hurt, so it tells us which to build first.

name: Tenant setup without waiting: 2 choices made
sub: Built 2026-10-21: tenant_not_ready, a sweep with a lease, stuck reported in 4 places, health degraded
explain:
Your 2 answers turned into 3 clearer asks. Setup took 0.4 s median and 1.6 s at most on CI, so most people never notice it.

  • The app developer decides what to show; Ordo gives them the status
  • Deployment-space things work before the tenant is ready
  • Only tenant writes must wait

What I'd change from today. Today a stalled setup is resumed only when a server boots, and after 15 minutes it is marked failed. Instead, any running server sweeps for stalled setups on a timer and takes one with a lease, so a dead server's job is picked up within a minute. Setup never ends by timeout. After ORDO_PROVISION_STUCK_SECS it is reported as stuck, while retries carry on with growing pauses.

Where the feedback goes. The person sees it through the status the page reads. The app developer gets it from the same status in the SDK and as an event in their security and event stream. The deployment owner sees stuck setups in /health/deep and the metrics.

What "nothing can be written" means. A write to a tenant that is not ready is refused with a retryable class, so the SDK can wait and resend it. Reads of the deployment space and the person's own account work as normal.

asks.text: Should Ordo give app developers a tenant status hook and a gate component, and refuse tenant writes before ready with a retryable "tenant not ready"?
asks.suggest: Yes. The hook gives state, step and time waited; the gate shows its children once ready and anything else meanwhile. Deployment-space screens are not held back.

asks.text: Should any running server keep retrying a stalled setup with no time limit, and report it as "stuck" after a set time to the person, app developer and owner?
asks.suggest: Yes. The job is stored, so it never silently ends. "Stuck" after a setting's time (default 5 min) shows on the status, in the app's event stream and in health.

asks.text: If a tenant can never be made, should the account stay (sign-in works and the person sees why) rather than be undone?
asks.suggest: Keep the account. Undoing it loses the person's passkey or sign-in for nothing; the status says what happened, and a retry can still finish it.

asks.text: Should a stuck setup go to the security-event stream (built), or to a separate app event stream?
asks.suggest: Security-event stream. It already reaches the app developer and needs no new feed; a separate stream adds a second thing to watch.

asks.text: Should a stuck tenant setup mark /health/deep as "degraded"?
asks.suggest: Yes. A stuck setup is a person who cannot use the app; health checks and alerts should see it without reading a new field.

name: Settings in layers: deployment, app developer, tenant, person
sub: Ordo v2. Starts after the service-interface audit (audit-one-interface-and-one-typed)
decided: a way to define custom settings ... configurable across tenants or across the whole system ... editable in the console, via code and at apply time. A second kind (secrets). Agree on renaming or removing for safety. Feature flags, definitely; may integrate with the blue green system for rolling versions out to different tenants.
explain:
One layered settings mechanism for Ordo's own settings and for app-defined ones (owner, 2026-10-22). Ordo v2.

  • Layers: deployment, app developer, tenant, person; the most specific allowed one wins
  • Declared in the program; edited at apply, in the console, or by code and CLI
  • Secrets are a second kind; feature flags are settings

Owner, 2026-10-22: "a way to define custom settings ... configurable across tenants or across the whole system ... a dynamic interface in our ... console ... editable via code and possibly via ordo itself at apply time." And: "we should have a second kind" (secrets), "agree on renaming or removing for safety", "Feature flags, definitely ... might in part have to integrate maybe with our green blue system when deploying different branches or trying to roll out different versions to different tenants."

Shape so far:

  • Declared in the program, e.g. setting maxAttachmentMb: int = 25 { range 1..500; tenant may change }: type, default, range, a description for the console, which layers may change it.
  • Layering as ruled for sessions (2026-10-21/22): a tenant may go looser or tighter inside the app developer's optional range; the deployment's absolute limits bound everything; the app developer can block a layer through the access template.
  • Three ways to edit, one path: program defaults at apply; the console on the fly; code or ordo settings set. Every change on the security stream, with who, history and undo.
  • Read in ops and routines (setting.name) and from the SDK and ordo-react; a change reaches open pages live, like data.
  • Secrets, a second kind: sealed at rest, write-only in the console, never in logs, the SDK or an export.
  • Renaming or removing a setting at apply follows the schema change classes: safe ones apply, risky ones refuse and name the fix.
  • Feature flags are boolean (or enum) settings per tenant or person. Targeting may join tenant-builds (27t): named tenants, groups, a percentage.
  • Ordo's own 31 hardcoded values and 15 deployment-only values (docs/settings.md) move onto the same mechanism.
  • The console (18o) is unbuilt; its Settings screen comes with it. Today the same edits go through platform ops and the CLI.

asks.text: Should feature flags and tenant builds (a version for chosen tenants) share one way to pick who gets what: named tenants, groups, or a percentage?
asks.suggest: Yes, one targeting model. A flag turns a feature on for some tenants; a build serves a version to some tenants. One rule set means one console screen and one audit trail.

name: Ordo Lang: the language as a library, without the platform
sub: Future, 2026-10-03. Planned in tooling-and-embedding-plan.md Track B
explain:
Use the language alone, in any language's app. What it includes decides what it is (owner, 2026-10-03: "Is it just to make writing SQL easier? Is it a better spring boot?").

  • Compiler alone: typed functions and guarded SQL.
  • Engine: chain, undo, sealed fields, live.
  • Platform: sign-in, tenants, deploys.

The compiler already lowers guards into SQL and builds the language's null and ordering rules into it, so a compile-only tier carries permissions with no runtime: the caller is passed in. What needs code at run time is the hash chain, sealed fields and keys, undo, live updates and retry safety. The chain's byte format is frozen, so those parts should be one shared core (WASM or a C ABI) rather than rewritten per language. A Postgres extension (27ae, native-datastore) could move the chain and live updates into the database, which would let the compile-only tier keep them. Plan: docs/tooling-and-embedding-plan.md Track B.

asks.text: Should the compile-only tier include permissions, by compiling guards into the SQL with the caller passed in?
asks.suggest: Yes. Guards already compile to SQL, so permissions cost nothing at run time, and that is what sets it apart from a plain SQL generator.

asks.text: Should live sync come with the embedded engine but not the compile-only tier?
asks.suggest: Yes. Live updates need something listening while the app runs; compile-only has nothing running. A Postgres extension could change that later (27ae).

asks.text: Which comes first: typed functions for every language (compile only), or the embedded engine?
asks.suggest: Compile only, for every language. Each language is mostly templates over the interface file, so it is cheap and proves the language works on its own.

asks.text: Should the engine's chain, keys and live parts be one shared core (WASM or a C library), never rewritten per language?
asks.suggest: Yes. The chain's byte format is frozen; one core keeps every language byte for byte identical, and a rewrite per language would drift.

name: How far back may a lagging tenant be, and what ends the contract?
sub: Settled 2026-09-21. One version, with a snapshot behind it, and the downgrade walks one step at a time
decided: One version back + ability for snapshots (for requesting customers on the app dev side) and ensure step by step downgrading in schema.
explain:
One version back is the bound. A deployment holds two artifacts at most, and a tenant two behind quarantines regardless, because a window that has been missed is not a window. That keeps this a bounded build rather than a platform that serves whatever anyone is still on.

The snapshot is the safety net, and it is requested rather than universal. Your words: for requesting customers on the app dev side. That follows from your correction to D-B — the contract is app-developer to customer — so the app developer asks for a customer’s snapshot and the platform makes one available. Generating one for every tenant by default would be a storage cost and a disclosure surface imposed on people who never asked.

Step by step downgrading is the sharpest clause, because it decides the shape of the build rather than whether to do it. A cross-version restore walks the chain one version at a time and never diffs the ends. Three reasons it has to: the diff engine only ever compares adjacent versions, so an end-to-end diff would need a second classifier that could disagree with the first; a step that cannot be carried then names itself, so an operator learns where it stops rather than only that the ends disagree; and downgrade loses at a specific step, since a field added at version 5 has no values before it.

What it obliges, stated plainly: the diff engine plans forward. Each step has to state its own down path, or state that it has none, and no artifact carries that property today. That is the real work in 11-10b and it is larger than lifting the version check.
suggest: Scope the down path before building 11-10b. Everything else in that item is mechanical once each version can say what coming down through it costs.

Quarantine is now the default, for a tenant with no contract, and it is what the plan already builds. A tenant whose deployment or maintenance window has not opened is served the artifact their database matches until it does.

The cost, said plainly, because your ruling moves onto it. I recommended unconditional quarantine precisely to avoid this: a deployment that can serve a lagging tenant the older program is a deployment holding two artifacts. Today it holds exactly one, swapped whole, and every request assumes it resolves the same artifact as every other. Contracted lag means the previous version stays loaded and the resolver picks per tenant. That is a real increment and it is not in the eleven already planned.

I am not arguing the ruling. A maintenance window is a thing customers buy and a platform that cannot honour one is a platform with a gap. But the bound on it is now the question, and it is open above as D-B2.
suggest: Build the default quarantine first, with T0 to T10 as planned, and hold the contracted path until D-B2 pins how far back it reaches. Building the tolerance before its bound is how one previous version becomes every previous version.

name: Per-tenant buckets: the requirements, and four defects found on the way
sub: U0–U6 built. The attach op is now reachable through the door; U7 to U10 remain
decided: recomendation + above.
explain:
The storage side mirrors the database side (built as libraries, binary wires the single variant), with one gap the databases do not have: the blob pipeline holds a store rather than a resolver, and the export path reads the same field, so the serving path has no per-space seam at all. The sweep, the re-seal pass and space erasure already resolve per space and are correct as written.

Where storage genuinely differs. The store interface has no listing, so the database is the only enumeration of objects and a bucket without its database is inert. An unreachable bucket refuses the blob routes rather than quarantining the tenant, because everything else about that tenant still works. A write is object first and reference second, so a half-succeeded upload leaves an object nothing names. And bytes stored is summed from the references in the tenant’s database, so the gap-not-zero ruling attaches to the database being unreachable, never to the bucket.

Four defects found while specifying, which is the useful part. 1. Nothing records which store an object went to, while the attach op promises a split population, so the sweep can delete against the wrong store, succeed (deleting an absent key succeeds), remove the reference and strand the bytes; erasure then reports a deletion that missed them. 2. The attach op returns the credential label to a tenant. 3. The S3 configuration derived Debug over its access key and secret, so any formatted line carried the credential. Fixed 2026-09-21, with a test. 4. Plaintext HTTP is admitted to a fixed local list; every other host must be HTTPS, which means a BYO endpoint may still point anywhere until the attach-time allowlist lands.

Eleven increments, U0 to U10, four of which must ship with their database twin.

Built 2026-09-24 (U6): a tenant can be given a bucket of its own, through the door. std.space.attachBucket has existed since the blob tier shipped and no deployment could reach it. It is registered now, and only on a deployment that will actually honour an attachment: blob routing set to attached, a store configured, and a credential provider installed. On a deployment without those, the op stays absent and the startup census says which piece is missing — because the sentence the op prints for a consent page says the objects are in the tenant’s bucket, and a deployment that recorded that while putting every byte in its own bucket would be making a promise rather than missing a feature.

Seven checks before anything is written, in the same order the database side refuses in: the target’s shape, the endpoint is on your allowlist, a plaintext endpoint needs a development flag, it is not the deployment’s own bucket, the credential is one you installed, the space holds no objects yet, and no other tenant is in that bucket. Then a probe: the platform signs one request at the bucket and only stores the attachment if the credential worked. A tenant does not find out at their first upload, after their bytes are already on the wire.

Two defects from the earlier list are closed by this. Defect 1 (nothing records which store an object went to, so the sweep can strand bytes) is closed by refusing to attach a space that already holds objects, which is your D-S2 ruling. Defect 4 (a BYO endpoint could point anywhere) is closed by the allowlist and the development flag.

Two things need you rather than the next implementer. D-S2’s carve-out for a one-for-one migration is not built and is described on its own row. And the custody record is written to both the tenant’s own security stream and the deployment’s; your D-F ruling removed the tenant’s chain entry, and its reasoning — that a tenant showing where their data went belongs to the app — arguably reaches the tenant’s security stream too. Keeping it preserves what the op has always done; removing it is a one-line change if you want the narrower reading.
suggest: Refuse an attach over existing objects, because the alternative is adopting bytes nobody can enumerate. Leave the objects when the tenant owns the bucket, and say so in the disclosure: the platform should not delete from a store it does not own, and destroying the epoch already makes them unreadable. Refuse the second tenant on a bucket declared as one tenant’s own, since that is what “own” means. The other five are mechanical and my recommendations are in the plan.

Erasure deletes every object in the resolved store today. The disclosure for a tenant who owns their bucket says the objects are theirs and removing them is theirs to do. Both cannot be true, and the disclosure is the half the tenant has already been shown.

It is also what makes the custody choice mean anything: under platform custody, erasure destroys the keys and the objects become unopenable wherever they sit; under the tenant's own perimeter, erasure destroys the keys and the objects stay readable because the tenant holds them.

name: Which KMS, and what the master key does about it
sub: Dissolved 2026-09-21: there is no KMS to choose. The deployment reads a mount, and whatever fills it is above and invisible

explain:
You ruled credentials are KMS first, with environment or file optional. The provider abstraction is unchanged; what changes is which implementation ships first, and that needs a name.

The inconsistency to settle at the same time: the deployment’s own master key already opens from a sealed file or the environment. Requiring a KMS for a tenant’s database password while the key that wraps every tenant’s data still opens from a file is backwards, since the master key is the more valuable secret by a distance.

The cluster already reads its secrets from GCP Secret Manager through the external-secrets operator, which is the shape a deployment here would use.
suggest: Your answer removes the inconsistency rather than settling it: if the service reads a mount and never knows what filled it, the master key opening from a file is the same mechanism rather than a weaker one. Rotation has two different answers and they must not be confused. A credential rotating (a database password, a bucket key pair) is ordinary: the value in the mount changes and the deployment must pick it up without a restart, with the rotator leaving the old value valid until the new one lands. The master key rotating is not that: it is rewrap-master, which is built, transactional and proved not to move a search digest. A tenant’s data keys are a third thing, the re-seal pass, also built.

name: Erasure proof belongs to the app, and what Ordo collects for it
sub: Confirmed 2026-09-21, and extended: the platform gives the application the tools to prove it, filed as 17ab
decided: Confirm. There should be the ability to match in some zero trust chain. The decision in these cases would be a transaction between app dev and client, but we should enable them with tools to do it.
explain:
You said erasure proof belongs to the application rather than to Ordo, and that the platform can collect something for the audit log automatically. That resolves the contradiction cleanly and I agree with where the line falls.

What Ordo does under a tenant-owned bucket: destroy the keys, leave the objects, and write what it left into the audit chain as a custody action: how many objects remained, which store they are in, and the epoch whose destruction made them unopenable. That is a fact the deployment can honestly assert, because it is about its own act.

What Ordo does not do: claim the bytes are gone. It did not delete them and cannot see into a perimeter it was told is the tenant’s, so the application makes that claim to its own user, using the record above as its evidence.

Under platform custody nothing changes: erasure destroys the keys and the objects become unopenable wherever they sit, which is the same act with a different disclosure.
suggest: It is the only version where every sentence is true. The alternative, deleting from a store the tenant owns, is the platform reaching into a perimeter it was told was not its own, irreversibly, on a call that reads as routine.

name: Must the custody disclosure state occupancy, and is a second tenant on an own-perimeter database refused?
sub: Ruled 2026-09-25: one tenant per database, same for buckets, and the unit is the database rather than the cluster. Broader than the question asked
decided: 1 tenant 1 database. same for buckets. database/schema not cluster.
explain:
The ruling is broader than the question, and the code changed to match. What was asked was whether a second tenant inside a declared own perimeter is refused. What was answered is the general rule: a database holds one tenant, custody does not enter into it. So the two refusals built first (one per direction, distinguished by which side declared OwnPerimeter) collapsed into one, DatabaseOccupied, and the test that asserted two platform-managed tenants could share a database was inverted rather than deleted — the behaviour it named is the behaviour that changed.

“database/schema not cluster” is the half that keeps this affordable. Many tenants on one Postgres server stays the ordinary case; what may not be shared is the database. That is why ORDO_PG_ATTACH_HOSTS is still a list of hosts, and why a tenant costs a database rather than a server.

What the question actually is. A pool is per target, not per tenant: a hundred tenants attached to one database share one pool and one credential, and inside that database the only separation is the $space column and the software defences. DbCustody says who runs the cluster and nothing about whether the tenant is alone on it. So a consent page can print “your data is in a database your organisation runs” to a tenant sharing it with three others. The sentence is true and reads as something stronger.

What is built. Two refusals, from both directions: a second tenant into a database already held as someone's own perimeter, and an incoming own-perimeter claim over a database someone is already in. Both end in one database holding two tenants with one told the perimeter is theirs, and arrival order is not a difference worth two outcomes. Occupancy is exposed as a fact (spacedb::occupants) rather than written into a sentence, which is your occupancy ruling: the platform records and exposes, the developer writes the words. DbCustody::disclosure is unchanged.

What this leaves open is its own row, db-default-tier: a tenant created without $db still shares the control database, and whether that must end is a much larger change than this one.
suggest:
Occupancy survives the ruling as a fact rather than a disclosure. spacedb::occupants stays, because it is what enforces the refusal and what R-S2's fleet view reads; it just cannot return more than one attached tenant any more. DbCustody::disclosure is unchanged, and the ambiguity it was going to need a clause for — “your own database” printed to a tenant sharing one — cannot arise.

“Same for buckets” lands on U6, which is the bucket attach op and is not built yet, so it arrives as a requirement rather than a change.

explain:
Your ruling on occupancy says the platform records and exposes the fact and the developer writes the sentence. This is the half a developer cannot write their way out of: a second tenant placed inside a perimeter the first was told was theirs is not a disclosure that can be corrected afterwards.

Built 2026-09-24, and it is wider than this row asks. The question here was a second tenant inside a bucket declared as one tenant’s own. Your later ruling — “1 tenant 1 database. same for buckets.” — makes it general: a bucket holds one tenant, and which custody either side declared does not enter into it. One refusal, not one per direction. The database tier built the narrow reading first and had to collapse it; this one was built general from the start.

A per-tenant key prefix is not a way around it, and this is a judgement worth your eye. A prefix looks like what a schema is to a database — a namespace inside the container — but a database schema is a line the server draws through its own privilege system, while a key prefix is enforced only by a bucket policy on the tenant’s side that the platform cannot enforce, and the credential behind that prefix signs for the whole bucket. So two tenants in one bucket under different prefixes are two tenants in one bucket, and the second is refused.

What this does not touch: tenants who attach nothing still share the deployment’s own bucket, separated by their space id in the key. That is the exact twin of the open question about the shared default database and nothing here assumes an answer to it.

name: Attaching a bucket that already holds objects
sub: Refusal built 2026-09-24. The exception is ruled 2026-09-29: allowed when every object matches a record. Not built
explain:
The attach op promises today that existing objects are adopted. That promise is what makes the sweep dangerous: it can delete against the wrong store, succeed (deleting a key that is not there succeeds), remove the reference, and leave bytes nothing can ever name. Erasure then reports a deletion that did not reach them.

Recording the store on each reference is the right answer later: it is what moving a tenant between buckets will need.

The refusal is built (2026-09-24). A space that already holds object references cannot be pointed at a new bucket: the platform records no per-object store, so the sweep would delete against the wrong bucket, succeed (deleting an absent key succeeds by design), retire the reference, and leave bytes nothing can ever name. A retry of an attachment that is already standing is not refused by this — otherwise the same call would stop working the moment the tenant started uploading, which is the opposite of what a retry should do.

The exception you named is not built, and it needs you. “unless everything matches i.e. a 1 for 1 migration would be indistinguishable” is right and is not free: the store interface has no listing, deliberately, so the only way to prove a one-for-one copy is one existence check per object reference against the new bucket. For a tenant with a hundred thousand objects that is a hundred thousand requests inside one door call. Two things are unspecified: what bounds that work, and what happens on a partial match — most objects present and three missing is neither a migration nor an empty space, and the answer decides whether this is a parameter on the attach or a separate migration command.
suggest: Refuse. One query, it matches how row-holding is already checked elsewhere, and it makes adopting a full bucket a migration rather than a side effect.

name: Per-tenant databases: the requirements, and two calls
sub: Ruled 2026-09-21. T0 to T9 built: a tenant can be given a database of its own through the door, an operator can see what version each database is at, resolve a restore by the tenant's id instead of a hostname, and read a per-target report with names beside ids. T10 (the record) remains
decided: Since it is configurable that belongs to the app developer to disclose. A gap. But if it is unreachable transactions cannot happen, unless we mean the local ledger? A gap would be better.
explain:
The gap, stated precisely. The routing seam, the attachment table, provisioning onto a target and the routed variants of the directory, the invalidation bus, the replay cache and the security drain all exist. The binary builds the single-database version of every one, so no tenant can have its own database today whatever the design says. No environment variable selects routing and nothing installs a credential.

A landmine worth knowing about. Turning routing on alone would deny every request in an attached tenant: its founding membership row is written to its own database, and the door reads memberships from the control database. The routed reader exists and nothing calls it. That is the kind of defect that looks like an authorisation bug for a day.

Credentials, answered. The attachment table holds a label and never a secret, which is already asserted by a test. The label names a provider, the way the key provider is named today, and the first provider is a mounted directory with the label as the file name, on the same reasoning that makes the database password prefer a file over an environment variable. Five things the door must never return, each with its own test, including that the text of a failed dial never reaches a caller.

Eleven increments, T0 to T10, smallest first, each with files, named tests, a done-when and a model tier: pin the current behaviour, fix the directory, collapse to one resolver, credentials, the switch, quarantine, the jobs table, schema everywhere, the attach op, operator surfaces, and the record.

T7 finished 2026-09-25. Its last two pieces landed: R-S5, which serialises attaching a tenant against applying a schema (and reuses the apply lock that already existed rather than adding a second one), and R-S2, the fleet view — one row per target in the control database saying which schema version it is known to be at and when that was last confirmed. The fleet view is a cache and the code enforces that: nothing routes, gates or refuses from it, and there is no way to read a version out of it without the timestamp that says how old the answer is.

Built 2026-09-24 (T8): the gap above is closed. The landmine described in this row was real and is gone; a tenant created with $db now gets a database of its own, its schema, its founding member and its $spacedb row, through one call at the door. It is a parameter of std.space.create, not a separate attach op, and that follows your own 2026-09-13 ruling: there is no owner yet to consent at provisioning and no space without a place to store it, so the system chooses. A database attach op gated on owner consent would have refused every space that had ever been written to.

One new setting an operator must know about. ORDO_PG_ATTACH_HOSTS is the D-E allowlist and it denies by default: unset, no tenant can be attached to any host. That is deliberate and matches how every other address-shaped control here behaves, but it means the feature does nothing until the hosts are named.

What was not built, because you ruled it away. The plan had the attachment fact joining the tenant’s own founding group; D-F says no, so the record is the deployment’s stream alone. Occupancy is recorded and exposed rather than written into a sentence, which is your occupancy ruling applied to the database tier the same way D-S8 applied it to buckets.

Built 2026-09-24 (T9): the operator surfaces. ordo restore --record --tenant resolves the tenant’s database through $spacedb instead of trusting a typed hostname, and prints which database it found. An unreachable target now leaves an explicit gap in the usage ledger — your own ruling above, word for word — in a new $usage_gaps table rather than a row of zeros in $usage, and a bigger defect fell out while building it: the rollup used to abort every tenant’s metering the moment any one target was unreachable, not just that target’s own tenants. Fixed alongside the gap, since the gap mechanism has nothing to prove without it. A new ordo fleet command reads the control database and prints each target’s schema version, its custody and which tenants are on it, every tenant with its name beside its id.

Partial, honestly. R-O6 named six facts an operator must see in one place; ordo fleet answers three (version, occupancy, custody) because it opens a database connection, not a socket into a running replica. The other three — the live quarantine list, the connection budget, which credential labels a node holds — are a replica’s own memory, and belong on /health/ready instead (T5 already built the quarantine half there). Printing a stale snapshot of those as if it were live would read as complete and would not be.
suggest:
Occupancy: the platform records and exposes the fact (which target a space sits on, and whether it is alone); the developer who configured it writes the sentence for the person whose data it is, in their own product’s words. Ordo does not invent a disclosure on their behalf and does not let the fact be unavailable.

The ledger, and your question was the right one: “unreachable” means two different things. Requests and rows returned are counted at the door, in the replica’s memory, and land in the control database: a tenant whose own database is down still generates those, because its callers arrive and are refused, and that is real activity. Writes, rows written and bytes are a measurement of the tenant’s database, taken at rollup. If it cannot be read, the measurement did not happen, and that period records a gap rather than a zero. A zero asserts nothing happened, silently discounts the bill and hides the outage. When the target returns the period can be measured again, because the command log it measures is still there.

name: The console, the operator, and how deployments are packed
sub: Ruled 2026-09-21: a private fork that pulls upstream carries the operator; the open repository carries the server and the console
explain:
Names. “Control plane” means a deployment’s own system space and nothing else. The surface above is the console. The software that creates and configures deployments is the operator. “Platform service” is retired.

A correction to the definition you read back. A deployment is not a process: it is one database, one program, one master key and one space of its own, served by one or more replicas. Several replicas are ordinary, which is why the supervisor elects a leader and flushes usage per replica. Scaling out adds replicas, not deployments. And an Ordo deployment is not a Kubernetes Deployment, which is one way to run its replicas.

One console, two modes. Bundled with a deployment it manages that one, which is what a self-hoster gets. Run by an operator it manages many. Same surface, and in both it reaches a deployment through the door as an owner with a token, never into its database. Otherwise it is a privileged back door around your own rule, and it has to be built twice.

On packing to save cost. Several deployments may share a pod, a node or a Postgres cluster, as long as each keeps its own database, its own master key and its own process. One process serving several deployments is the shape that trades away the custody perimeter and needs the engine changes 18n found. Worth knowing where the money actually goes: a deployment’s cost is its database and its idle memory, not its pod. Ten small pods against one shared Postgres cluster is cheap; ten Postgres servers is not.
suggest:
A fork that pulls is a different animal from a long-lived branch, and the objection to branches does not apply. What makes it work is the seam: the operator must attach through interfaces the open repository already has, the door, the configuration surface and the usage ledger. The obligation that creates is upstream’s: if the fork ever has to patch engine code to do its job, the seam is in the wrong place and the interface is what to fix, not the fork.

On packing: the saving from two deployments in one pod is the pod’s own overhead, which is small. What costs is the second set of everything a replica holds: its pool, its supervisor, its access engine, the live program and its schema graph. So the first lever is one replica per deployment by default, and the second is one Postgres cluster with a database each. Two replicas is availability you switch on for a deployment that has earned it, with the complexity you suspected: leadership handover, and a quarantine or a swap that has to be true on both.

asks.text: Nothing open. Answered 2026-09-21: a private fork that pulls upstream, not a branch, with the open repository carrying the server and the console and the fork carrying the operator.
For launch, should the console manage one deployment (bundled with it, as a self-hoster runs it), leaving many-deployment management to the operator later?
asks.suggest: Yes. It is what every open-source user needs, and it matches the 2026-09-21 ruling: the open repo carries the console, the private fork the operator.

asks.text: Should the launch console cover: health and deploys, tenants and people, sign-in settings, shares and links, the security log, usage, and settings?
asks.suggest: Yes, read first, then the edits Ordo's ops already offer. Each screen calls existing platform ops through the door, so the console adds no back door.

asks.text: Should the console be built with ordo-react and served by the deployment itself, at its own path, signed in by passkey like any app?
asks.suggest: Yes. It proves our own SDK on a real app and needs no second server. Its sign-in is the deployment owner's passkey, with step-up for changes.

asks.text: Should the deployment owner see every tenant's name, status, counts and usage, but not its members or shares unless they hold a role in it?
asks.suggest: Yes. It keeps tenants' privacy as Ordo has it today. Searching people across tenants waits for v2, with a logged break-glass.

asks.text: The console shows Ordo data read through the deployment's API. Should its page use ordo-sdk for those calls and plain React for the rest?
asks.suggest: Yes, ordo-sdk only, no ordo-react data hooks. The calls go through the console's own server with its key, so the SDK client fits; the hooks assume a page on its own Ordo backend.

asks.text: Should the console ship as its own container beside the deployment (same pod, own address), with one compose file and Helm chart for both?
asks.suggest: Yes. Separate app and origin, as ruled, yet one thing to install. A self-hoster can still run it anywhere else.

asks.text: Should the console's address share a site with the deployment's (e.g. console.example.com beside api.example.com)?
asks.suggest: Yes, recommended in the docs. The renewal cookie is same-site only, so on another site every reload of the console asks for a passkey touch.

asks.text: At launch, should settings that only exist as environment variables show read-only, with how to change them, until v2's settings mechanism?
asks.suggest: Yes. Settings that already have an op are editable at launch. The rest need settings-layers to change safely while running.

asks.text: Should the full caps page wait for v2, with limits on the settings screen and hit counts on the monitoring screen at launch?
asks.suggest: Yes. Launch shows every limit and how often it was hit; the page with history and alerts comes in v2.

asks.text: At launch, should query performance be a "slow ops" table from the metrics Ordo already keeps, with full tracing in v2?
asks.suggest: Yes. Ordo keeps per-op timings today, but no slow-query log or query plans. Tracing is a large piece of its own.

asks.text: Should the launch console have rollback to an earlier version and a preview of what an apply will change?
asks.suggest: Yes, both. Rollback is a small wrapper over code that exists; a preview is what a less technical owner needs before applying.

asks.text: Should the console's runtime drivers ship in this order: Docker first, then Kubernetes, with a "manual" driver (shows the commands) always?
asks.suggest: Yes. Docker covers most self-hosters and the quickstart; Kubernetes covers the Helm chart; manual covers every other platform.

asks.text: Should the console's own database default to a SQLite file, with Postgres optional? This changes the 2026-09-25 default (the shared cluster).
asks.suggest: Yes. Then the console still runs when the deployment's database cluster is what broke.

asks.text: Should the console hold a revocable key for reads and plain changes, while every platform change still needs your own passkey touch, passed through?
asks.suggest: Yes. The alternative, the console keeping a long-lived owner session, would make your presence a stored thing anyone with the console's database could use.

asks.text: Should the docs lead with 2 containers from 1 image (deployment and console), with "both in one" for trying it out?
asks.suggest: Yes. One image as you wanted, and the console keeps running when a redeploy or a crash takes the deployment down.

asks.text: If the console owner loses every passkey, should the failsafe be a command run inside the image (ordo console recover) that prints a one-time setup code?
asks.suggest: Yes, plus recovery codes at setup and a second owner. Shell access to the image proves you run it; the command is logged and ends every old console session.

asks.text: When a console owner signs in with a recovery code, should their old passkeys be removed?
asks.suggest: Yes, remove them. A recovery code is used when a passkey is lost or stolen; keeping it leaves a stolen device able to sign in. The owner enrols a fresh one on the spot.

asks.text: Should the console run succession only in tenants where you hold the owner role?
asks.suggest: Yes. Succession runs in the deployment's space, so through the console it could reach any tenant. Every other console action in a tenant needs your owner role there; this keeps one rule.

name: Heavy writes to a tenant can lock every member out
explain:
Seen: under about 100 concurrent writes, every member of a tenant got 403 for seconds (two-instance test, 3 of 4 runs).

  • Cause: each door rebuild dialled the tenant with Pool::connect, which runs the platform tables' DDL in one transaction. Its ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS deadlocked with a blob write. An unread space is denied for everyone.
  • Fix: the rebuild reads with Pool::connect_without_ddl.

Regression looks like: deadlock detected in the log beside "members could not be read", and a whole tenant refused.

Guarding tests: the_doors_read_does_not_deadlock_with_a_blob_write in crates/ordo-host/tests/provision_target.rs; scripts/two-instances.sh concurrent_writes_stay_consistent (4 of 4 after). Still open: a writer's first connection per instance runs the same DDL; a failed rebuild answers 403 instead of 503.

asks.text: When a rebuild fails for a passing reason (deadlock, timeout), should the door keep serving the last good member list?
asks.suggest: Yes, for a bounded time (default 60 s, a setting), retrying meanwhile; deny past that bound or on a lasting error. A removed member keeps access at most that long, similar to the session refresh today.

where: Deadlock fixed (dcb7c3fb, 5dde8f36). Door keeps the last good member list up to ORDO_DOOR_STALE_GRACE_SECS (60) on a passing failure; test door_stale_grace.rs

name: Tenant database grouping: many tenants in one database (v2)
explain:
Owner, 2026-10-27: Ordo v2. A deployment may group tenants into one database on a cluster, with as many groups as it wants, at its own choice.

  • A tenant still lives in exactly one database; a database may hold a group.
  • Inside a group, tables are named however makes sense.

Why: 1 database per tenant costs a catalog per database (about 7.5 MB empty), autovacuum across every database, and a migration per database on every deploy. A notes-style app (1 user, 1 tenant) with a million users would need a million databases.

asks.text: How are tenants kept apart inside a grouped database?
asks.suggest: A schema per tenant (t_<space>.notes). Each tenant keeps its own tables, keys and command log; moving one out is a schema copy. Shared tables with a tenant column scale further but mix rows; keep that for later if schemas run out.

asks.text: Is a single database per tenant still the default, with grouping opt-in?
asks.suggest: Yes. Grouping is the deployment owner's choice per group; with nothing set, behaviour is today's.

asks.text: Can a tenant move between a group and a database of its own?
asks.suggest: Yes, as a recorded, step-up operation, using the live-move work already planned (18e). A tenant that grows leaves its group.

where: Ordo v2 (owner, 2026-10-27)

name: Ordo mass-scale single-tenant application (v2 design)
explain:
Owner, 2026-10-27: Ordo v2 design. A plain app where tenants make no sense is first-class, and must be able to reach the scale.

  • Walls: the member snapshot in memory, one log chain per space, feeds waking every follower, central sign-in, one database per space.
  • Most users only read, so reads should be served near them.

asks.text: What should one space handle?
asks.suggest: Design for 10 million users and 5,000 writes a second, measured; then 100 million and up with partitioning and log lanes.

asks.text: In what order should the walls fall?
asks.suggest: Access checked in the database instead of a member snapshot, then group commit on the command log, then feeds that wake only those who can see a row, sign-in on its own database, and partitioning within a space.

asks.text: How should reads that are not public reach the edge?
asks.suggest: ETag and 304 on every read first. Then a stable marking on ops, cached per tenant at the CDN with the token checked at the edge, purged by tag on change. Signed links for private files are already ruled.

asks.text: Should app users' tokens be verifiable at the edge?
asks.suggest: Yes, signed with a key whose public half a CDN worker holds, as the identity service's tokens are. Without it, nothing private can be served from the edge.

where: Ordo v2, going into design (owner, 2026-10-27). Includes edge caching beyond the public path (docs/design-public-path.md).

asks.suggest: Yes. Both manage the deployment; one cluster fewer to run. It stays a separate database with its own role.

asks.text: Q2. May a machine key do platform writes that need a passkey touch from a person?
asks.suggest: Yes, for the deployment's own space. A machine cannot touch; its key is the proof. Every use is recorded under its name and it can be revoked.

asks.text: Q3. Is a 10-minute token lifetime enough to end someone's access, with no live revoke check?
asks.suggest: Yes, for v1. Ending access takes effect within 10 minutes. A live check can come later if needed.

asks.text: Q4. Should deployment admins keep today's read-only tenant admin views (gated by a touch)?
asks.suggest: Keep them. They are the console's tenant screens; they never open tenant data.

asks.text: Q5. ordo login by browser with a local callback only, and a device code later?
asks.suggest: Yes. A local callback works on any developer machine. A device code is for remote shells; add it when someone needs it.

asks.text: Q6. Remove the claim code, while app tenants keep their own first-comer setting?
asks.suggest: Yes. The claim code goes from the deployment. A tenant's first-comer option is the app developer's and stays.

asks.text: Q7. On upgrade, do existing console owners re-enrol through an invite?
asks.suggest: Accept it. No live deployment has console owners yet, so nobody is affected today.

asks.text: Q8. Should the identity service have its own address and port (8082)?
asks.suggest: Yes. Passkeys bind to an address, so it needs its own. Behind the TLS proxy it can be a path or a subdomain.

asks.text: Q9. Lifetimes: tokens 10 minutes, CLI sessions 30 days idle and 90 days at most, invites 7 days?
asks.suggest: Yes, as stated, each a setting with these defaults.

asks.text: Q10. Should the console be able to restart only the deployment, not itself or the identity service?
asks.suggest: Yes. The console never controls the service that signs people in to it.

name: Deployment people: sign-in, machines, CLI, and an audit of every door act
explain:
Owner, 2026-10-27: Ordo is set up for others from the back end, with no claim. One admin role for now. Every door act records who did it, in a log that cannot be changed.

  • Two account lists for now: the console's own, and deployment accounts.
  • The console creates deployment accounts by expiring, single-use invite links.

asks.text: How should a machine (your provisioning service, CI) act on a deployment with no person present?
asks.suggest: A key issued by the Ordo server, like the console's key: a key pair per machine, admin role, revocable, every use recorded under its name. Your provisioning service gets one when it creates the instance.

asks.text: How should the CLI sign in?
asks.suggest: A per-machine token the console mints for a deployment account, revocable and recorded. A device login (ordo login with a code you approve) can come later.

asks.text: How is the first admin of a new instance made?
asks.suggest: By the call that creates it: the provisioning service, or a one-time command on the host, names the first admin or machine key. No page to claim, no code to type.

asks.text: Should the door's audit log be signed by default, so an edit shows?
asks.suggest: Yes. Every door act goes to the deployment's hash-chained security log with who, what and from which client. The signing key is generated at first boot instead of being optional.

name: Usability and performance audit: what to fix first
explain:
Fable audited usability and performance (2026-10-25), measured. Full list: docs/audit-2026-10-25-ux-perf.md.

  • Worst: access guards scan whole tables, so a read at 5,000 notes takes 450 ms and a device sync 33 s.
  • Also high: stuck uploads, no first-run guide for you, offline reload looks like sign-out.

asks.text: Should the index fix go first, ahead of everything else?
asks.suggest: Yes. It is quadratic in a tenant's data, so every real user past a few hundred rows feels it. It keeps null comparisons exact: plain = only where neither side can be null.

asks.text: Then the other 3 highs, one at a time, before the mediums?
asks.suggest: Yes. Stuck upload and offline reload are quick page fixes; the first-run guide and boot message are a docs pass. The mediums follow in the audit's order.

name: After a contest: what comes back, what stays
explain:
Follow-up to the contest fix (2026-10-25). A contest now removes every sign-in method and second factor linked since the case opened.

  • That includes a password or outside sign-in the thief linked.
  • A "second step after a passkey too" setting the thief turned on stays on.

The owner's own second factors were removed when the recovery completed and do not come back; their secrets are gone, so they are enrolled again.

asks.text: Is removing every sign-in method linked since the case opened right, not only passkeys and second factors?
asks.suggest: Yes. A Google sign-in the thief linked is as much a way back in as a passkey.

asks.text: Should a contest also reset sign-in settings the thief changed during the case, back to their value when it opened?
asks.suggest: Yes. Otherwise the thief's choices outlive them.
