name: Guessing a password or a link password has no limit
explain:
Found by two pen tests (2026-10-24), both confirmed.

  • Password sign-in: 200 wrong passwords, all 401, no delay, no lock.
  • Share-link password: 60 wrong in 13 s, no limit. Lockout is off by default, per your 2026-10-22 ruling, and nothing stands behind it.

asks.text: Should both have an always-on slowdown per account or per link, separate from the lockout, so a guess cannot run fast but the real person is never locked out?
asks.suggest: Yes. After 5 wrong tries each further try waits longer (1 s, 2 s, 4 s, up to 60 s), per account or per link, across nodes. Your lockout stays off by default; this only slows guessing.

asks.text: Should a link password's minimum length rise from 4 to 8 characters?
asks.suggest: Yes. A 4-character password falls to an online guess in hours even with the slowdown; 8 takes years.

name: What health checks tell a stranger
explain:
Found by the deployment audit (2026-10-24). Anyone can read /health/ready and /health/deploy in full.

  • They show each check's detail, credential_labels, quarantined tenants, node id, version and pending deploys.
  • Ruling 17t says the body reports whether a program is active; it does not say who may read it.

asks.text: Should a caller without the deployment owner's token get the status alone, with the full body for the owner?
asks.suggest: Yes. A probe needs only the status. The detail maps the deployment for an attacker. ordo deploy --host keeps working; it already holds the owner's token.

name: Three answers the matrix found no rule for

asks.text: A manager or owner asks for another person's private file they may not read. Should the answer be not_found, the same as a handle that does not exist?
asks.suggest: Yes. Today it answers 403 access_guard, which tells them the file exists. howto-files.md already promises not_found.

asks.text: Should a share-link guest, a link token or an agent be able to list the tenants a person belongs to (GET /auth/spaces)?
asks.suggest: No. These tokens act inside one tenant for one purpose. Listing every place the person belongs leaks their memberships.

asks.text: Should a signed-out or revoked token be refused before the door says whether a live stream exists?
asks.suggest: Yes. Check the token first, then the stream. Today an unknown stream answers 404 to any token, even a dead one.

name: What a contest undoes after a stolen recovery
explain:
Follow-up to the recovery fix (2026-10-24). A contest now voids unused codes and ends the thief's sessions.

  • It does not remove second factors the thief enrolled after the quarantine ended.
  • After the 72-hour window, a passkey added by recovery is an ordinary passkey.

asks.text: Should a contest also remove every second factor and passkey enrolled since the case opened?
asks.suggest: Yes. Otherwise the owner may face a step only the thief can give. The record names each one removed.

name: Short-lived signed links for files
explain:
Owner, 2026-10-24: newcomers will not have a second domain, so signed links are the way, as on denizens.ellanor's R2.

  • A link opened in a browser carries no token, so private files cannot be plain links today.
  • A sealed file is ciphertext in the bucket, so its link must be the door's.

An unsealed file could use the bucket's own presigned link, which also serves from a separate domain at no cost to the deployment owner.

asks.text: Should signed file links come now, before release, or in Ordo v2?
asks.suggest: v2, unless an app needs private files opened as links before release. Notes v2 shows files through the SDK with a token, which works today. Signed links change every file URL, so they deserve their own design pass.

asks.text: Should an unsealed file's link be the storage provider's own presigned link (R2, S3), and a sealed file's the door's?
asks.suggest: Yes. The provider's link moves the bytes off the door and gives a separate domain for free. A sealed file has to pass through the door to be opened, so its link stays the door's, with the sandbox headers.

asks.text: How long should a signed link live by default?
asks.suggest: 5 minutes, a setting the app developer may change within a ceiling. Long enough to open or start streaming a video, short enough that a leaked link soon dies.

where: Ordo v2 (owner, 2026-10-24): provider presigned links for unsealed files, door links for sealed, 5 min default within a ceiling

name: Upload rules set per file field: size and type
decided: Render vs provide is up the to the app dev and theres good cases for either situation.
explain:
Today one deployment-wide cap (100 MiB) covers every file, and the type is whatever the uploader claims.

  • An app with avatars and a video library needs 2 MB on one field and gigabytes on another.
  • The size check before and during the upload already exists; only the limit's source changes.

asks.text: Should the program declare each file field's size limit, within a deployment ceiling the deployment owner sets?
asks.suggest: Yes. avatar: blob max 2MB, video: blob max 20GB. The door checks the declared length against the field before reading a byte, as it does today against the one cap.

asks.text: Should a file field's allowed types be checked against the file's first bytes, not only the type the uploader claims?
asks.suggest: Yes, for fields that declare types. It catches a renamed or mislabelled file. It proves the format, not that the content is harmless; safe serving does that part.

where: Ordo v2 (owner, 2026-10-24). Ask 2 open.

name: A person's own download: past 1 GiB, compression, and parts
decided: Move all of those including the asks to v2
explain:
GET /download streams one zip, entries stored uncompressed, capped at ORDO_OWN_DOWNLOAD_MAX_BYTES (1 GiB, at most 4 GB).

  • A file past the cap is listed missing, and nothing lets the person get it.
  • Every row is read into memory before the first byte, with no cap.
  • No resume: a dropped connection starts over. 6 a person an hour, per node.

asks.text: Should a download past the cap come as numbered parts, each within the cap, that together hold everything?
asks.suggest: Yes. The manifest lists every part and each part's files, and GET /download?part=N fetches one. The order is fixed, so a part fetched twice is the same part.

asks.text: Should the rows (the JSON) be compressed, with files left stored?
asks.suggest: Yes. JSON shrinks several times over; photos and PDFs are already compressed, so compressing them costs CPU for almost nothing.

asks.text: Should rows be written as they are read, a page at a time, instead of all held in memory first?
asks.suggest: Yes. Today a tenant with a million rows holds them all in memory before the first byte. One page at a time keeps memory flat.

asks.text: Should a part be resumable after a dropped connection, by byte range?
asks.suggest: Yes, per part. Parts make it cheap: the part is rebuilt the same way and the range is skipped. A full-file resume would need the server to keep a copy.

asks.text: Should the hourly limit count per person across all nodes, instead of per node?
asks.suggest: Yes. Today 3 nodes allow 18 an hour. A count in the control database makes the setting mean what it says.

where: Ordo v2 (owner, 2026-10-24); asks kept open for then

name: Owner succession: what the app developer sees and the tenant can stop
explain:
Succession exists today without the console: std.space.succeedOwner, deployment owner only, a 1-day delay, recorded in both streams.

  • It names an existing member; it admits nobody and touches no credential.
  • Not built: the managers' notice and their objection during the delay.
  • The departed owner's grants and delegations stay live.

asks.text: Should the tenant's managers be told of a succession and able to object during the delay, before the console offers it?
asks.suggest: Yes. Without it a tenant learns of a new owner only after the fact. The plan already has this rule (plan-passkey-recovery.md ask 8); it was never built.

asks.text: Should the console's succession form take the successor's id from you, with no list of that tenant's members?
asks.suggest: Yes. You hold no role in most tenants, so listing their people would show you who is inside. The person asking for succession supplies the id.

asks.text: Should completing a succession end the departed owner's grants to apps and their delegations?
asks.suggest: Yes, as an option on by default. A dead or departed owner's app grants keep acting in the tenant. The new owner can re-grant; the record names each one ended.

name: Move the CI runners from a personal token to a GitHub App
explain:
On 2026-10-23 CI stopped for about 5 hours: the runners' personal access token stopped working (401 Bad credentials), so no runner could register.

  • A personal token is tied to one person and expires
  • A GitHub App is tied to the org; its tokens renew themselves
  • ARC, the runner system, supports and recommends it

Steps: create a GitHub App in HominemAI with organization permission "Self-hosted runners: read and write"; install it on the org; store app id, installation id and private key in GCP Secret Manager gha_runner_secrets (keys github_app_id, github_app_installation_id, github_app_private_key); point ARC's scale sets at those keys instead of github_token in smg_infrastructure gha-runner values; delete the personal token after one green CI run. The runner token is never read by Claude.

asks.text: Should the CI runners log in with a GitHub App owned by HominemAI instead of a personal token?
asks.suggest: Yes. No expiry to forget and no dependence on one person's account. You create the app and its key; I write the steps and the config change in smg_infrastructure for your approval.

name: Audit: one interface and one typed error per service
explain:
Owner, 2026-10-23: done before any Ordo v2 work starts. Checks AGENTS.md rule 9 across Ordo.

  • Services: database, mail, file storage, outside sign-in providers, key custody, the door from the SDK
  • Looks for: errors kept as text, causes stripped, per-site handling
  • Sign-in is being fixed now and is the pattern

Rust shape to check against: one error enum per service client; From conversions so ? carries it; the cause kept through source(); classification by methods on the type (busy, retryable, refused, bad input), never by matching message text; one IntoResponse at the edge; #[non_exhaustive] on public enums. Known today: carries_server_busy matches message text; CredentialStoreError(String) keeps errors as text; sign-in had about 50 sites mapping errors to their own words. SDK side: one request helper per service with one retry policy.

asks.text: Should the audit report first (each service: what is wrong, the fix, its size), with fixes built after your ruling?
asks.suggest: Yes. One read-only pass of about 1 session gives you the whole picture and a fix order; fixes then follow the sign-in pattern, one service at a time.

asks.text: Should the 6 bugs the audit found be fixed now, before the structural work: lost rate-limited mail, provider hiccups shown as failed sign-in, and 4 more?
asks.suggest: Yes, now. Rate-limited mail is deleted and lost today, and a busy key store is reported as a destroyed key. Each is small; the list is in the report.

asks.text: Should the structural fixes go in this order: database error type, remaining text stores, sign-in providers, file storage, mail, the server edge, the SDK?
asks.suggest: Yes. The database type is what the rest build on; the SDK goes last because it consumes what the server sends. About 6 to 8 sessions in all.

asks.text: Should every public error enum be marked #[non_exhaustive], and ordo-react import ordo-sdk's code instead of carrying copies of it?
asks.suggest: Yes to both. None of 45 enums is marked, so adding a case breaks callers; and the copies drift, which is how ordo-react ends up with its own error shapes.

asks.text: When a sealed value fails to decrypt (key present, data wrong), should Ordo say "unreadable, possibly tampered" instead of "destroyed"?
asks.suggest: Yes. "Destroyed" should mean the key was deliberately erased. A decrypt failure with the key present is corruption or tampering, and should alert the deployment owner.

name: How a tenant comes into being
sub: Ruled 2026-09-21: a tenant is a minted globally unique id, public rather than secret, with its name an attribute below it
decided: Names are irrelevant, everything should be by id and there can be attributes under the id that are not global. Only the ID is globally unique for a tenant.
explain:
You ruled that a first tenant cannot exist until something is applied. Building it turned up a rule pointing the other way, enforced three times over: space is a reserved word with no parser arm, the binder refuses a $space parameter, and the planner compiles the space as a slot rather than a literal, because a literal “would be a compiled-in tenant” and would change the artifact’s hash for every tenant. That is what lets one compiled program serve every space.

So a program cannot name a tenant, and should not: the day it can, the artifact stops being tenant-independent and every tenant needs its own build.

The reading that fits both. Your sentence is about order, not authorship: a tenant cannot exist before a program, because a tenant’s tables come from a program’s DDL. Creating the tenant stays a separate act on the deployment, an owner-gated op that provisions custody and writes the founding member row. bootstrap.md already settles that op with a caller-supplied slug, name and owner, and provision_space is built and tested with no production caller. So: apply first, then create the space, both through the door, neither in the program text.
suggest:
Your answer is better than the reading I proposed. Uniqueness stops being a promise and becomes a property: mint with enough entropy and no registry has to allocate ids, two deployments cannot collide, and the hazard 18n found (three tables keyed on space alone, where a collision is two tenants on one chain rather than an error) cannot arise. A self-hosted deployment with no console mints its own safely.

A rename stops being a migration. With the name as identity, changing it means rewriting every row’s space column, the chain’s lock key and custody. With the name as an attribute it is an update.

An id is not a secret (your clarification: they do not have to be sealed). A space id travels in headers, metric labels, logs and refusal messages, so it is public by construction; it may even carry a readable fragment to help a human place it, as long as nothing keys on that fragment. Authority never comes from knowing an id: a call is authorised by a token and a membership.

And it is cheap: the door still takes a space in a header, the character set is unchanged, every existing deployment keeps working because a minted id is a well-formed space string, and the system space stays a compiled constant. What changes is how a new tenant’s id comes into being. One thing it obliges: operator surfaces must show a human which tenant they are looking at, because an opaque id is unreadable and the name is now the only thing that reads.

asks.text: Nothing open. Piece 3 of 17aa is unblocked.

where: 17aa piece 3: crates/ordo-host/src/tenants.rs mints the id, tenant_ops.rs serves it (738c633); ordo space create over the door (3b75ad8).

name: What runs where, and what points at which database
sub: Ruled 2026-09-21. Per-tenant databases are wired into the binary since T4 and T8
decided: Each deployment can be pointed to any particular postgres cluster. The console can have its own postgres cluster connection for its own data. Public release = one ordo console pod, runs a deployment within itself, and the deployment can point to a database and the console to another.
explain:
Three layers, each pointed at a database independently. A deployment takes a Postgres connection as configuration and has no concept of the console, so nothing about the console’s storage constrains it. The console keeps its own data in its own database for the same reason. A tenant may sit in the deployment’s database or in one of its own, because the design is indifferent to where data lives as long as it is reachable.

The correction. The third layer is built and not connected. $spacedb exists, the routing code exists, the directory reads attachments, and the tests exercise them, but the shipped binary constructs SinglePool, so today every space resolves to the one configured database. A tenant that must have its own database cannot have one yet, whatever the design says. Filed under 18c/18d.

Packing is operational, not architectural. A pod may run one deployment or several; they are processes and should not care. If a pod runs out of room, they spread. Availability inside a deployment is replicas, switched on per deployment rather than by default. None of it reaches the engine.

The public release shape: one pod, the console and one deployment inside it, each pointed at its own database.
suggest: A console in the same pod still reaches the deployment through the door, as an owner with a token, over localhost. Sharing a pod is not a reason to share a process or to read the deployment’s database. The moment it does, there are two ways to operate the platform and only one of them is audited, and the rule that the system is the source of truth quietly stops being true.

asks.text: Nothing open. One constraint recorded rather than asked, because it is what keeps the rest true.

where: Deployment and tenant clusters configurable: ORDO_PG_* and ORDO_PG_TENANT_* (dcd4579), routing wired via T4 (2a42d00). The console with its own cluster and the one-pod release are filed under 18o.

name: Can one control plane serve more than one deployment?
sub: Ruled 2026-09-21: hosting many deployments is a product requirement, and the shape is a service above them. Not an overhaul, because nothing inside a deployment changes
decided: 1. Is it forbidden / would it require a massive overhaul to support. 2. The control plane exists out of the concept of the deployment / tenants, it should be able to serve more (I intend to host this as a paid service). 3. No, 1 deployment 1 separately managed master key. 4. Yes, globally ID'd and managed by the control plane; the deployment should have no concept of the control plane, just that it gets to live somewhere. Think docker service abstraction.
explain:
There is no deployment identifier anywhere in the codebase. A deployment is defined implicitly by one process, one database, one ORDO_SPACE and one master key. Much of the platform is already keyed by space and would tolerate a second deployment: the chain, checkpoints, custody, security events, quotas, usage, the witness, membership. Four things assume exactly one and have no key at all: the program’s activation pointer (one database is one program), identity (a login has no space, so it reaches everything), the access engine (built from one unfiltered membership read), and custody (one master key, loaded whole).

The security finding is the one to sit with. Every boundary in Ordo is enforced by space, never by deployment, so tenant isolation already survives a shared process. Deployment isolation does not, and it rests on a single check in the apply op: the bound space must be the deployment’s own home. The code says why in a sentence worth keeping: being the owner of a space you were given is not being the owner of the deployment that serves it. Remove the single home and every tenant owner can replace the program.

Two supporting facts from the tree: the token key’s own doc argues that sharing it is one authentication boundary shared by strangers, and the page key binds the space into its signature while the token key cannot, because principals and sessions carry no space. That asymmetry is exactly where the identity tier stops being keyed.

Three shapes were weighed (a process per deployment over a shared control database; one process serving many; a separate control-plane service deployments register with). The recommendation is to build none of them now and build 17aa, whose three pieces are prerequisites for all of them and are worth having at one deployment. If a second is ever needed, the separate service is the shape, because it keeps one process equal to one custody perimeter.
suggest:
Filed as 18o, the platform service. It owns the global namespace, the registry of deployments and where each lives, provisioning (generating a master key and handing it over once), the control database each deployment writes its witness into, and billing, which the usage ledger already produces per space. It must never reach into a deployment’s spaces, keep a master key after provisioning, or become something a deployment discovers rather than is configured with.

Three prerequisites in the engine, each worth having anyway: a deployment id on the four unkeyed tables, the identity tier keyed so one login cannot span deployments, and 17aa, because a hosted service multiplies one tenant’s failure by every customer on it.

asks.text: Answered. Your first question back: not forbidden, and not an overhaul in this shape. The overhaul only appears if many deployments share one process, which your own answer 3 forecloses. A service above them leaves the engine alone.

where: Filed as checklist 18o (the service above deployments), evaluation in 18n. Its 'cheap now' deployment id on $artifacts, $activations, $jobs, $schedules is not done (no deployment_id in crates/).

name: What the CLI promises against what it ships
sub: Ruled 2026-09-21: proceed in the recommended order, import over the wire first
decided: Continue with suggestion.
explain:
Every command, subcommand and flag checked against the dispatch rather than against the documents. The good news first: the compiler commands, the operator commands, custody, quotas, usage, restore and verify are all built and behave as documented.

What hurts, in order. 1. ordo import has no CLI verb. The engine is built and the server can call it, but the operator tool cannot, because it has no way to choose a master key and an import that cannot seal cannot write a sealed field. A customer can get data out and not in. 2. Only apply reaches a deployment over HTTP, so every other operator act still wants database credentials on a laptop, which is the thing this week set out to remove. 3. migration.md reads as a runbook for two commands that do not exist. 4. A trap: exporting ORDO_HOST silently selects the door, so a documented database invocation then fails with a confusing usage error. 5. A third of the shipped surface is missing from the tool’s own help, so running ordo with no arguments does not show you quotas, usage or four custody verbs. 6. ordo dev --gen quietly does nothing without --out. 7. The plan documents understate what ships by seven commands, so they cannot be used to decide what to build next. 8. ordo fmt is promised under two different spellings and exists as neither.

Four stale passages were corrected the same day: the metering plan’s “nothing is built”, the deploy guide’s claim that every schema change resets, the migration runbook, and a flag named --correlation that is really --group.
suggest: Order: import over the wire first (the server already holds the master key the CLI lacks, which is what has been blocking it), then the help text, then rollback, deploys, migrate --apply, quota, usage and restore --record, then the two traps.

asks.text: Nothing open. Ruled 2026-09-20: the CLI triggers actions on the server, not locally, so the door is the default for every command that acts on a deployment and the database path becomes break-glass, named as such, for the acts that must work when the door is down.

where: Finding 1 built: std.space.import and ordo import over the door (d8e941c), crates/ordo-cli/src/wire.rs. Findings 2 and 4 to 8 open in checklist 17y.

name: Most operator commands still need database credentials
sub: Ruled 2026-09-20, not built. A started table of which commands take --host is kept at tag salvage/cli-door-table
explain:
Ruled 2026-09-20 (17y, finding 2): the door is the default for every command that acts on a deployment, and the database path is break-glass. Built so far: apply, import and space create. Still owed, in the ruled order: rollback, deploys, migrate --apply, quota, usage, restore --record. Finding 4, the ORDO_HOST trap, is open as well.

An agent began the per-command table in crates/ordo-cli/src/wire.rs on 2026-09-20 and was stopped by the spend limit. Its 187 lines were never compiled, no command calls them, and they predate import and space create. The commit is kept at tag salvage/cli-door-table as a starting point and the branch is deleted. It was not merged, because unused and untested code on main would read as built.

name: The CLI works only through the door, and what that leaves uncovered
sub: Ruled 2026-09-21: the control plane boots without the deployment under it, which dissolves the circularity rather than working around it
decided: We should only work around the door. System is the source of truth and errors. If someone needs to break glass they can just work in the database. System UI can provide a url string that can be used with credentials for break glass.
explain:
The rule is clean: the CLI speaks to the deployment and nothing else, the system is the source of truth and of errors, and break-glass is a database session the system hands you rather than a mode of the tool. What follows is what that leaves open.

The sharp one, live today. The binary refuses to boot when the chain has been rewound without a marker explaining it, and the command that writes that marker talks to the database. Door-only makes recovery circular: the deployment will not start until the marker exists, and the marker cannot be written without a deployment. Recording a restore should be a deliberate one-shot act of the server at boot, audited as a custody action, not a request to a door that is not there.

Day zero has no door either. Custody for the first tenant is written by the CLI today, and the server refuses to boot without it. The system space solved itself (17v); a tenant has not.

Verifying a server you do not trust cannot be done by asking it. The offline verifier is the answer and needs a path to a proof that does not depend on the suspect cooperating.

Operator lockout: one owner credential, lost, and door-only means no way back in. This is where your break-glass URL earns its place.

Then the shape problems. Long operations (apply, migrate, import) outlast a proxy timeout, and this deployment sits behind one that cuts them: a job id and a poll, not a held request. An import bundle wants chunked upload with resume rather than one request carrying gigabytes. CLI and server versions will routinely differ. A tenant promoted to its own database makes “which database does this act on” a real question. And quotas must never apply to the operator surface, or an over-quota deployment refuses the call that would fix it.
suggest: Both as deliberate one-shot acts of the server at boot, set by the operator and written into the audit trail as custody actions, rather than as anything a laptop does to a database. That keeps your rule intact (the system is the source of truth) and keeps the property that a typo cannot mint a tenant. Your break-glass URL then covers the genuine emergencies, and it should be minted on request, recorded when minted, short-lived, and loud about the fact that using it can break things.

asks.text: Two to settle before the database path goes: how a restore is recorded when the deployment will not start, and how the first tenant gets custody when there is no door yet. The rest can be built in order.

where: The circularity ruling is built as 17aa pieces 1 and 2 (ee5a37e). Scenarios 3 to 9 (untrusted-server verify, operator lockout, long ops, large payloads, version skew, limits) stay open in checklist 17z.

name: Two acts that have no door to go through
sub: Ruled 2026-09-21: everything happens in the server, and a tenant comes into being through an apply rather than before one
decided: Correct - everything happens within the server. But a first tenant (non system) can't exist until something is applied.
explain:
You ruled that the CLI works only through the door and that break-glass is a database session the system hands out. Two acts cannot obey that, because in both the deployment is not running and cannot start until the act is done.

Recording a restore. The binary refuses to boot when the chain sits below a head the witness remembers with nothing explaining it. That refusal is the whole point of the restore work: a silent restore is impossible. But the command that writes the explanation talks to the database, and under door-only there is no door to write it through, because the deployment will not start. This is live today, not a design worry.

Creating the first tenant’s custody. The server mints the system space itself at boot, so a bare deployment starts. A tenant is different: its keys are written by the operator today, and the server refuses to serve a tenant that has none, on purpose, so that a typo cannot mint a tenant.
suggest: Server at boot, both of them. A one-shot boot act keeps your rule intact (the system does the work and owns the error), keeps the audit trail complete, and keeps the typo protection, because the operator has to say the tenant’s name deliberately in configuration rather than in a command. Break-glass stays what you described: the fire axe for the cases nobody designed for, rather than the documented way to do two things we know we need.

asks.text: Should both become deliberate one-shot acts of the server at boot, set by the operator (an environment variable or a flag) and written into the audit trail as custody actions? Or should they be the first two uses of the break-glass URL?

where: 17z scenario 2: rewound tenant quarantined, door stays up (ee5a37e). Scenario 1: a tenant is created through the door, crates/ordo-host/src/tenant_ops.rs (738c633).

name: Signed provenance on releases waits
sub: Ruled 2026-09-20: off for now. It needs an Enterprise plan while the repo is private, and is free once it is public
decided: I'll leave it off for now. Maybe I'll just do some manual signing at some point - but it will end up public anyways at some point.
explain:
The first release built every binary and then failed on GitHub’s build-provenance step: artifact attestations need GitHub Enterprise Cloud for a private repository, and are free for a public one. A plan limit took down a release that had already succeeded.

The step stays in the workflow, made non-fatal, and the release now prints whether provenance was actually attached, so a green release never implies a signature it does not have. Tarballs ship with SHA-256 files, which catch corruption and not substitution by someone who can write to the release page.
suggest: Manual signing is a reasonable stopgap if a consumer appears first: a detached signature beside the tarball answers the same question, with you rather than GitHub as the root of trust.

asks.text: Nothing open. Revisit when the repository goes public, which turns it on for free, or sooner if someone outside this organisation starts consuming the artifacts.

name: Old blob objects clear on the sweep, not at once
sub: Ruled 2026-09-20: accepted, and disclosed in howto-custody.md. Old objects clear on the sweep, and because destroy refuses until they are gone, the retired key stays alive until then
decided: Accept with disclosure in docs? If that makes sense. We can revisit if it needs to be removed from docs or a new solution proposed later.
explain:
A re-sealed blob is written as a new object under a new handle, and the row points at it. The old object is left for the garbage sweep, which deletes on its own horizon rather than immediately, because the handle is the object’s key in the store: there is no way to rewrite the bytes in place without an extra layer of indirection between a row and its object.

So after a rotation, a copy of the old ciphertext survives in object storage until the sweep passes. It is still ciphertext, and its key epoch can be destroyed, which makes it unreadable, so the window is about storage cost and tidiness rather than about readability.
suggest: Accept. Destroying the retired epoch already makes the leftovers unreadable, and the indirection would put a lookup on the path of every blob read forever to tidy a window that the sweep closes anyway.

asks.text: Accept the sweep horizon for old objects, rather than adding an object-key indirection so they can be replaced in place?

where: Disclosed in docs/howto-custody.md (6150544); destroy refuses while objects remain (11-11, 17i). Ruling in docs/corpus-rulings.md.

name: When keys rotate, and what counts as exposure
sub: Ruled 2026-09-20: rotation stays an operator act with no clock; exposure is an event that may have put a data key in front of a party who should no longer hold it
decided: Take Suggestion
explain:
Rotation is built as an operator act: ordo keys rotate mints a new epoch, and a background pass moves every ciphertext onto it, resumably, without changing a value or a search digest. Two questions the code deliberately does not answer:

Cadence. Nothing rotates on a clock today. A scheduled rotation would mean the platform decides when a tenant’s keys change, and the pass it starts is the same one an operator would start by hand.

Exposure. rotate --reason takes free text. The question is what an operator should be told to treat as exposure.
suggest: Yes to both. A clock-driven rotation spends real work on every tenant on a schedule nobody chose, and the thing that makes rotation urgent is an event, not a date. reseal stays the repair tool for a pass that was interrupted, and rotate is the response to exposure. If a compliance regime later demands a calendar, the worker already exists and only needs a schedule.

asks.text: Leave rotation as an operator act with no clock, and define exposure as any event that may have put a data key in front of a party who should no longer have it (a departing administrator, a leaked backup, a compromised host)?

where: Documentation only: docs/howto-custody.md rotation steps and 'Force a re-encrypt after an exposure' (43fe89a, 6150544). Ruling in docs/corpus-rulings.md.

name: Two checkpoints at one position
sub: Ruled 2026-09-20: accepted. $checkpoints admits an orphaned and a current checkpoint at one position, through an additive key change
decided: Accept suggestion
explain:
After a restore, the chain grows again from an earlier point, so a new checkpoint can be signed at the same position as an orphaned one from the discarded timeline. Today $checkpoints allows one checkpoint per position, so the new, current one cannot be stored and the space stays parked on the orphan with no current anchor. The plan changes the table’s key to (space, position, head), through an idempotent ALTER, so both can exist and the verifier tells them apart by whether the stored chain agrees.

A limit to know about, from the same design: in a single-database deployment the control-plane record of checkpoint heads lives in that same database, so a restore of the whole database still cannot be caught at boot. That case is caught by the offline verifier checking against the attestation receivers’ copies. With spaces routed to their own databases (18c/18d), the boot check catches a space’s restore directly.
suggest: Yes. Without it, the first restore leaves a quiet space with no current anchor until it happens to write past the orphan’s position. The change is additive for existing deployments.

asks.text: Change $checkpoints’ key to admit an orphaned and a current checkpoint at the same position?

where: $checkpoints keyed (space, upto, head) by an additive ALTER, 17j R2b' (8ebf120).

name: Which checkpoints still count after a restore
sub: Ruled 2026-09-19: a checkpoint counts when the stored chain agrees with its head; no format change
decided: Take reccomendation
explain: After a restore, some signed checkpoints describe history that no longer exists (they were signed on the timeline the restore discarded). The plan treats every checkpoint signed after a restore marker as orphaned and never uses one as an anchor again. The build showed three problems with that rule: pruning across the restore point makes verification fail; a later, unannounced rewind can be misread as explained by the earlier marker; and signing a new checkpoint misbehaves when the new chain reaches an orphan’s position.
suggest: Yes. It needs no format change, fixes all three problems, and asks the question the verifier actually cares about (“is this signed head part of the chain I hold?”) rather than a timing rule that stands in for it.

asks.text: Classify checkpoints by what the stored chain says instead: a checkpoint whose head matches the stored hash at its position is current history and may anchor; one that does not match is orphaned. And have the restore command record the newest stored checkpoint as the pre-restore head by default?

where: 17j R2b': a checkpoint counts when the stored chain agrees with its head (8ebf120).

name: A restore can hide its own evidence
sub: Ruled 2026-09-19 (C): checkpoint heads also recorded in the control plane for the boot check; the verifier also compares against the attestation receivers
decided: Take reccomendation
explain:
The restore plan’s central promise is that a silent restore cannot happen: at boot, if the chain’s head is behind a checkpoint that was signed earlier, and no restore marker explains it, the space refuses to load. The check needs a signed checkpoint that the restore did not also roll back.

The problem: signed checkpoints are stored in $checkpoints, in the space’s own database. A point-in-time restore of that database rolls the checkpoints back together with the chain, so after the restore the chain and its checkpoints agree again and the check reads intact. The check only catches restores that roll back the chain without the checkpoints, which is exactly the case that does not happen in practice.

What survives a database restore: copies of checkpoints already sent elsewhere. The attestation layers (built, 11-12) push signed checkpoints to webhook receivers and serve chainProof, and the deployment has a control-plane database separate from each space’s own once spaces are routed (18c/18d).
suggest: C, built as A now and B as a verifier check. A keeps boot local and fast and closes the realistic case (one space restored from its own backup). The attestation receivers already hold signed heads, so letting the offline verifier compare against them costs little and catches the rarer case where the control plane is restored too. I would have Fable write this into the plan before R2d is built, since it moves where checkpoint heads are written.

asks.text:
Where should the boot check read its “last checkpoint I know was signed” from, so that restoring a space’s database cannot roll it back?

  • A. The control-plane database: every signed checkpoint’s head is also recorded there, per space. A space restore does not touch it; a restore of the control plane itself is a separate, louder event.
  • B. An external witness: the attestation receivers. Strongest, but the boot then depends on a network party answering.
  • C. Both: A at boot, B audited later by the verifier.

where: 17j R2d-i to R2e: signed heads recorded in the control database, boot refuses an unaccounted chain, verifier reads the receivers (28e4188, 27a957d, a132367, 16b44e0, b1d3126).

name: Quotas on writes wait for a later version
sub: Ruled 2026-09-19: v1 quotas on requests and rows returned; write quotas are 18i, post-deployment
decided: Take reccomendation - Add the remainder to the post deployment roadmap
explain: A quota gate runs at the door after the access check. Requests and rows returned can be counted at the door the moment they happen, so a quota on them is exact. Writes are counted from the command log at rollup, so a quota on writes would only notice an overrun up to a rollup period (an hour) late. A tenant could exceed a write quota by an hour’s worth of writes before being stopped.
suggest: Yes. A quota that is enforced late does not do what its name says it does, which is worse than having none. Writes are still measured and reported from day one. A write quota can come later with a door-side counter if a customer needs a hard cap.

asks.text: Ship v1 quotas on requests and rows returned only, and defer quotas on writes?

where: Write quotas filed as checklist 18i (post-deployment). v1 request and row quotas built in 17n M2 (fe600a1, 68d2d5f).

name: How often usage is counted
sub: Ruled 2026-09-19: 60 s flush and 1 h rollup by default, both configurable and documented with their trade-offs
decided: Take recommendation as default - making sure it is configurable - document the feature / configuration and its implication
explain: Metering counts requests, rows returned, writes and blob bytes per space. Each replica keeps its own counts in memory and flushes them to a per-replica table; the leader then rolls them up into the $usage table that quotas and billing read. The two intervals set how fresh usage is and how much database traffic the counting costs. A crash loses at most one flush interval of counts.
suggest: Yes: a 1-hour rollup and a 60-second flush. An hour is the billing grain most platforms use and keeps $usage small. A minute bounds what a crash can lose while adding only one small write per replica per minute. Both are configuration, so they can change later without a migration.

asks.text: Roll up hourly and flush every 60 seconds?

where: ORDO_USAGE_FLUSH_SECS (60 s) and ORDO_USAGE_ROLLUP_SECS (1 h) in crates/ordo-host/src/runtime.rs; documented in docs/howto-operating.md (8d80642).

name: CI images: how much to build on every push
sub: Ruled 2026-09-19: option B. amd64 built, smoked and pushed on every push to main; both architectures on v* release tags
decided: Take reccomendation
explain:
R4 (plan-ci-images.md increments 1–3) replaces ci.yml with the stricter proposed pipeline, and switches on images.yml: three images (host, CLI, playground), each smoke-tested by booting it, pushed to GitHub’s container registry (GHCR) under this repo. GHCR needs no secrets, and on a private repo the images are private too. The release workflow later turns a v* tag into tarballs plus image digests.

The cost. The test suite already uses about 11.5 minutes a run. The plan builds each image for both amd64 and arm64, and arm64 under emulation is slow: expect roughly 20–40 extra minutes a push until the build cache warms, and more whenever dependencies change. The repo is private, so those minutes count against the organisation’s monthly allowance (2,000 free).
suggest: B. Every push still proves the deployable image boots and passes its smoke gates, which is the check that matters day to day, for about 5–8 extra minutes. arm64 is only needed when something ships, so it runs on release tags. Switching to A later is one line in the workflow.

asks.text:
On every push to main, what should run?

  • A. Everything the plan says: both architectures, built, smoked and pushed on every push.
  • B. amd64 only on every push (built, smoked, pushed); both architectures only on a v* release tag.
  • C. Images only on release tags and on a manual button; pushes run the tests alone.

where: .github/workflows/images.yml: amd64 on push to main, amd64+arm64 on v* tags (8866a53).

name: The security drain stays outside the supervisor
sub: Confirmed 2026-09-19: the security drain stays standalone, listed in the census, never quarantined
decided: Take reccomendation
explain:
The plan's worker table says R3 wraps the security-event drain in the same worker shape as everything else. It was kept standalone instead. It is listed in the supervisor’s census on /health/deep with supervised: false and its own counters, and its reasoning is recorded in corpus-rulings.md.

The reason: supervised workers are quarantined after ten consecutive failures. The drain already has its own bounded buffer, and a failure today is a counted, reported loss of a bounded number of events. If it were quarantined, it would stop draining altogether and the loss would become unbounded. Adopting it would also move when it starts and when it flushes at shutdown, which the drain’s own guarantees depend on.
suggest: Yes. Security events are the one stream where stopping is worse than retrying forever, and quarantine is designed for loops where stopping is the safe default. It stays fully visible, so nothing is hidden by the exception.

asks.text: Keep the security drain standalone (visible in the census, never quarantined), as built?

where: secevent.drain started standalone in crates/ordo-host/src/runtime.rs (step 11) and listed in the census, per checklist 17d.

name: Every `policy` block in the language is documentation
sub: Ruled 2026-09-16: mark the six blocks unbuilt in the language doc now; the grammar is roadmap 18g when policies are wanted.
decided: Take reccomendation
explain:
The keyword is lexed and there the trail ends. lexer.rs and token.rs know policy. There is no parser arm, no AST node, and no consumer in ordo-schema or ordo-plan. So every policy block definition-language.md documents is prose: policy spaces, policy commandlog, policy vault, policy llm-egress, policy retention, policy compliance. security-hardening-review-2.md already noticed one corner of this — it says policy mirror and policy keys are “referenced but absent from the policy grammar” — but the gap is wider: none of them parse.

It surfaced building C7, whose fourth item is policy mirror { keep 90d | keep <n> rows | full } scope and eviction. The other three items are built. This one cannot be: eviction enforcing a policy nobody can write is a dial no deployment can set, and policy retention’s own comment promises a nightly platform sweep that likewise does not exist.
suggest:
Do not build mirror eviction alone. It would need a spelling invented for one policy, and then five more policies would arrive later wanting a grammar that had already been shaped around the narrowest case.

A. Build the policy grammar as its own increment — lex, parse, an AST node, validation, and the descriptor projection — then mirror scope and retention become ordinary consumers of it. Honest cost: it is a language change, and every keyword is forever.

B. Build mirror scope alone with a bespoke spelling, and accept that the grammar gets shaped by the first caller.

C. Leave all of it, and mark the six documented policy blocks proposed in the language doc so nobody reads them as shipped. This is the cheapest and it is also the one that stops the documentation lying.

Recommendation: C now, A when policies are actually scheduled. C costs an afternoon of doc edits and removes a class of false expectation; A is real work that should be scheduled deliberately, not smuggled in under a cache increment.

asks.text: Mark the policy blocks proposed (C), build the grammar (A), or give mirror scope its own spelling (B)?

where: The six blocks are marked unparsed in docs/definition-language.md (around line 3018, 1a565a4). The grammar itself is filed as checklist 18g.

name: Your id ruling conflicts with a settled ui-gen rule
sub: Ruled 2026-09-16 after the review you asked for: follow ui-gen §1. My earlier ruling rested on a claim that is false in code.
decided: Take reccomendation but launch fable to go through it and confirm its the right choice and reconcile the conflicts.
explain:
I recommended that a synced op must list id in its projection, saying otherwise a feed would send something the op itself does not return. ui-gen.md §1, settled, says the opposite: the anchor's id rides every list row even when unprojected, because it already underwrites the page cursor, so delivering it costs nothing. The executor has not implemented that yet (it reads the id for the cursor and drops it), which is what I described.

As ruled, only the derived std.E.list and std.E.get ops in the fixture can be synced. Every hand-written list, such as taskBoard, is refused until its author adds id.
suggest:
Confirmed by review, 2026-09-16. The reviewer found the earlier ruling rests on a false premise: the page cursor is authenticated, not encrypted (base64url(JSON) . base64url(HMAC)), so every caller already reads the last row’s id on every page. id is reserved and implicit, can never be sealed, and is the tiebreak of every row plan, so no caller is entitled to a row but not its id. Two amendments taken: the predicate must name distinct and many-side joins as refusals rather than catch them by accident, and the id must be attached to every paged read row so an ordinary call and a feed still agree. The cost is three crates and every read op re-versioning, not the one clause I claimed. Filed as C4e.

Follow ui-gen.md §1. Any anchored, ungrouped read can be synced, and the feed carries the anchor's id on every row. C4a is built to your ruling as recorded; switching is one clause of the rule, plus the id in C4b's frames.

asks.text: Keep the ruling (authors add id), or follow ui-gen §1?

where: C4e: the anchor id rides every row, crates ordo-plan project_row_key (287b5cc, 5ede5ea; predicate ddda3b2). Plan: docs/plan-replica-feed.md C4e.

name: The device now answers refinements the door refuses
sub: Ruled 2026-09-16: the device keeps answering, and server-side Tier 0 is scheduled with the refinement feature.
decided: Take suggestion.
explain:
Tier-0 refinement is specified, validated, cost-gated and served by nothing. api-engine-design.md §7 settles the envelope; ordo-api/src/refine.rs implements the tier check, the manifest validation and all three sealed rules; refine.rs raises invalid_refinement and refinement_unbounded exactly as specified. And then: interface.rs hardcodes tier: “none” for every op, so the door refuses $refine across the whole catalog; @ordo/react builds a valid envelope it can never send; and ordo-host’s executor takes a validated refinement and ignores it — its own test says so (tests/cost_class.rs: “the executor does not yet APPLY $refine”). None of this is new breakage. What is new is that C6 is the first working Tier 0 in the system, and it runs on the device.

The descriptor already carries the other half: ops[].refine.fields lists each op’s refinable output fields, and 75 of the 165 ops in the golden descriptor have a non-empty list even though every tier is none. So the manifest is real and only the permission is withheld.
suggest:
What I built, and why: the device validates a filter against refine.fields and does not consult refine.tier. The tier governs work the server does — a refinement lands after the op’s take and after the page window, so the door charges for it, and none means “this op did not buy that”. Rows already on the device cost the server nothing. Honouring the tier would have refused every op in the catalog and shipped C6 inert.

The cost of that choice, stated plainly: the same envelope now behaves differently in two places. {where:[{field:‘price’,op:‘gt’,value:1000}]} answers on the device and earns invalid_refinement at the door.

A. Keep it (what is built): the device answers, the door still refuses, and the divergence is documented. B. Honour the tier: one rule everywhere, and C6 does nothing until some op declares a tier. C. Land server-side Tier 0 (the executor applying $refine, and a spelling for the per-op opt-in) so both agree — the largest, and the only one that makes the feature real on both sides.

Recommendation: A now, C when the refinement feature is scheduled. A is the only option that makes the replica useful this increment, and it throws nothing away: when C lands, the device’s evaluator is already the same rules, and the gate becomes one line.

asks.text: Does the device keep answering refinements the door refuses (A), wait for the tier (B), or should server-side Tier 0 be scheduled now (C)?

where: Server side: crates/ordo-plan/src/interface.rs:657 (basic tier), crates/ordo-host/src/refine_call.rs; tests crates/ordo-host/tests/refine_door.rs, refine_paging.rs. Device side: refineOp (db6e1ca). Corrected by audit-2026-10-09 finding 22

name: Resuming a device after a reconnect without a reload
sub: Ruled 2026-09-16: build it on a shared hash; the reload becomes the fallback. Filed as C4d.
decided: Can it share a diff hash or version hash and if they disagree on reconnect reconcile. Add it to C4 work.
explain: With the ruled state model, the server's memory of what a device holds lasts as long as the connection. A reconnect reloads every op that device syncs, paced like a first load. The device keeps working from its own store meanwhile, and only synced ops are affected: an ordinary call has no connection to lose. With no cap, a reload grows with the results. A resume would send only what changed since the device's position, either from a summary the device sends or by working forward from the command log.
suggest: Not in v1. Build C4 on the ruled model, measure what reconnects cost once the paced load exists, and build the command-log resume if they dominate. The frames stay the same either way, so nothing built now is thrown away.

asks.text: Leave resume for later, or build it into C4?

where: C4d: a reconnect sends its result hash, an unchanged result sends no rows (dbc731f). Plan: docs/plan-replica-feed.md C4d.

name: Generated UI
sub: Ruled 2026-09-16: 14a and 14b stand; 14c moves to the post-deploy roadmap as 18f, lexing question included.
decided: Lets build this later on - add it to the post-deploy roadmap. At that point all the system bits will be settled.
explain:
Step 1 landed as 14a: ordo interface, GET /interface, and a descriptor that is a projection of the catalog manifest, now at ordo.interface/2. Catalog scoping is one filter: the route filters manifests with the same check the door runs, asserted as an equality in both directions, so a manager-only op’s name appears nowhere in a viewer’s document. DL §13 versus ui-gen.md resolved toward ui-gen, as proposed.

Step 2 landed as 14b: @ordo/react, the headless runtime in clients/ordo-react/, the first JavaScript in the repo. It reads the descriptor at run time and derives everything from it, with no op-name heuristic anywhere: the wire method from call.method, the verbs from call.terminal, the form from params[]. CAS is unavoidable rather than offered: a CAS op committed without rev is refused before the wire, cas_miss becomes a conflict state with exactly one refetch, and a retry re-asserting the stale rev is refused locally. cas_miss and version_skew are kept apart (one refetches a row, the other restarts a listing). Paging terminates on a missing next and nothing else. 89 vitest tests against the 165-op golden descriptor and a mock door. Building it found seven facts a renderer needs that /1 did not carry; all seven closed by /2, and the package refuses /1 loudly.

Owed from 14b and deliberately not done there: live (?live=1) and page-level snapshot coordination, which need a log position on the read path that nothing carries (11-17); optimistic apply and typed rollback; hook-level render tests; and the JS build is not wired into cargo or CI, so a descriptor shape change can break the package silently.

How Watermelon works, looked up: it is built on the shadcn registry standard, JSON over HTTP: a catalog of items, each carrying its source files, dependencies and cssVars for theming. npx shadcn add writes the source into your project, so the code is yours. The registry schema carries no data contract; Ordo’s interface descriptor is the data contract, and ui-gen §5’s binding grammar is where descriptor fields meet component props. “Support the standard” therefore means: consume items as the skin, and emit per-deployment items whose props bind from the descriptor.
suggest:
Step 3, surface descriptors (14c), is blocked on the language, and I would unblock it by lexing the five annotations rather than by a sidecar file. ui-gen.md §1 says a surface descriptor is the interface descriptor plus label, desc, order, choices and danger. DL §10.3 marks all five inert and the lexer carries none of them, so 14a emits none: an always-null danger would be a producer-less field a renderer would learn to trust, and “this is destructive” would come to mean “nobody wrote one”.

Why the language and not a sidecar. An annotation describes one field or one op, and it changes when that declaration changes. In the schema it is versioned, diffed and refused with the declaration; in a sidecar it drifts, and the descriptor stops being a projection of one source. The five keywords are also already reserved, so the cost you named (every keyword is forever) has been paid at the reservation; lexing them adds meaning, not surface. The cost that remains is real: five keywords in the grammar for the benefit of a renderer.

Order from here: (1) wire the JS build into CI so 14b cannot break silently; (2) 11-17 log-positioned reads, which 14b’s live and snapshot half is specified on top of; (3) lex the five annotations, then 14c; (4) the Watermelon skin via one cssVars token set; (5) registry emission, so ordoc serves each deployment’s surfaces as shadcn items and ejection is already in your tree.

asks.text:
Your words: generated UI should be a feature we deploy, basic components built from data; consider Watermelon; needs further discussion.

The Watermelon question is researched in the Explain panel: it is a shadcn registry, so consuming it is the skin and publishing per-deployment registry items is the bigger move, and both fit. What discussion is left is the one decision the language needs: lex the five annotation keywords (label, desc, order, choices, danger), or keep them in a sidecar file. Steps 1 and 2 of the order in Suggest (wire the JS build into CI; log-positioned reads) proceed either way. If you want the discussion in a document rather than this box, say so and it gets the same treatment as the blob explainer.

name: How the server knows what a device already holds
sub: Ruled 2026-09-15: the subscription remembers what it sent; a reconnect reloads, paced.
decided: take reccomendation
explain: When a synced op changes, the server has to send the device the difference. (A) The subscription remembers what it last sent and diffs against it; on reconnect the device gets everything again. (B) The device sends a summary of what it holds and the server sends only what changed, which needs a summary protocol that gets hard for large results. (C) The server works forward from the command log and re-evaluates only the rows touched, which is the most efficient and needs every guard's dependency set, since one access change can hide rows no command named.
suggest: (A) for v1. Every frame comes from an ordinary read at a known position, so it is correct by construction, and the cost of a full resend on reconnect is bounded by the size cap. (C) is the upgrade path behind the same frames.
where: C4b: the subscription remembers per-row digests and a reconnect reloads, crates/ordo-api/src/sync.rs (merge 17b3976).

name: Must a synced op include its id in what it returns
sub: Ruled 2026-09-15: a synced op must return its id.
decided: take reccomendation
explain: A device keys synced rows by entity and id. The id is in the paging cursor today, but inside an authenticated token the client cannot read. If the server added it to sync frames on its own, a feed would send something the op itself does not return.
suggest: Yes. An op can be synced only if its projection includes the anchor entity's id, so a feed never sends more than an ordinary call would.

asks.text: Require the id in the projection?

name: How large a synced op may be
sub: Ruled 2026-09-15: no cap; large loads arrive in paced pages, with honest progress.
decided: I think a cap like that would be arbitrary - instead it should paginate over time and be honest that over 10k will take a while - add in some waits to not overload the db (first loads)
explain: A synced op's whole result goes to the device, so it has to be bounded: provably bounded, or acknowledged unbounded by its author, and in both cases under a cap. Truncating instead of refusing would leave a device holding a partial result that answers offline questions wrongly without knowing it.
suggest: 10,000 rows per synced op by default, configurable per deployment, refused above it with a typed sync_too_large error rather than truncated.

asks.text: 10,000 by default, or another number?

name: What a device's replica may receive
sub: Ruled 2026-09-14: op-scoped sync, with the whole-space feed as its special case.
decided: Take all reccomendations and update doc
explain:
Guards are evaluated on the server, and a device may only hold what its person may read. A membership or acl write can change what someone may read without touching those rows, so the feed also has to take rows away.

(a) Whole-space command feed, the definition language's literal wording: safe only for someone who may read the whole space; everyone else gets no replica. (b) A per-person filtered command feed: fully Jazz-like, and the server must work out every person's difference after each access change. (c) Op-scoped sync: the app names the ops a device keeps in sync, and the server sends row-level changes to each op's result for that person. The device stores the rows once and answers new questions over them. This is how ElectricSQL and PowerSync do it.
suggest: (c), with (a) as its special case. Safe by construction, because a device only receives what an ordinary call would return; access changes remove rows for free, because they already invalidate the op; and it reuses the live and position machinery that exists.
where: Op-scoped sync built as C4a to C4c: syncability in ordo-plan, crates/ordo-api/src/sync.rs, syncOp in @ordo/sdk (17b3976).

Level 2: Ordo pipelines evaluated in JavaScript: a second implementation of the language, which the vault plan warns against. Level 3: Postgres in WASM (PGlite): the same SQL the server runs, a multi-megabyte download and a slower first load. The vault plan already recommends it for F7.

sub: Ruled 2026-09-14: a device-local key now, shaped for the passkey wrap and the server-released key of 5g-rev.

A key the server releases only while access holds is 5g-rev's third layer.

sub: Ruled 2026-09-14: replication, like Jazz. The plan is being revised against the design documents.
decided: This is supposed to function like jazz - so yes replication - that's the whole point of the indexdb and fast responsive usage -  its pretty critical.
explain:
A, a cache of answers: each entry is one op's response for one set of parameters, for one person in one space, with its chain position. Instant reads and offline reads of anything already fetched. Needs one small server change and nothing heavy on the device.

B, a replica of rows: rows mirrored to the device and queries evaluated there, which answers new questions offline. Needs a change feed that does not exist, the device engine F7 prices at 8 to 12 agent sessions, and a per-person copy of the data, because guards are evaluated on the server and a device may only hold what its person may read.

name: Where a key release is recorded
sub: Ruled and built 2026-09-14: option (a). A key release about a space is recorded in that space's own stream.
decided: Take the reccomendation
explain:
A key release is the platform asking to use a space’s key, for one stated purpose, on behalf of one request. It is recorded at deployment scope today, because the routing rule sends an observation to the deployment whenever the subject has no relationship with the space, and the platform never has one. Since D2 it also carries the space it touched, as about.

So under the new topology it would live centrally, and not in the tenant’s own record. That is the reading of the existing rule, and it may be the wrong outcome: a tenant auditing their own custody is exactly the party who should see “the platform opened my key, for this purpose, at this time”, and under your positioning it is plausibly the single most important line in their audit trail.
suggest:
Three options. (a) Route them to the space stream, which puts the record where the interested party is, and weakens the rule that the deployment stream holds every platform custody act. (b) Dual-write, which gives both readers the fact and creates two records that can disagree, which this codebase works hard to avoid. (c) Keep them central and give the tenant a derived view, filtered to their own space, which keeps one record and costs a reader surface that does not exist yet.

Recommendation: (a). The routing rule exists to stop a stranger writing into a tenant’s record, and the platform is not a stranger to a space whose key it holds. Routing custody acts about a space into that space’s stream honours the rule’s purpose rather than its letter, and it keeps one record with one reader.

Note this interacts with growth: key releases are the dominant volume and do not collapse, so moving them into tenant streams moves that volume with them.
where: Key releases recorded in the space's own stream (9ea5d26, merged 5d1bd92), crates/ordo-secevent/src/event.rs.

name: The record grows 256x under a sweep
sub: Ruled: your recommendation taken.
decided: I will take your reccomendation.
explain:
Answered in docs/opslog-growth-explained.html, with the diagrams and the worked table. The short version: the 256x is not the growth that matters. Only denials collapse. Every other event writes one entry, and the dominant producer is key releases, one per lease, on any read or write touching a sealed field. Roughly 170 MB a day at a hundred tenants against about 2.3 MB an hour for a capped sweep.

And a caveat that makes those numbers conditional: MeteredKeys::with_stream() has no production caller, so key releases do not reach the log in any deployment built through this tree today.
suggest:
The tenancy ruling changes this, and in your favour. The cap logic is unchanged, since there is still one deployment scope. But the volume now lands in the control database rather than anywhere a tenant feels it. And if key-release-home takes option (a) and routes key releases into space streams, the deployment stream’s steady state falls to near nothing, so the sweep growth stops being a spike on a large baseline and becomes nearly all of what the stream holds. That makes it a clearer signal and makes a generous retention number affordable: a stream quiet at rest can keep a year of sweeps where one carrying every key release cannot keep ninety days.

Standing recommendation: take the growth, keep the cap keyed on the scope (capping per target hands the attacker the ability to size your record by choosing space ids), and set the deployment retention number independently, which D1b already landed as ORDO_DEPLOYMENT_SECLOG_RETENTION_DAYS.

Separate recommendation, the real fix for the rate: collapse key releases the way denials collapse, keyed on (deployment, space, purpose) with the count inside the hashed body. Sampling is refused, because the design settled “nothing is sampled” and argued why.

asks.text: Confirm the cap and the retention approach, and say whether key releases should collapse.

where: Collapse key (scope, about, subject, op) and its own retention number, crates/ordo-secevent/src/collapse.rs (D1+D2, 6d453ca). Plan: docs/plan-opslog.md Q-4.

name: The reader of the ops log is also its pruner
sub: Ruled: the reader is not the pruner, and every read is auditable. Separating them needs a deployment-level role, which is its own build.
decided: This should be auditable and NO - the reader should not be the pruner.
explain:
You ruled the backend's own admin may read the deployment artifact. That is right and it is the artifact's purpose. The residual: the same admin can also prune it and switch it off with the toggle.

The plan's rule that every read of the artifact appends an entry to the artifact helps, because “who looked at the cross-tenant probe record, and when” becomes answerable. It does not close it: whoever can prune can prune the read records too.
suggest:
File it rather than pretend append-on-read solves it. The honest fix is a role that reads and cannot prune or configure, and there is nothing to build it on today: roles resolve per space and there is no deployment-level role concept. Building one is its own item and probably its own ruling.

The only thing available now that changes the shape: keep the reader offline, where it needs database credentials rather than a role, so no token, session or capability grant ever reaches it. That does not separate the powers, it just means they are not reachable over HTTP.

asks.text: Accept the concentration for now, or keep the reader offline only until a role exists?

name: Reading another space without replicating it
sub: Ruled in conversation 2026-09-13: host-side merge only. A case that needs a real join reopens it.
decided: Confirm suggestion (in conversation, 2026-09-13).
explain:
The catalogue must not be replicated (your ruling), so a tenant reading it reads somewhere else. Three mechanisms, ranked by what they cost the model.

Host-side merge. Fetch from your space, fetch from the other, merge in the host. No join, so no invariant is touched. This is what the marketplace already does: three lists unioned client-side. Costs an extra round trip and an N+1 risk.

A foreign data wrapper. postgres_fdw lets one Postgres query another as if local, so real joins work. Costs a shared dependency (the catalogue target down means every tenant’s joins fail), weaker planning across the boundary, and a connection per backend per remote. It also needs an extension, which Ordo currently requires none of.

A cross-space query in the planner. Real joins, no extension, and it costs the invariant that makes everything else checkable: the planner returns a table and its predicate as one value, and every statement is re-verified before it leaves the crate. Punching a hole for “read-only shared entities” needs the placement syntax you already rejected.
suggest: Recommendation: host-side merge, and treat the absence of joins as the constraint it is. The marketplace, the catalogue and the public site are all unions rather than joins, which is why this has not bitten yet. If a genuine join across the boundary ever becomes necessary, that is the moment to reopen it, and the honest answer then is the foreign data wrapper rather than weakening the planner.

asks.text: Confirm merge-only, or name the case that needs a real join.

where: Host-side merge is an application pattern; nothing to build. Recorded on the board only (no entry in docs/corpus-rulings.md).

name: The third home: a system space
sub: Ruled: confirmed.
decided: Confirmed.
explain:
Ordo names two homes and needs three. The control plane holds identity, access and grants: infrastructure, not entities, no chain. Packages hold code, distributed as signed git artifacts and installed rather than queried. Tenant spaces hold customer data. Nothing holds platform-owned runtime content: a tool catalogue, system agents, reference data, a third party’s app listing.

The catalogue case forced it: you ruled it should not be replicated, and a singular catalogue needs a home that is not a tenant and not the control plane.
suggest:
Make it a space. Platform-owned, with a universal read window. It gets a chain, guards, versioning, deploys and export for free, and needs no entity kind and no placement syntax. Its only distinguishing properties are that nobody erases it and everybody reads it.

Third-party content does not go there. A third party is itself a tenant: what they publish lives in their space and is shared outward, so their chain records what they changed and their erasure removes it. Putting their listing in a platform space would make the platform the author of record for something it did not write.

The test for which home a thing belongs in: is the platform genuinely the author? Tool catalogue, yes. A third party’s app listing, no.

And one new artifact is needed: discovery across publishers you have no relationship with is the case windows and feeds cannot serve. A derived projection in the control plane, rebuilt from what publishers consented to expose, never a source of truth, pruned when a publisher is erased.

asks.text: Confirm the three homes and the authorship test, or name a different split.

where: The system space exists at boot and the first apply completes it: 17v (5d33177, b265988). Ruling in docs/corpus-rulings.md, The third home (2026-09-12).

name: A tenant cannot install an app
sub: Ruled: apps are versioned and a tenant selects among versions; denizens is part of the system, not a marketplace.
decided: Denizens is a bad exampel because "denizens" would be simply a part of the system not a third party market place. But apps can be versioned and tenants should be able to select between those versions.
explain:
There is one schema for the whole deployment. $artifacts and $activations carry no $space column, and the registry says plainly that activations record “which version the deployment points at, one”. Every space runs the same artifact.

So a marketplace of installable apps is not expressible. If a third-party app is a package (shapes, ops, routines, triggers), installing it is a deployment act, and tenant A cannot have it while tenant B does not. This is a sharper gap than where a listing lives, and it is structural rather than missing plumbing.
suggest:
Three ways out, in ascending cost. (a) Apps are deployment-level, chosen by the operator, and the marketplace is a catalogue an operator installs from. Honest, cheap, and not what “marketplace” usually promises. (b) Per-space activation: $activations gains a space, so spaces run different versions. That touches the artifact registry, the planner’s cache, deploy propagation and every assumption that one schema describes the deployment. (c) Apps are data rather than code: an app declares no shapes, only configuration over shapes that already exist, so installing is a row. Cheapest at runtime and the least capable.

Recommendation: decide what an app is allowed to be before choosing. If apps may define their own entities, (b) is the only honest answer and it is a large build. If apps are configuration over a platform-defined model, (c) costs almost nothing and covers the denizens case exactly, where a “denizen” is config over a fixed shape.

asks.text: Are third-party apps allowed to define their own shapes, or are they configuration over yours?

where: Filed as checklist 18u for after the first deployment. You ruled it twice, 2026-09-13 and 2026-09-29. Nothing built.

name: Windows get more expensive, feeds get cheaper
sub: Answered in conversation: a window stops access, not memory. Taking data back off a device is the revocable local cache (5g-rev).
decided: I guess my questions is what allows "you can no longer see my data" Is that even possible?
explain:
A window resolves its grant in the control plane, then opens the owner’s target and runs the guarded query there. Under routing that is a second connection to a second database, and it can never be joined to the guest’s own data. Collaborating across five owners is five reads.

A feed copies into the receiver’s space, after which every read is local, in their own target, joinable with their own rows.

In a single-database deployment a window is the cheaper mechanism. Under routing it is the more expensive one, and the guidance to app authors inverts.
suggest: Say so in the modelling guidance rather than letting authors discover it. Windows for small, live, revocable views where freshness matters. Feeds for anything read often or joined against local data. And note the cost feeds carry that windows do not: revocation stops a feed and already-copied data stays, which is stated at consent and cannot be undone.

asks.text: Confirm, and I will put it in the modelling guidance.

where: Owed: docs/modeling-guidance.md must say windows cost more than feeds under routing; it does not mention routing. Ruling in docs/corpus-rulings.md. Checklist 22g.

name: High-volume data does not belong on the chain
sub: Ruled: confirmed, as recommended.
decided: Confirmed. Do as reccomended.
explain:
A real app has tables that want no audit chain: call logs, cost telemetry, events. Modelled as entities in Ordo, each row costs a command group, two images and a chain append under the space’s advisory lock. You pay for revertibility and tamper-evidence on data nobody reverts, and a busy tenant hits the per-space write ceiling with its least valuable writes.

I said last week Ordo lacks an unchained tier. It does not. The blob tier is exactly that: bulk data batched behind a reference. Since C4 an upload is an ordinary converge, so a batch of a thousand records is one chain append instead of a thousand.
suggest:
Batch into sealed objects, reference them from a row, keep aggregates as rows. The batch is sealed under the space key before it leaves the process, so R2 or S3 holds ciphertext and crypto-erasure reaches it. It is swept when unreferenced. Aggregates stay chained because they are small, rarely written, and are what reporting actually reads.

The cost, stated: no ad-hoc query over the detail. “Which calls used model X last Tuesday” becomes fetch-and-scan. If that is a product surface rather than a debugging need, this is the wrong answer and you want an analytics store beside Ordo, with per-tenant erasure becoming your problem there.

This is modelling guidance rather than a feature, and the natural instinct is to make the log an entity and find the cost later.

asks.text: Confirm, and I will write it into the modelling guidance.

where: No build: the blob tier is the unchained tier. Recorded in docs/corpus-rulings.md, Bulk data belongs behind a reference (2026-09-12).

name: Moving a live space between databases
sub: Ruled. Routing refuses a move until the move exists (WouldMove); the full build is post-release item 18e.
decided: Make sure the routing can handle it, and add the full implementation to the post release roadmap.
explain:
The plan covers attaching a database at provisioning time. It does not cover moving a space that already has data from one target to another, and that is the feature a customer asks for the moment they hear a dedicated tier exists: “promote us”.

It is excluded because it needs a consistency argument the plan does not make. The chain must not fork. The undo horizon must survive the move. Blob references must be repointed or the objects moved with them. And the cutover has to be atomic from the caller’s point of view while spanning two databases, which no transaction can do.
suggest: File it as its own item rather than smuggling it into the routing build. The routing work is worth having without it, since new tenants can be provisioned onto any target from day one. Promotion is a second build with a real design problem in it, and pretending otherwise is how it gets half-built.

asks.text: Agree to file it separately, or is promotion a launch requirement?
