name: Deployment operational security log
sub: Ruled: a toggle, with its own artifact as the default.
decided: It should be a toggle. But its own artifact makes sense to me as a default.
explain:
The checklist row was stale and is corrected. This is not “a whole missing subsystem”. Scope::Deployment exists, the door routes to it on all three denial paths, and it is stored, signed into its own chain from its own genesis, and retained. The crate even argues your 2026-09-07 ruling in its own words: an unchained operator log is the one an attacker can edit.

name: Backfill audit encoding
sub: Ruled — summarised default, per-creator full images; 13c unblocked
decided: Let's go with option 2 - but i'd like the ability to switch to option one if an app creator wishes it.
explain:
This row exists because a coverage audit caught me claiming your answer was recorded when it was not. On 2026-09-06 you approved schema evolution and added: “the audit line should split and a summary should be created — the idea is that the data integrity is guaranteed so data before = data now in a different structure.” That is an answer to the one question plan-schema-evolution.md §9 leaves open. It was never written into the plan, never recorded in corpus-rulings.md, and §9 still reads [open] and still recommends the opposite option. Checklist 13c still says “blocked on §9”.

The question, plainly. A transforming backfill rewrites a column across every row of an entity — say, splitting name into first and last. The audit spine records every write with a before image, because the before image is the only record of what a value used to be. A backfill is millions of writes. So either the log grows larger than the data it describes, or it summarises — and a summary of a transformation does not say what any particular value was, which is the one thing the before image exists for.

Why it cannot wait: the barrier, the chunk cursor and the verify pass can all be built against either answer, but the group encoding cannot change afterwards without moving every chain hash it already wrote.
suggest:
Take your answer, and close Z-014 inside it rather than beside it — option 2 with a proof obligation.

Your sentence contains the fix. “Data before = data now in a different structure” is not a comment on the migration; it is a claim that can be checked. So the summarised group carries three things: the row count, the minted/touched id set, and a content hash of the pre-transform values under the same canonical encoding the chain already uses. That is one hash per chunk, not one image per row — the log stays proportional to the migration, not to the data.

What it buys: the guarantee you actually asked for becomes verifiable. Anyone can recompute the hash from the post-transform rows by applying the declared inverse and see that the claim holds. What it does not buy: point recovery of one row's old value. That is genuinely lost, and it should be disclosed by ordo plan — “this migration is verifiable but not row-revertible” — rather than discovered by someone who needed it.

And keep option 1 available per migration. A small transform over a sensitive entity should be able to say “full images” and pay for them. One knob, defaulting to the summary, is honest; forcing every migration onto one encoding is what makes this irreversible.

Confirm this reading and it becomes a ruling in corpus-rulings.md, §9 stops being [open], and 13c unblocks.

asks.text:
Your answer maps onto the plan's option 2 (summarised batch groups), and option 2 has a recorded defect I owe you before you confirm it.

The three candidates §9 weighs:

1. Full per-row images. Correct, revertible, and produces a log larger than the data for every large transform.
2. Summarised batch groups — a count, an id set and a content hash instead of per-row images. Cheap, tamper-evident, and it is settled already for creates, on the grounds that “creates have no before, and the after is the database”. A backfill is all converges, which do have a before. This is the option your answer describes.
3. A pre-transform snapshot outside the chain, with the chain carrying only its hash. Restores revertibility and invents a second durable record with its own retention, pruning and erasure story — the thing this platform has been careful not to have.

The defect, recorded as Z-014 and still open: a corrected rerun converges an existing row with no before image; delete-by-minted-ids destroys the prior row, and keeping it cannot restore the old value. So under option 2, a botched backfill is not revertible — the data is transformed and the record of what it was is gone.

Does “data before = data now, in a different structure” mean the summary must prove that (a verifiable content hash of the old shape, kept), or that it may simply assert it?

The part that made me file this rather than note it. name: The last process-wide refusal over one tenant's state
sub: Built 2026-09-21, and it found the same defect in readiness one layer up
decided: okay execute
explain:
A deployment used to refuse to boot when ORDO_SPACE named a tenant with no custody — the last place one space’s state decided whether a whole process started. It now quarantines that one space, names it in /health/ready with the command that fixes it, and serves everything else.

Writing the test found that readiness had the same defect. Its custody check probed ORDO_SPACE, so the first run came up, quarantined the space correctly, and then answered 503 — a load balancer would have pulled the whole deployment out of rotation because one tenant was not provisioned yet. It now probes the system space, which the boot always creates and whose custody failing genuinely does mean the deployment can serve nobody. That is the split continuity already had: the check answers for the control plane, the register answers for tenants.

And the master-key probe was narrower than it read. It checked only ORDO_SPACE, so a deployment whose tenant was not provisioned never verified its master key at all — which is now the ordinary first-boot state. It checks the system space always, and the configured space too when that one has custody.

The property the old refusal protected is untouched and is asserted: the binary reads custody and never creates it, so a typo in ORDO_SPACE still mints nothing.
suggest: Nothing further. deploying.md is corrected in the two places that described the old refusal, one of which printed it verbatim.

name: The control plane boots without the deployment under it
sub: All three pieces built 2026-09-21. A tenant can now be created through the door, and a tenant's failure is no longer the deployment's
explain:
You answered the recovery question by changing the shape rather than routing around it: the system space is the control plane, a tenant’s state is a fact about that tenant, and dependence runs one way. Pieces 1 and 2 made a rewound tenant a quarantine rather than a refused boot, and gave the boot a reconciliation pass that prints what it found and repairs nothing.

Piece 3 is std.space.create, on the same gate the apply op uses: owner, step-up so no capability token reaches it, and the bound space must be the deployment’s own, because the first two are deployment-wide policy installed in every space and a tenant’s owner passes both. You supply a name and an owner; the deployment mints the id. Seven tests, four of them the gate.

Building it found a defect that would have shipped quietly. The door builds its memberships from members.id and ignores the principal column beside it, so the first version — which minted a member id the way it mints a space id — would have produced a tenant reachable only by an identifier nobody holds a token for, with the named owner locked out of the space created for them. The test now rebuilds the engine from the real rows rather than asserting on the row it just wrote.

A new tenant is reachable immediately, without a restart: the create announces itself on its own channel and every replica rebuilds its door the way it already does after a deploy. The answer tells you which — reachable: true, or that it lands at the next restart — rather than leaving you to assume.

What it leaves owed is on the checklist: a CLI verb for it, the creation record on the security stream, and 17ac above.
suggest: The CLI verb next, because the op is reachable over the wire and ordo has no word for it, so the only way to create a tenant today is to hand-roll the HTTP call.

Billing (invoices, payment, tax) is explicitly a product on top. Self-host: off by default, never phones home — telemetry outside the egress pins is the SSRF path §7b closes.

name: What the platform must do before anything is deployed to it
sub: All three built 2026-09-20: readiness means ready to deploy, boot creates the system space, and the CLI applies over the wire with no database credentials
decided: Readiness is not a measure of is a deployment running - it is a measure of are we ready to apply and run deployments. CLI should interact with the endpoint - should be adjusted with a flag. System space should exist at boot because nothing can really exist without it.
explain:
Standing the cluster instance up exposed three places where the binary still behaves like a server that serves one program rather than a platform that receives them.

17t, readiness. Built 2026-09-20. It now gates on five checks, none of them about a running program: the database answers, custody opens, the configuration a live program needs is present (a blob field with no store attached is named entity and field), no required worker is quarantined, and the deployment can still create schema. The body carries program_active either way, plus a line per check saying what is wrong without disclosing a credential, a host or a port. A deployment with nothing deployed is ready, which is the point.

17u and 18l, the CLI over the wire. Built 2026-09-20. std.deployment.apply is the door: owner only, presence required so a capability token can never apply, refused unless the caller is bound to the deployment’s own space, and serialized by a lock taken before the first schema read, so two applies cannot interleave their decisions rather than merely their statements. The CLI takes --host (default ordo.inf.smg.icu), a token from an ordinary sign-in, and falls back to the database when no host is given. No HTTP client was added: it reuses the hand-rolled client already in ordo-blob, so no native TLS and no image growth. The headline test compares the two paths’ reports as text, so the wire cannot quietly say something different from the database path.

17v, the system space. Built 2026-09-20, and the cluster proved why it was needed: the first real deployment crash-looped on $keycustody does not exist, because the binary read its own custody table without creating it. Boot now creates the platform’s tables and mints custody for the system space, whose name is a constant compiled into the binary and therefore not something an operator can mistype into existence. A tenant named in ORDO_SPACE that has no custody still refuses, now saying the system space is fine, which tenant is missing, and the command that creates it.
suggest: Building in this order: 17v first, since a deployment with no system space has nowhere to keep what it knows; then 17t, which makes the readiness probe honest and lets the cluster manifest point back at it; then 17u with 18l, which retires the apply job rather than building one.

name: Restore & disaster recovery
sub: Built 2026-09-20, R1 through R3: a restore is recorded in the chain, a silent one is refused at boot against a witness a space restore cannot roll back, and the drill runs as a test
explain:
The promise, now kept: a restore cannot happen quietly. Every signed checkpoint head is also written to the control database before the checkpoint itself, so a restore of a space’s own database cannot roll the evidence back with the data, and the boot refuses when the chain sits below a head the witness remembers with no marker explaining it. ordo restore --record writes that marker.

A checkpoint counts when the stored chain agrees with it, which is your ruling of 2026-09-20, and the anchor is the newest one that agrees. Orphans from a discarded timeline are judged on every run rather than by when they were signed.

The drill is a test, on a real copy-restore of an attached database: the refusal fires, exactly one discontinuity appears where it should from both anchors, the schema has not drifted, the rows equal the pre-backup snapshot with the discarded groups gone, and the bundle re-hashes against its manifest. Three more variants pin a missing, a doubled and a misplaced marker.

Five places the plan disagreed with the code, each followed toward the code and recorded rather than papered over, including one where the plan’s own rule would have broken an earlier increment’s done-when.
suggest: Queued behind the runtime go (the drill wants a bootable binary). No decision owed.
where: 17j R1 to R3: export digest, witness in control database, drill test in crates/ordo-cli/tests/operator.rs (8ebf120 to 4378135); docs/howto-operating.md Backup and Restore.

name: A developer cannot call their own op locally
sub: Fixed 2026-09-20: `ordo dev` prints a ready-to-paste token and the curl line to use it. The quickstart now shows the working path
explain:
ordo dev compiles and serves in under a second, and then a developer cannot call the op they just wrote. The door requires a bearer token on every call and refuses for lack of membership before it ever looks at a row guard, so even an entity with no access rules at all is unreachable. The tokens ordo dev would accept are signed with a secret it derives from its own process id and never prints, and it mounts no login route, so there is no way in from outside the process. What you get is a correct, well-shaped refusal: missing bearer token.

The quickstart written today documents this rather than pretending a copy-paste curl works, which is the honest thing to publish and a bad thing to leave standing.
suggest: Built as recommended: a development principal is seeded into the local database on reset, and its token is printed with a line saying it is local only and signed by a key that dies with the process. ORDO_TOKEN_KEY is accepted too, so a script can mint its own, and a malformed one is a refusal rather than a silent fallback. What keeps it local: the seeding lives in the dev loop’s own reset, which ordo apply, ordo migrate and the server binary never call, so no path puts that row or that token into a real deployment. The end-to-end test drives a real HTTP request against a real server on a real port, and was watched failing first with 403.

name: Key rotation & epoch lifecycle
sub: Built 2026-09-19 (K1–K3): rotate mints a new epoch, a resumable re-seal pass moves every ciphertext off the old one, and destroying an epoch is refused while anything still reads under it. Ciphertext stays readable and no search digest moved
decided: Envelope encryption it is - with built in ability to force re-encrypt after exposure.
explain:
Found by the 2026-09-07 coverage audit: no row, and the checklist closed only the half it named.

ordo-crypto/src/custody.rs has rotate, retire, destroy_epoch and a Purpose::Reseal. Items 8b, 8c and 8d closed the per-space master key, DEK rotation, and the key-release stage. What implementation.md and deploying.md §4 additionally settle, and what nothing in crates/ does:

1. The lazy resumable re-seal job. Rotating an epoch does not re-encrypt anything; old rows stay sealed under the old key. A worker is supposed to walk them and re-seal under the current epoch, resumably. grep reseal across every crate finds a Purpose variant and one unrelated test. So an epoch can never actually be retired — there is always live data under it.

2. Master-key rotation as a blind-index re-index. Blind-index digests are keyed off the master key and are deliberately epoch-independent, so rotating the master invalidates every blind index at once. It needs an offline rebuild and an atomic swap under a write barrier. Nothing does this — and f7-vault-plan.md §3.4 closes a departed member's equality oracle by saying a master rotation clears it. That closure currently has no mechanism behind it.

3. Retire-then-destroy driven by the undo-horizon gate rather than by a direct call.

Note the asymmetry the export work created: destroy_space is built and required, so deletion works and rotation does not.
suggest: No decision owed — your sketch matches K1–K3 as planned. The one open build question stays: wiring the trigger, since rotate() currently has no production caller at all. It rides the supervisor (17d/17i).

asks.text: You said: envelope encryption, with a built-in ability to force re-encrypt after exposure. That is what K1–K3 in plan-production-ops.md build: per-space DEKs wrapped under the master, a new epoch on rotation, and the chunked resumable re-seal worker that an operator can force after an exposure. It has no production caller until R3 exists, so it is queued behind the supervisor as 17i.

name: Concurrent writes to one row can freeze the server
sub: Fixed 2026-09-18: each write attempt has its own log; six writers to one row sharing a log now all return, land as +6, and all six groups reach the chain
explain: Every write in a space shares one in-memory write log behind a standard mutex. The executor holds that mutex while the write waits on the database for a row lock, and a second writer that already holds the row lock needs the same mutex to commit. Each waits on the other. Because the blocked mutex call runs on the async runtime’s own threads, the whole process stalls: the reproduction’s own 20-second timeout never fires. ordo-host gives one log to every request in a space, so ordinary contention at the served door reaches it. The log also has one “pending group” slot shared by all writers, so one write can discard another’s group.
suggest: What was built: give each write attempt its own pending group and staged payloads, and touch the shared log only to mint ids and to record a committed group, never across database I/O. Done when the reproduction passes as an ordinary test. It goes before the runtime binary, because the binary is what puts real concurrent traffic on the door.

name: A space on another database hears no invalidations
sub: Built 2026-09-14 (S7): a listener per database, and a node refreshes its bus when a database is attached.
decided: Performance costs? Network layer, PG handling etc (Then, after the measurements: acknowledged.)
explain:
A NOTIFY reaches only listeners connected to the same database, so a space on an attached database would publish invalidations nobody on the control database hears, and its ?live subscriptions would go silently stale.

You asked what it costs, and it was measured: establishing a listener takes about 0.7 to 1.3 ms, delivery is about 0.08 ms at the median and 0.30 ms at p99, and each listener holds one backend per target per node. So the cost scales with the number of distinct databases, not with spaces, the same property the rest of the routing rests on.
suggest: S7 builds a listener per attached database, pinned by a test that proves an invalidation on an attached database reaches a subscriber. Its failure mode is silence, which is why it is not deferred.

asks.text: Nothing open.

name: The isolation suite stops at the write protocol
sub: Done: built 2026-09-12, its last finding closed 2026-09-13 (11-27).
decided: Build
explain:
spaces.rs is the two-space isolation suite and it is well built: the fixture seeded twice with identical row ids, differing in reads, guards, tree walks, writes and uniqueness, on the stated ground that isolation must not rest on ids being lucky. It reaches the write protocol and nothing above it, and names neither ordo_exec nor ordo_host.

Three bugs in two days lived exactly there. The revert applier addressed rows by id alone in seven statements. The write protocol NFC-normalised space literals and the revert applier did not. And the platform surfaces authorized against a caller-named space header, which returned 200 where it owed 403.

Behind it sits a larger fact: deployment_engine hardcodes one space id, so nothing provisions a second space into a running deployment. Three separate test justifications now lean on “no deployment provisions two spaces”, which is a fact about today rather than a property to rely on.

The same discipline one layer up: a two-space suite over ordo-exec and ordo-host with the identical-ids construction, covering the revert applier, the blob door and its collector, the platform surfaces, and security-event routing. Run by default, so the next bug of this shape fails a test rather than a tenant.

Cheap now. When multi-space provisioning is built, every latent single-space assumption lights up at once in a deployment instead of one at a time in tests.

name: Where each log lives when a tenant has their own database
sub: Ruled and built: S4 writes each space's security stream to its own database, and the deployment's to the control database.
decided: Control plane / data plane splot makes sense.
explain:
In the tenant’s database, because they travel with the data. $commandlog and its checkpoints: exit-ops already ships a space export as schema, per-entity JSONL, blob bytes and a command-log archive bundle, so the chain is part of what a tenant takes with them; erasure destroys it with the space; verify --space reads it; the undo horizon is per space. The space-scope security stream and its checkpoints, for the same reasons and because the design says a space owner reads both and verify() checks both independently, which only holds if one connection reaches them. $blobref, $blobtomb and $sealedpayload follow the chain that references them.

At the control plane, because they are about more than one tenant. The deployment-scope security stream, which is the ops log. This one must not sit in a tenant database: it holds denials by non-members and anonymous callers, and the cross-space sweep, and putting a stranger’s probe into a tenant’s record is exactly what that rule exists to prevent. Identity and authentication events, since a principal exists deployment-wide. Access, grants and share grants, which link a principal on one side to a space on the other.
suggest:
Control plane and data plane, which is the right split rather than a compromise. A small control database holding identity, access and grants, and N tenant databases holding nothing but that tenant’s data and that tenant’s history.

One concrete consequence to plan for: $secevents is currently one table with a scope column carrying both halves, and it becomes two physical tables in two databases. try_scopes walks one table today and hands every scope to one retention pass. The new shape is that the control plane prunes its own stream and each tenant database prunes its own, which incidentally makes the read/prune custody split cleaner, since the two streams can have different signers.

asks.text: Confirm the placement, or name an artifact you want on the other side.

name: Grant pinning
sub: Done — DL §8's form, the escalation executed and refused
decided: Implement reccomendation  - make sure the escalation is not possible.
explain:
Landed and verified. The pin carries the field set and the row-scope shape, because §8's counterexample is real and now runs as a test: delete member == $caller from an op body and the field set is byte-identical — the §5 comparison would apply the widening silently. Now it classifies Expanded and the whole grant dies until re-consent; narrowing applies silently and is audit-noted. Fail-closed at every edge: a changed guard walk is a different set of rows, an undeployed op is expansion-equivalent. One recorded boundary: a loosened take bound is volume, not shape, and neither half of the pin can see it — DL has no clause for it, so it is documented rather than invented.

A capability grant is how a third-party app gets scoped access. Someone consents, and the platform mints a grant into a token: one space, a listed set of ops, a mandatory expiry, and a pin of what those ops looked like at consent time. Every later call compares pinned against current, so you cannot quietly widen what an integration can reach — widening revokes it.

Grants are now recorded in a registry, so they can be revoked before expiry. Before that, a grant's only end was expiry and nothing recorded one had been issued.
suggest:
DL wins — the language authority, the only one that argues rather than asserts, it supplies the counterexample, and security-hardening-review-4.md corroborates. §5 and §10 then need editing, and the manifest needs a row-scope shape (9l's field-scope work is the foundation).

Implementing §5 as written would introduce a silent privilege escalation. Current behaviour is over-strict and fails closed, so waiting is safe.

asks.text:
security-logging-design.md §5 and api-engine-design.md §10 both pin an ordered field-set comparison per op. definition-language.md §8 says that form is “decidable and wrong”: delete member == $caller from an op body and the output field set is byte-identical, so a field-set comparison reads it as narrowing and applies it silently — “this app may read my expenses” becomes “this app may read everyone's expenses”.

All three are marked settled. Which wins?

where: 8s: crates/ordo-host/tests/pinning.rs; ruling recorded in docs/corpus-rulings.md (86393f9).

name: Keyset paging as a row bound
sub: Done — ruled, and the golden move audited op by op
decided: OKay continue as needed.
explain:
Landed. The gate accepts paging as a row bound, and the loosening is a recorded ruling in corpus-rulings.md (2026-09-05) that states exactly what counts as paging, because the gate is shared and security-bearing. The 1,803-line golden move this row used to warn about is explained and audited: it was row_scope arriving on the 16 listings, checked op by op rather than regenerated. Nothing else moved.

You asked for this one plainly, so here it is plainly.

Every operation has to promise it will not return an unlimited number of rows. If it cannot promise that, the author has to write unbounded on it — an admission that says “yes, this one can get big.” The point is that nobody accidentally ships an operation that tries to return a million rows.

An operation proves the promise in one of a few ways: it has a take 50 on it, or it collapses everything to a single row, or it looks up exactly one thing by id.

The problem. std.E.list is the built-in “show me these rows, a page at a time” operation. It genuinely cannot return a million rows — it returns twenty, then you ask for the next twenty. But the checker does not recognise paging as one of the ways to prove the promise, so it refuses.

And the obvious fix does not work. You cannot just put take 20 on it, because of where the take lands: it caps the whole listing at twenty rows forever, rather than giving you twenty per page. Row twenty-one becomes unreachable by any page you ask for. So the list would quietly stop at twenty items and look like that was all the data.
suggest:
Yes, and the reasoning is short: a paged operation cannot return unbounded rows in one response — that is what paging means. The promise the gate wants is genuinely kept, just by a mechanism the gate does not currently recognise.

The care needed is that the gate is shared and security-bearing, so the change should be a recorded ruling in corpus-rulings.md saying exactly what counts as paging, not a quiet loosening somebody finds later and cannot explain.

asks.text:
Should “it is paged” count as proof that an operation returns a bounded number of rows?

The catch, and the reason I did not just do it: this checker is shared. Teaching it to accept paging changes the rule for every operation anyone writes, not only for the built-in list.

where: 9k': keyset paging as a row bound and std.E.list (0f9fe56, landed after b43e3ca). Ruling in docs/corpus-rulings.md.

name: `check` row invariants
sub: Done — row-local checks execute; the rest refuses by name
decided: okay continue as neededs
explain:
Landed. check used <= seats lowers to a real CHECK constraint; a violation is check_violation (409) typed by SQLSTATE — never internal — and the constraint name carries the condition (teams$chk0$used<=seats) so you learn which check failed. Ref-walking and time-dependent forms refuse by name with the reasoning recorded; three more classes fell out of building it. Two-valued logic is executed inside the constraint: a null in a checked column refuses, where naive SQL would silently pass. Found on the way: DL’s own used: used + 1 spelling still waits on P5’s computed RHS, and unique/index never validate their column names.

Plainly, as asked.

A check is a rule a row must always satisfy, written once in the schema so it holds no matter which piece of code does the writing. “A discount is never above 100.” “An end date is never before its start date.” The database enforces it, so no forgotten code path can slip a bad row past it.

Why it is not built. Everything Ordo refuses has a named reason — not_found, access_guard, cas_miss. That list is deliberately closed, so a caller can handle refusals without reading error text, and so nobody invents a new one casually.

There is no name for “a check failed.” If I built the feature now, a violation would come back as internal — a 500, the code for “the server broke.” That is exactly wrong: the server did not break, it worked correctly and told you your data was invalid. We spent real effort removing that same failure elsewhere, so building it back in would be a step backwards.

Worth knowing: an audit named the missing piece — check_violation — two audits ago, and nobody added it.
suggest:
Yes to both.

The name is really just confirming a decision already made and never carried out.

On the split: Postgres can enforce a rule about a row's own columns directly and cheaply. A rule that has to go and look at another table cannot be done that way at all — it needs triggers, which are only now being built. Two of the three things the spec asks for fall on that side.

The simple half is most of the value and is honest on its own. Building all three now would drag in a whole unfinished subsystem to deliver the least-used part.

asks.text:
Two things. Add check_violation to the closed list of refusal names?

And accept that only the simple half gets built now — rules about a row's own fields, like “discount ≤ 100” — while rules that look at other rows wait for triggers?

where: 9e: row-local check invariants, crates/ordo-conformance/tests/check_invariants.rs (b58b153).

name: Authentication providers
sub: Done — passkey/WebAuthn ships, so step-up is satisfiable
decided: Ordo owns the door and ships one real provider.
explain:
Landed. ordo-identity carries passkey.rs, webauthn.rs, session.rs and directory.rs, 93 tests, and one end-to-end run that drives ceremony → subject → directory → token → verify → AccessEngine::check with nothing stubbed between the signature and the door — its control runs the identical plumbing with a password and gets StepUpRequired. Two finds nobody was looking for: provider ceremony handles had no expiry at all (one-shot was enforced, one-time was not; every handle now expires at 300s), and the COSE parser decided what label -1 meant before reading alg, so an RS256 key came back “malformed CBOR” instead of “algorithm not offered”.

Left to the deployment, deliberately: the browser ceremony itself (no test can fake a user gesture), the HTTP login and enrollment endpoints, the Postgres-backed credential store, and reading ORDO_APEX_DOMAIN at boot.

Before this: an AuthProvider trait, a password provider using a test hasher rather than argon2id, a stub OIDC provider, and no passkey provider at all — which made the door's sole step-up source unsatisfiable.

Make the engine refuse to start without it. A deployment that boots on a default apex mints passkeys against the wrong relying party, and the failure is discovered at the worst possible moment — when the domain moves and every enrolled authenticator stops working, irreversibly. A one-line boot assertion is the cheapest possible insurance against a class of loss that has no repair.

If you would rather leave it optional, then the ordering has to change instead: no passkey may be enrolled until an apex is configured, so the value is pinned before the first credential depends on it.

name: Durable idempotency
sub: Done — and the measurement corrected the plan itself
decided: Make it so ensign!
explain:
Landed, made so. idempotency_applied (409, terminal, “retrying will not change this answer”) is minted, produced at exactly one site, and proved in both directions — a crash-window retry gets it stably, a verbatim replay never does. And the measurement corrected the plan’s own audit: the journal’s completion UPDATE is not “small and inside the critical section” — it is outside the lock entirely (the lock is taken as late as possible, after the lease completes), proved from pg_locks rather than call order. The ~29% share is kept as a counterfactual. The decisive argument against folding the response store into the transaction got stronger: in-transaction, the seal must succeed before the effect can commit, so a KMS outage stops every write. Two spec lines in api-engine-design.md that still demanded the fold-in are narrowed in place, dated.

The audit came first, as you instructed, and it changed the recommendation. Reading the write path end to end found the re-execution hazard already closed: a fenced $replay journal rides the write’s own transaction (AA-004’s third leg), a retry after a crash answers instead of executing, and a stalled node that wakes up late cannot commit. What the crash window loses is only the verbatim response body, answered honestly by a named refusal. So the plan (docs/plan-idempotency.md) recommends not moving the response store into the transaction — the audit’s two unsafe rows: it would put an unbounded INSERT and a KeyProvider round trip inside the global append lock’s critical section, making a custody outage a total write outage, to buy back a convenience.

Retry the same request under the same key and get the stored response instead of a second execution. The in-memory version was wrong for more than one node in a way invisible to one process. The durable store claims a key in one statement (the unique constraint decides, in the statement that acts on it), seals responses at rest, and answers InFlight rather than Reserved when unreachable.
suggest: Yes, mint it. The inventory exists so a machine can act on the class alone, and this is a case where the class and the truth disagree. It is one enum variant, one inventory row, one producer at the router’s already-applied arm, and one test — small, and it makes the rarest, most confusing case in the retry story self-describing. The rest of the plan needs no decision: it recommends leaving the response store outside the transaction, and the docs-truth and measurement steps are just work.

asks.text: One decision, severable: the “effect committed, response lost” answer currently reuses idempotency_in_flight. That class name says retry later; the truth is this will never change — a client polling on the class polls forever. Mint idempotency_applied (409, terminal: the effect is committed, the body is gone, stop retrying)? It widens the closed wire inventory, which is why it comes to you rather than being done.

name: `allocate()`
sub: Done — four modes, both venues agree, ruling recorded
decided: Yep. A dev decides in which way to allocate and when that happens not the spec. Continue as needed
explain:
Landed and verified (93 suites green). Four modes — largestRemainder (default) · first · last · largestShare — and the invariant that makes them safe: a mode is not a second algorithm, every mode floors the shares and hands the leftover out one apiece, so the parts always sum exactly and no part is ever more than one minor unit off. Rotation is excluded with its reasoning in the ruling: it needs memory, and memory in an expression function breaks determinism. A misspelled mode is a compile error, never a silent default. One catch the lexer made: the literature spells largest_remainder, and DL §1 has no underscores — the first draft shipped four modes nobody could type.

The money-split primitive. allocate(100.00, (1,1,1)) gives 33.34 / 33.33 / 33.33: floor each share, then hand the remainder out by largest fractional part, so the parts always sum to the total exactly. Never floating point.

Its rule is built and golden-tested including host/SQL agreement — which nothing had checked, there being no second venue. Its site is not: the only legal caller is each over a list parameter, which is [lean].
suggest:
Agree with the principle, and I would go further than a parameter.

Largest-remainder is the right default — it is what regulators and accounting texts assume, and it is the only rule where the parts provably sum to the total with the smallest possible dispersion. But which party absorbs the odd penny is genuinely a business rule, not a mathematical one. Real cases differ: some split to the first party, some to the last, some to the largest share, some rotate it across invoices so it evens out over time.

My recommendation: a named-mode second argument — allocate(total, weights, largest_remainder) with that as the default — rather than a family of functions. One name to learn, the modes are a closed set the grammar can check, and an unknown mode is a compile error rather than a silent fallback.

But it needs a ruling before it is built, because DL settles the current single form. And it is blocked behind the same [lean] construct either way — there is still no legal place to call allocate. So I would record the decision now and build it when each is settled, rather than adding a mode to a function nobody can invoke yet.

One caution worth stating: rotation is not expressible as a pure function of (total, weights) — it needs to remember what it did last time. That one is application state, not a mode.

asks.text:
Your question: could different forms be offered — a parameter — so the implementer decides which split gets the extra penny, rather than the platform? You are right that this affects financial viability.

You are also right on the merits, and I want to be honest that this is a language change, not a parameter I can add quietly: it means either a second argument to allocate, or a family of named functions. Both widen the closed grammar, which is the thing the whole design is careful about.

Landed, generator-first as you ruled. One generator (ordo gen ts), two outputs: clients/ordo-sdk (typed client from the descriptor) and clients/ordo-cdk (the builder — language layer from the compiler’s closed tables, schema layer from the descriptor). Both ratchets are live: no-wildcard matches proved by three real mutations (a new language variant fails the generator’s build until its TS spelling is decided — the gen button is enforced by the compiler), and isomorphism 31 of 31 — every corpus program machine-rebuilt through the builder synthesizes back to AST-equal .ordo, with the synthesized files checked in so cargo test verifies without node. The corpus caught two real builder bugs before anyone typed a line. The demo page’s panes are rewritten in the real API and each one is synth-verified through ordo check. Owed and stated: live/refinement/whole, an @ordo/wire consolidation, and JS gates in CI.

The typed TypeScript embedding — entity("x", { amount: money() }), q.source(…).group(…) — that synthesizes canonical .ordo rather than executing at runtime. Two doors into one room: teams pick per taste, artifacts stay identical, and the platform never knows which frontend authored a definition. It now features on the converter demo page as a clearly-labelled planned pane, and you asked why it wasn’t on the roadmap — it was untracked by rule (Track C is a plan, and “a plan is not a gap”), and is now 14f, gated behind 14d.
suggest: My recommendation: yes, as the step after 14d — say “go” and I start 14d now with the CDK as its named second consumer, so the generator is built once for both. The ship bar stays the plan’s own: isomorphism (builder output ≡ hand-written .ordo, both directions) as a conformance-tested property, or it does not ship.

asks.text: Schedule it? The honest sequencing: build 14d (the generated TS SDK) first — the CDK’s core guarantee is that its API is generated from the grammar so it cannot drift, and that generator IS 14d’s machinery. Building the CDK first would hand-write what 14d generates. The plan calls the builder “nearly mechanical” once that exists.

where: 14f: clients/ordo-cdk, corpus isomorphism (1373f98, 6548b45).

name: Making the repository public
sub: Private; CI: 2 upgrade baselines missing, GHCR access, 1 timing flake (asks 10, 11)
explain:
The repo is private now and will be public, linked from the hominem page and a resume. An audit found no real secrets.

  • Untracked today: .DS_Store, compact.md, review run output, local paths.
  • Old history still holds those and a 10 MB node_modules.
  • The CLI's default host is the live deployment.

asks.text: Should the public repo be a fresh export with one clean commit, while this private repo keeps its full history as the working copy?
asks.suggest: Yes. Rewriting 2,417 commits on 6 branches is slow and risky; a fresh export drops every old file at once, and the private repo keeps the board and agent workflow unchanged.

asks.text: Should the public export leave out the board's raw files (board.jsonl, answers, marks, grief notes) and .claude/, keeping plans, rulings and the checklist?
asks.suggest: Yes. Plans, rulings and the checklist show how decisions were made; the raw answer log is working state, and leaving it out avoids reviewing every line of it.

asks.text: Should the CLI drop its default host (ordo.inf.smg.icu), so --host or ORDO_HOST is required and the refusal names both?
asks.suggest: Yes. A public tool should never point at the author's own deployment by default; the refusal tells anyone what to set in one line.

asks.text: Should the agent skill in skills/ordo/ be Apache-2.0 like the docs and SDKs, since ordo skill install copies it into app developers' projects?
asks.suggest: Yes. Today it falls under the AGPL default, so every app that installs it carries AGPL text in its repo. The docs it is built from are already Apache-2.0.

asks.text: The "Protect active branch" ruleset now blocks every push to every branch. May I narrow it to main, keep no-delete and no-force-push, and let admins bypass?
asks.suggest: Yes. As set, nothing can be pushed and a pull request needs a second person's approval. Narrowed, main still cannot be deleted or rewritten, and the release work flows again.

asks.text: Since the repo went public, our runners get no jobs. May I ask you to tick "Allow public repositories" on the k8s-ordo runner group?
asks.suggest: Yes. That setting defaults to off, which matches what we see. Forks stay guarded: their runs need your approval, and self-hosted jobs skip fork pull requests.

asks.text: The repo went public with its full history before you answered ask 1. Should I still replace it with a fresh one-commit public repo?
asks.suggest: No, keep it. The history has been public since 10-30 and may be cloned already. A swap means 2 repos, a sync step and re-pointing CI and images.

asks.text: If the repo stays as it is, should the board's raw files leave the public tree now, though they stay in its history?
asks.suggest: No. They stay readable in the history, and the board tools need them in the tree. An audit skim found product reasoning only.

asks.text: Will you add the new HominemAI/ordo to the k8s-ordo runner group's selected repositories? It still lists the old repo, now ordo-history.
asks.suggest: Yes. GitHub tracks the group's repos by id, so the new repo's jobs sit queued. Org Settings, Actions, Runner groups, k8s-ordo, Repository access. Removing ordo-history there too is fine.

asks.text: Will you give the new HominemAI/ordo write access to the 3 GHCR packages (ordo, ordo-cli, ordo-playground)? Pushes are refused with permission_denied.
asks.suggest: Yes. Each package page, Package settings, Manage Actions access, add HominemAI/ordo with Write. Until then main cannot publish images.

asks.text: The 2 upgrade tests build old Ordo from commits the 1-commit repo lacks. Should their baseline become the public first commit?
asks.suggest: Yes. Nothing has truly deployed, so the first public commit is the real starting point. Old trees as tags would put the old history back in public.

asks.text: The identity upgrade e2e starts from a pre-identity console that only ordo-history holds. Retire that job?
asks.suggest: Yes. Nothing ran that console publicly, and the public repo cannot build it. It now runs only by hand with an old_ref, which this repo cannot resolve either.

where: HominemAI/ordo (root f0246551); old history private at HominemAI/ordo-history; local branch history-main

name: CI Postgres: a dedicated instance on the cluster, or memory for the runners
explain:
A CI Postgres crashed mid-run with 10 runners. The pool is back to 8.

  • Runner pods reserve no memory or CPU, so busy nodes get overfilled.
  • 2026-11-01: test shards run together took 28 to 30 min; alone, 8 to 10.
  • Tests use 893 fixed database names, so a shared instance needs a per-job prefix.

asks.text: Should runner pods reserve memory, so the cluster places no more jobs on a node than fit?
asks.suggest: Yes, first. It addresses the likeliest cause at its root and is a small change in runner.yaml. It may let the pool go back to 10.

asks.text: Should CI move to one dedicated Postgres instance hosted on the cluster?
asks.suggest: Not now. It needs a per-job name prefix across 893 test databases, a connection budget for 8 jobs, and a sweep for leftovers. One crash would then fail every running job. Revisit if crashes continue after memory is reserved.

where: Ruled 2026-11-01: no memory reservation; move CI to a dedicated cluster Postgres. Held while the test strategy is rethought (owner, 2026-11-01)

name: Entities, fields, refs
explain: The closed grammar's core. Typed-id keys derived per entity, refs with ->, owned marking the parent edge, tree for self-edges. Everything else builds on this shape.
where: Parser crates/ordo-syntax/src/decl.rs and declparse.rs, binder crates/ordo-sema, DDL crates/ordo-schema/src/ddl.rs; exercised by crates/ordo-conformance/fixtures/market.ordo through tests/corpus.rs.

name: Pipelines & steps
explain: filter, project, sort, take, group, reduce, distinct, append. One spelling per concept — the parser refuses synonyms and names the Ordo spelling, so sort total desc answers “desc is not Ordo — sort -key”.
where: Steps parsed in crates/ordo-syntax/src/parser.rs, planned in crates/ordo-plan/src/lib.rs; exercised by the corpus runners crates/ordo-conformance/tests/corpus.rs and corpus_stage*.rs.

name: Named-query composition
explain: Ops compose. The callee is flattened at bind, so its guards inline and appear in the caller's disclosed scope — you cannot compose your way past an authorization rule.
where: Composition binding in crates/ordo-sema/src/ir.rs and lib.rs; composition ruling for take bounds 7c671f5; cases in crates/ordo-conformance/tests/corpus_c_extra.rs.

name: Keyset pagination
explain: Cursors over the language's guaranteed total order — declared sorts plus a tiebreak, NULLS LAST always. Page while rows are inserted and you get no duplicates and no skips, unlike OFFSET. Tokens are authenticated and bound to op and caller.
where: Keyset paging in crates/ordo-api/src/page.rs and crates/ordo-plan/src/artifact.rs; door tests crates/ordo-api/tests/api.rs.

name: Aggregates
explain: percentile, distinct x, joined. Identities asserted against real Postgres rather than hand-written expectations — median is p50, reversing the sort reverses the parts. Found on the way: a sort before a group was carried into the outer ORDER BY and Postgres rejected the statement outright.
where: crates/ordo-conformance/tests/aggregates.rs; checklist 9f closed (d3898a5).

name: Expression functions
explain: A closed set, and their arguments are now type-checked at bind. lower(price) used to bind, plan and emit SQL Postgres would refuse — caught only at load, as “the database would not describe this statement” rather than as the author's mistake. The class is argument_type_mismatch, a deliberate addition to the closed inventory.
where: Argument typing in crates/ordo-sema, test crates/ordo-conformance/tests/argument_types.rs; checklist 9v closed, ruling in docs/corpus-rulings.md.

name: `hash(x)`
explain: SHA-256 of the UTF-8 bytes, first eight big-endian, top bit cleared. The earlier SipHash pin was withdrawn: it is not in core Postgres, and the database computes hash in a condition. Three details are ours and are where a second implementation goes wrong — the sign mask, convert_to rather than ::bytea, and the restricted text/id domain.
where: hash() emitted with convert_to in crates/ordo-plan/src/lib.rs; typed in tests/argument_types.rs (crates/ordo-conformance).

name: `since` windows
explain: Anchors to execution time, folded at bind into an exact date literal so no NOW() reaches SQL and plans stay reproducible. It was frozen: all eight binder sites hard-coded the corpus's pinned date, so since 30d was a 154-day window widening daily. The clock is now a required argument — a default here is the shape of the bug.
where: The window folds at bind time against a supplied clock: crates/ordo-sema/src/lib.rs, test crates/ordo-conformance/tests/clock.rs. Checklist 9z closed.

name: Two-valued null logic
explain: null == null is true, null != 5 is true, ordering against null is false. It was not compiled: the planner emitted = and <>, so every comparison against a nullable column got SQL's three-valued answer and the row was silently dropped. Recorded once before as X-011 and closed as a document fix while the planner never changed.
where: Distinctness-family comparisons in crates/ordo-plan; test crates/ordo-conformance/tests/null_logic.rs. Checklist 9y closed.

name: Decimal scale 12 & money
explain: Money is integral minor units — write 2999, not 29.99, and the compiler refuses the latter. Division holds a fixed scale of 12. No implicit rounding anywhere: the conversion is the author's to write.
where: Decimal at scale 12: 8ad8018, test crates/ordo-conformance/tests/decimal.rs. Checklist 9c closed.

name: NFC normalization
explain: Stored text is normalized on write, so é and e+combining-acute are one value. Nothing did it — they sorted apart, compared unequal, and could both occupy a unique column. Three doors: the lexer for literals, the door for caller values, the write path's SQL funnel. Migration hazard probed, never repaired: normalizing can merge two rows a unique column keeps apart.
where: crates/ordo-syntax/src/text.rs and crates/ordo-exec/src/nfc.rs, test crates/ordo-exec/tests/nfc.rs. Checklist 9u closed.

name: Text collation
explain: COLLATE "C" — codepoint order, so Z sorts before a. Not because every Postgres has it, but because codepoint order is the only order that is a function of the value alone; every alternative depends on a collation table on someone else's release cadence, and keyset paging turns that into skipped and repeated rows.
where: COLLATE "C" emitted in crates/ordo-plan/src/lib.rs and artifact.rs; covered by crates/ordo-exec/tests/nfc.rs and the corpus goldens.

name: `whole` object graphs
explain: Returns an entire object graph in one call. It inlined no read guard at all — a total authorization bypass on the one op that returns everything, and the members signpost handed out principal, role and status to anybody. Also aborted the process on a tree with owned, via a stack overflow on the self-edge.
where: crates/ordo-plan/src/whole.rs (one row_guard since a77cf1a); guard bypass fixed f6b0249. Checklist 9a closed.

name: Parameter bounds & `take $n`
explain: $n: int <= 5, enforced at the door. ParamSpec::bounds had no producer at all — the whole enforcement path existed with nothing to enforce, so every bound in the docs was a promise the compiler could not make. An unbounded take $n proves no row bound and is refused.
where: a6f5c93 parameter bounds and take $n (crates/ordo-sema, crates/ordo-plan/src/cost.rs); test crates/ordo-host/tests/take_param.rs. Checklist 9e closed.

name: Guards
explain: access read / access write, compiled to nested EXISTS semi-joins. Both verbs required or it will not compile — “read-guarded, write-open” reads as secure and is not, so if writes really are open you spell it.
where: Guards compiled in crates/ordo-sema and crates/ordo-plan; tests crates/ordo-conformance/tests/guards_corpus.rs, guards_multihop.rs, guards_compiler_joins.rs.

name: Parenthesised guard groups
explain: Distributed into DNF rather than kept as a nested node, because “a disjunct” is the unit three separate rules quantify over — a nested node would make all three read past the parens. Sound because the guard grammar has no not. Found on the way: the guard parser had a precedence table, so a and b or c parsed silently as (a and b) or c.
where: b77011e, crates/ordo-syntax/src/declparse.rs; test crates/ordo-conformance/tests/guard_groups.rs. Checklist 9e closed.

name: Guard literal typing
explain: guard_atom_cond was the one place the binder built a comparison without consulting what it compares against. qty == "seven" on an int field registered, planned and 500'd on every read — on the authorization path. Survived because the realistic shape is a well-formed guard with one ill-typed conjunct.
where: Test crates/ordo-conformance/tests/guard_literal_types.rs; checklist 9f closed.

name: Inherited guards
explain: A child owned by a guarded parent is guarded automatically, rebased through the ownership chain however deep. taskNotes declares no guard and gets a two-hop one. This is why you grant on the project and the tasks follow — and why revocation is instant and total.
where: Inherited guards in crates/ordo-sema/src/ir.rs and crates/ordo-plan/src/lib.rs; cases in crates/ordo-conformance/tests/guards_corpus.rs.

name: `acl` derivation
explain: One line — acl (read, write, admin) — derives the link entity, its guards, its unique key, the level enum, and the grant/revoke/setLevel ops. The container mechanism: if a human would say “add Sam to the project”, do not hand-roll it.
where: acl derivation in crates/ordo-schema/src/lib.rs and crates/ordo-plan/src/interface.rs; tests crates/ordo-conformance/tests/group_membership.rs and owner_admin.rs.

name: acl level ordering
explain: Thresholds are positional and compile to a closed disjunction of ==, because level >= "write" is unspellable in the closed grammar. The middle rung of every three-level acl was previously decoration — write was a level that could not write.
where: At-or-above rung tests in the derived guards (crates/ordo-schema/src/lib.rs); checklist 10a closed, docs/definition-language.md.

name: Derived admin ops
explain: grant / revoke / setLevel, named by rule, gated at the top level. Found while building: a raw unique violation would have leaked once the composite index existed; and revoke compiled to a ranged delete, which over an empty write view is a vacuous no-op — a non-admin's revoke would have reported success having deleted nothing.
where: ordo_schema::acl_admin_ops in crates/ordo-schema/src/lib.rs, registered with authored ops; test crates/ordo-conformance/tests/owner_admin.rs. Checklist 10h closed.

name: Space tenancy
explain: $space in every primary key, every composite foreign key, every unique constraint — and audited on every emitted statement. A cross-tenant reference is not refused at runtime; it is unrepresentable. Enforced by the schema, not by care.
where: The space column: 232410d (merged 5ad4f5e), predicate in crates/ordo-plan/src/lib.rs; tests crates/ordo-conformance/tests/spaces.rs and crates/ordo-plan/tests/scoping.rs. Checklist 9h closed.

name: Platform entities
explain: members and groupMembers are read-only to domain code. They were not: set members { role: "owner" } compiled and ran, and the door builds its access engine by reading that column — so an editor could promote themselves, and everyone else. Refused at registration and at the write path's one dispatch point.
where: platform_members in crates/ordo-schema/src/lib.rs makes members read-only to domain code; test crates/ordo-conformance/tests/platform_entity.rs. Checklist 8y closed.

name: Derived write modes
explain: create / addressed / bulk are derived from the statement's own shape, never a keyword. No condition is a create; id == is addressed; anything else ranges.
where: crates/ordo-plan/src/writes.rs derives the write modes; exercised by crates/ordo-conformance/src/write.rs and tests/corpus_stage5.rs.

name: Mode labels
explain: Per statement, unioned on the wire. Every conditioned set used to print converges, so a ranged write over a thousand rows and an addressed write over one were the same word. bulk is now sayable.
where: ordo_plan::writes::stmt_label in crates/ordo-plan/src/writes.rs; pinned in crates/ordo-cli/tests/golden/market.interface.json. Checklist 9s closed.

name: CAS and create-once
explain: rev mismatch answers cas_miss; a create-once whose key already matches answers expected_absent. Both have producers — a class with no producer is a recurring defect pattern here.
where: cas_miss and expected_absent produced in crates/ordo-conformance/src/write.rs and crates/ordo-plan/src/writes.rs, answered at the door in crates/ordo-api/src/error.rs; tests corpus_stage5.rs and std_ops_keyless_create.rs.

name: Trees & subtree delete
explain: Path and depth maintained by the platform. Cycles, depth overruns and ranged reparenting are each refused by their own class — a tree node moves one at a time.
where: tree and subtree parsed in crates/ordo-syntax/src/declparse.rs, planned in crates/ordo-plan/src/whole.rs and artifact.rs; cases in crates/ordo-conformance/tests/corpus_p0.rs and platform_entity.rs.

name: Write-valued `let`
explain: let p = set projects {…} — naming a freshly created row in the same op. Gives unbindable_write a producer for the first time. Ruled where the spec is silent: a rev: null create-once is bindable.
where: crates/ordo-syntax/src/declparse.rs; test crates/ordo-conformance/tests/write_let.rs. Checklist 9e closed.

name: `unique (a,b)` and `index (…)`
explain: Composite keys and declared indexes. Carries NULLS NOT DISTINCT — which was missing from every generated unique index, so a nullable unique field was not a unique claim at all for rows that left it out.
where: unique (a,b) and index emitted in crates/ordo-schema/src/ddl.rs; test crates/ordo-conformance/tests/entity_clauses.rs. Checklist 9e closed.

group: Done — custody and the audit spine

name: Key custody
explain: Per-space master keys wrapping per-epoch data keys. The provider exposes operations, never keys. DEKs are random and wrapped rather than derived, which is what makes destroying a retired epoch expressible — crypto-erasure.
where: crates/ordo-crypto/src/custody.rs and master.rs, crates/ordo-exec/src/keystore.rs; tests crates/ordo-crypto/tests/master.rs and crates/ordo-exec/tests/keystore.rs.

name: Sealed fields
explain: XChaCha20-Poly1305, AAD bound to entity:field, a fresh nonce per seal, never deduplicated — two equal plaintexts must not produce equal ciphertext, or the store becomes an equality oracle.
where: crates/ordo-crypto/src/sealed.rs and crates/ordo-exec/src/sealed.rs; test crates/ordo-exec/tests/sealed.rs.

name: Blind index
explain: A keyed digest lets a sealed field be found by exact match at index speed. Ranges and sorting stay impossible, which is the honest half of the trade. Found: the parameter path compared raw plaintext to a digest column — silent zero rows, because only the literal path was tested.
where: crates/ordo-plan/src/blind.rs and the blind index in crates/ordo-crypto; crates/ordo-conformance/examples/blind_report.rs; door cases in crates/ordo-api/tests/api.rs.

name: Sealed payload store
explain: Command-log images hold opaque handles rather than values. The handle is keyed-random, not content-derived — and the cheaper [epoch][random] spelling was rejected because rotation is mandatory on revocation, so an epoch byte in every image hands anyone holding the log a revocation timeline.
where: The $sealedpayload store, 1877ce9, in crates/ordo-exec/src/sealed.rs; test crates/ordo-exec/tests/sealed.rs. Checklist 8j closed.

name: Command log
explain: Every write appends an attributed, hash-chained group with before and after images, under a per-space advisory lock. Survives restart. This is what makes undo, audit and attestation possible at all.
where: crates/ordo-commandlog (chain.rs, store.rs, sign.rs) and crates/ordo-exec/src/commandlog.rs; test crates/ordo-exec/tests/commandlog.rs.

name: Undo / revert
explain: A revert is new history, not an erasure — the audit list gets longer. It re-seals under the current epoch rather than replaying the stored envelope, which would resurrect a retired epoch and partly undo a rotation a revocation forced.
where: crates/ordo-exec/src/undo.rs (revert); tests crates/ordo-exec/tests/undo_space.rs and crates/ordo-cli/tests/operator.rs.

name: Checkpoints & signing
explain: Ed25519 over the chain head at a position, verifiable from a public key alone.
where: undo::sign_checkpoint in crates/ordo-exec/src/undo.rs, signing in crates/ordo-commandlog/src/sign.rs; tests crates/ordo-exec/tests/commandlog.rs and cadence_prune.rs.

name: Layer-1 attestation pinning
explain: Every answered response carries a position and the signed head at it, so a client holds evidence the server cannot retract. Detects, does not prevent. Not read-your-writes — a position looks like a consistency token and is not. An empty chain pins genesis, because “always on” that switches on after the first write is not always on.
where: crates/ordo-host/src/replay.rs (PgReplayCache) and test crates/ordo-host/tests/pinning.rs; commit dae80d2.

name: Prune & archive
explain: History can be trimmed, and x-ordo-verifiable-from tells a client where recomputation still starts — disclose, don't prevent, since a pin is structurally unprotectable. Found: a prune could empty the chain entirely, and an empty chain reads two different wrong ways.
where: crates/ordo-exec/src/prune.rs and cadence.rs; test crates/ordo-exec/tests/cadence_prune.rs. Checklist 5f closed.

name: Access checker
explain: Status first, then role plus groups plus overrides, or a capability allowlist — the two paths are exclusive by token shape. Suspension takes effect on the next request, not at token expiry.
where: crates/ordo-identity/src/access.rs (AccessEngine::check) wired at the door in crates/ordo-host/src/lib.rs; tests crates/ordo-identity/src/tests.rs and crates/ordo-host/tests/auth_door.rs.

name: Roles & profiles
explain: Four fixed roles; the org chart lives in data as groups. Profiles map role to ops, with per-member overrides for the long tail of “this person specifically”. This is the layer your Jira example lives in — who may create tickets, manage automations, manage dashboards.
where: Roles and profiles in crates/ordo-identity/src/access.rs and principal.rs; unit tests crates/ordo-identity/src/tests.rs.

name: Grant registry & revocation
explain: Grants were minted into tokens and never recorded, so none could be revoked and callersOf could not be exhaustive. Deliberately not consulted to admit a request — the door decides from the token alone, so a registry outage cannot become an authorization outage.
where: crates/ordo-identity/src/grants.rs and crates/ordo-host/src/grants.rs; tests crates/ordo-host/tests/grants.rs and callers_of.rs (std.space.callersOf). Checklist 8r closed.

name: Page tokens
explain: Authenticated, op- and principal-bound. Version skew is a hard rejection here and a soft signal everywhere else, because a stale page token is the one place a version assumption silently corrupts meaning.
where: crates/ordo-api/src/page.rs: an HMAC'd, principal-bound token (SH-6); door tests crates/ordo-api/tests/api.rs.

name: Live subscriptions
explain: Cross-node invalidation over pg_notify, riding the write's own transaction so a rollback takes the signal with it.
where: live_capable in crates/ordo-api/src/spec.rs and router.rs, 2840a31; tests crates/ordo-api/tests/api.rs and crates/ordo-host/tests/invalidation_routing.rs. Checklist 9j closed.

name: Shape verification gate
explain: Poses every registered op to the database at boot and refuses to serve if the compiler and the database disagree. Enforced by type: serving takes a report obtainable only from a passing verification. It was correct and gated nothing — its only callers were its own tests.
where: crates/ordo-exec/src/shape.rs and crates/ordo-host/src/shape.rs, 2840a31; test crates/ordo-exec/tests/shape.rs. Checklist 8n closed.

name: Hot swap
explain: Swapping a registry without a restart, taking a Verified so a swap cannot walk around the shape gate. The deeper defect it fixed: the program lived in three places nobody moved together, so a registry-only swap left the door dispatching new specs into an executor planning the old program.
where: crates/ordo-host/src/deploy.rs swaps the served artifact (f294459, 540c29a); tests crates/ordo-host/tests/deploy.rs and lock_wait.rs. Checklist 5f closed.

name: Health endpoints
explain: live, ready and deep — each proving something different, with the shape report published so an operator can read the coverage rather than trust it.
where: Health routes in crates/ordo-host/src/serve.rs, 2840a31 and 3284328 (17t readiness); test crates/ordo-host/tests/health.rs. Checklist 8o closed.

name: Error inventories
explain: Wire and compile class sets, both checked two-directionally against the documents at build time. The wire check found two defects the day it was written. The compile census found 24 of 61 classes in no document at all — the set had stopped being closed. Now: 20 documented, one collapsed, two named as internal vocabulary.
where: crates/ordo-api/tests/inventory_is_closed.rs and crates/ordo-conformance/tests/class_inventory.rs; c2be766. Checklist 9x closed.

name: `ordo check` / `plan`
explain: Compiles a program and prints its shape, or emits the artifact JSON. The manifest is a projection of the artifact, so two derivations cannot print two numbers for one op.
where: ordo check and ordo plan in crates/ordo-cli/src/main.rs and lib.rs, c305074; tests crates/ordo-cli/tests/cli.rs and plan_against.rs. Checklist 9m closed.

name: `apply` / `rollback` / `deploys`
explain: The Postgres artifact registry with drift detection at the deploy path. Rollback is a re-point, not a special path.
where: apply, rollback, deploys in crates/ordo-cli/src/operator.rs and wire.rs; tests crates/ordo-cli/tests/operator.rs and wire_apply.rs. Checklist 5f closed.

name: `verify` / `revert` / `prune`
explain: Exit codes an operator's cron actually reads: 0 clean, 3 a broken chain, 2 usage, 1 everything else. 3 is separate from 1 on purpose — “the chain does not recompute” and “I could not reach the database” must page different people.
where: verify, revert, prune in crates/ordo-cli/src/operator.rs; test crates/ordo-cli/tests/operator.rs.

name: Golden files
explain: DDL, artifact and per-case SQL, updated only via ORDO_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1. A golden that moves is a question, not a chore — several real defects were caught by reading a diff line by line rather than regenerating it.

name: No-guards canary
explain: Strips every guard from the schema, then asserts the DDL is byte-identical and that guarded assertions now fail. Proves the guards are doing the work rather than the data happening to line up. No production code touched, no runtime flag added.
where: crates/ordo-conformance/tests/guards_canary.rs runs the corpus with guards stripped.

name: Doc-block parse harness
explain: Extracts Ordo blocks from the documentation and parses them — 61 of 81, ratcheted so the number can only rise. Three-category allow-list: settled-and-unbuilt, [lean]-and-not-owed, not-Ordo. Filing the second as the first is how a sketch becomes a work item nobody owed.
where: crates/ordo-syntax/tests/docs_parse.rs parses the tagged blocks in the docs.

name: How-to guides
explain: Four guides — custody, operating, the audit spine, and the six places Ordo differs from SQL. Written by cheap models against tight briefs, then verified: headers, exit codes and the null truth table all checked against source. Their Ordo examples are now read by the parse harness, so “copied from a real file” is checked rather than promised.
where: Documentation only: docs/howto-audit.md, howto-custody.md, howto-operating.md, howto-values.md.

name: Sign-ups are provisioned one at a time
explain:
Measured 2026-10-25: 150 to 300 ms each, so the 60th sign-up waited 14.1 s; 200 would wait about 50 s.
- Cause: one gate per process (`tenant_ops.rs:101` `own_gate`).
Fix: run preflight and database creation several at a time; serialise only the registry index.
where: Not started; audit item 5

name: Each read makes 5 database round trips
explain:
Found 2026-10-25: BEGIN, rows, `max(idx)` position, COMMIT (`ordo-exec/src/lib.rs:2589-2611`), then the attest tip query (`host/src/attest.rs:114-131`).
- About 5 ms floor on a cloud database with 1 ms round trips.
Fix: fold the position into the read; cache the tip per space, cleared on write.
where: Not started; audit item 6

name: Connections grow with tenants, with no total limit
explain:
Measured 2026-10-25: one pool per tenant database (`exec/src/route.rs:295`); 77 tenants held 54 of Postgres's 100 connections.
Fix: a deployment-wide connection budget setting, and sizing guidance per tenant count.
where: Not started; audit item 7

name: `ordo check --help` and friends fail
explain:
Found 2026-10-25: `ordo check --help` answers '--help: No such file or directory'; `dev` and `apply` the same. Bare `--help` is 300 lines.
Fix: per-command help, and a short top-level help pointing to it.
where: Not started; audit item 8

name: Boot refusals name the setting but not a value to set
explain:
Found 2026-10-25: `ORDO_KEY_PROVIDER`, `ORDO_SPACE` and `ORDO_PG_HOST` refusals give no example value; the passphrase file refusal names no setting; `bucket_ops.rs:297` names no setting.
Fix: every boot refusal names the setting and a valid value.

- A refused database at boot says only `Connection refused`.

name: Door operations that could break a hosted instance
explain:
For Ordo Cloud v1 (2026-10-27): settings tied to the hosting must not be changeable through the door, or a customer can lock themselves out.
- Find every door operation that changes such a setting: allowed origins, sign-in methods, the public address, the database, ports.
- Each one either moves to the environment or stays with a reason.
where: Not started; a quick audit before Ordo Cloud v1

name: Horizontal scaling and high availability: v2
decided: for more than one copy lets move that for v2. (I assume this is for HA)
explain:
Owner, 2026-10-27: before releasing v1. Multi-replica pieces exist, but no one page says how to scale, and nothing tests 2 replicas on one database.
- Built: leader lock, `$nodes` heartbeats, LISTEN/NOTIFY, serialized applies, per-replica usage rows.
- Gaps: per-replica limits, connections multiply per replica, revocation lag, in-memory metrics.
